sections.section: Dartvel — The Complete Vision, to be implemented

sections.absent: Absent: the glob patterns. The section offers glob patterns for file groups, directories and subdirectories under the dartvel: key, and nothing in dartvel_config.dart reads one -- the path options are plain strings with defaults, so a project whose pages live in two directories cannot say so. The rest is built: the default paths, the per-key overrides, and the Dart config file, whose public class extending DartvelConfig is found by the regex at dartvel_config.dart:189 and must start with an uppercase letter so the CLI can import it.

A box can be turned now, and could not: the chain faded, rounded, bordered and painted a gradient through a box and had no way to rotate one, so a design tilted badge and its angled price flash came through square -- rendered, plausible, and not the design, which is the kind of loss nothing reports. rotate takes degrees rather than radians, deliberately differing from Transform.rotate, because the number in a page document, the number a designer reads in an inspector, the number Figma reports for a layer and the number in exported source are then the same one, converted once where the widget is built; the parameter is named for its unit so somebody reaching for radians sees it before running it, pi over four in degrees being very nearly no rotation. Zero is not a rotation, since a Transform that turns nothing would be a layer in the tree of every page for the one design in ten that tilts something. Text can be underlined and struck through now, and could not: the chain carried every other text style a design uses -- size, weight, family, colour, letter spacing, line height, line limit, overflow -- and had no way to mark a link or a superseded price, so both arrived as ordinary text, which is the same silent loss the missing rotation was. One method taking Flutter's own TextDecoration rather than an underline flag and a strikethrough flag beside each other, matching overflow(TextOverflow) already on the chain: a design that underlines and strikes the same run is a real design, and two flags cannot say it. Text nobody decorated carries no decoration at all rather than TextDecoration.none, because naming none would override an underline an enclosing theme asked for, which is a decision the chain was never given. A box can be blurred now, and could not, which cost two different designs: a soft-focus decorative shape rendered sharp, and -- far more commonly -- a frosted card over a photograph rendered as a flat translucent panel. Two methods rather than one, because they are not the same picture: blur softens the box and what is in it, backdropBlur leaves it sharp and softens whatever shows through, which is the whole of the frosted effect, and a single blur() would have to guess which was meant. The unit is a standard deviation, which is what ImageFilter.blur takes and what CSS's blur() takes, and Figma's own CSS export writes the number from its Layer blur straight into blur(Npx) -- so the value a designer typed is the value in the document, in the chain and in the exported source. A background blur is bounded by the box's own corners, since an unclipped backdrop filter blurs the whole screen behind it: the page goes soft and nothing points at the card that asked for it. Nought is not a blur, for the reason nought is not a rotation -- a filter layer that changes no pixel costs what a real one costs -- and a negative one is refused before ImageFilter.blur asserts on it and takes the page down over a number a document can carry. The chain also reaches text now, and did not. DVText drew text and only text: a modifier carrying padding, a background, a corner radius, a border, a width or a fade reached it and did nothing, on a build that succeeded. This repository did it to itself four times -- the studio's Close button and a tab label, both asking for padding round a tap target and getting the glyphs; the site's own paragraph helper, whose maxWidth was the readable measure every paragraph on dartvel.dev was supposed to be held to and was not; and the framework's own prebuilt sign-in page, whose Sign in button asks for padding, a corner radius and a dark fill and rendered as the two words on their own. The test over that page expected exactly one DVBox and passed because of it, which is a count measuring the bug rather than the page; it now asserts the fill and the radius reach a decoration. There is a fifth, and it is the one with a claim attached: a page document says a text node is centred with align, that becomes DVModifier.align, and DVText looked straight past it -- so every centred heading in every imported design came through left-aligned while the feature list said centred text survives the import. That is the same shape as the bug the semantic fields had on this widget before they were read: the call goes where it naturally goes and the widget it goes to never looks at it. The box half is drawn by the thing that draws boxes rather than by a second copy of the code here, only when one was asked for -- a container round every DVText in every application, for the styling most of them do not use, is a cost nobody chose -- and the tap and the semantics are cleared on the way, because text already applies them and its handling of a role that owns its own label is the careful one. Left in, the box would carry them too: a callback that runs twice and a screen reader saying heading, then heading. A rounded box also rounds what is in it now, and did not: the radius reached the decoration and nothing else, so a box drew rounded corners and its child squared them off again. With a flat colour nobody notices, because the decoration is the only thing painted there. With a photograph everybody does, and it is the commonest rounded thing in any design -- every circular avatar came through as a square photograph inside a rounded outline. Clipped only where a radius was asked for, and in both the animated and the plain branch, because a rule applied to one of two is a box that clips until somebody asks it to animate. A box can also be told to crop what is in it without being rounded, which is its own decision in a design and the commonest version of it is a photograph cropped by a square frame. Without that the child paints outside the box and the page carries an overflow stripe, so an imported design arrives visibly broken rather than quietly wrong. Hard edges on a straight edge and antialiased on a curve: a rectangle needs no smoothing, and paying for it on every cropping frame is a cost with nothing to show for it. A border can be on one side now. The document could say a colour and a width and the width went to Border.all, so a box with a rule under it was a box with a line on all four sides -- not a missing style but a wrong one, and the commonest border in any design is a single hairline under a header or between two rows. Four widths beside the colour, in the shape the corners and the shadow already use: the colour owns the decision and the sides are its companions, because a side applied on its own is a line nobody chose a colour for. A document that names no side still draws all four, since one width has always meant a box and every page written that way has to keep meaning it; a side named as nought is not a side, because a BorderSide of no width renders as nothing and reads in the exported source as a decision. A page document can also name a wrapping row now. Three separate switches read a layout name -- the renderer, the Dart exporter and the editor's own canvas -- and a fourth list, the palette, decided what anybody could drag in. The wrapping row was missing from all four while DVBox.wrapLine had existed the whole time, so a chip row or a tag list, which is the commonest wrapping thing in any design, came through as a single row that runs off the side of a phone. The drift was silent because an unknown name falls through to a column in every one of them. There is one catalogue now and the palette is built from it, the way the palette was already built from the leaf types; the column keeps the label people call it, because its name in a document is list -- it is the default, and a page written before there were others has no layout at all. A wrapping row is aligned like any other row, which took a second change and would have been the same bug one level down: the alignment properties are written for every auto-layout frame, so a wrap that ignored them would be a property the inspector offers, the document carries and nothing applies. DVBox.wrapLine hard-coded start and gave a Wrap no alignment at all. A Wrap offers every alignment a row does, so the mapping is one for one and a wrapping row aligns exactly like the row it becomes when the line has space; stretch is the exception and becomes start, because a Wrap has no equivalent -- its children are as wide as they are, and there is no width to stretch them to. The surface a page is edited on draws it the way the page does now, and did not. "What is edited is what ships" is what the renderer's own documentation promises, and the canvas built its containers itself -- a switch over the layout name and nothing else. No padding, no background, no radius, no border, no shadow, no spacing, no alignment, and a stack piled its hand-placed children into the corner. So a card was a bare column while somebody was styling it and a card once the page ran, and the person doing the styling could not see what they were doing. Both surfaces call one layout function and one styling function now, which is also what removed the third reader of a layout name. The styling travels to the canvas and the behaviour does not: a canvas that navigates away when somebody taps the card they are editing is worse than one that shows the card unstyled. A grid can also be told how many columns it has. The renderer read that, the exporter wrote it, and a document could override it per breakpoint, while the inspector offered no control for it at all -- so a grid built in the builder was permanently two columns wide. It is the drift the layout-property list exists to prevent, in the layout-property list, and the guard over that list could not catch it because it asserted a set of names it already knew about. A layout property now says which layouts it means anything to, and the inspector offers it only there: a row has no columns, and a control that does nothing is worse than one that is absent, because the person who set it has decided something. The export guard holds each one to a layout it belongs to for the same reason. Absent: nothing named here.

Built: pages by file and config routes declared in lib/routes.dart (or dartvel.routes) mix in one generated router and one DVRoutes. The CLI reads the routes file lexically for paths and names, generates a typed target per route (derived from the path, or name:), lists config routes in dartvelRouteManifest so the web build writes their pages, and puts a route behind a redirect or the root guard in dartvelGuardedRoutes. DVRoute, DVShellRoute, DVStatefulShellRoute with DVShellBranch, and DVGoRoutes for an existing go_router list are mounted by dvConfigRoutes with route state, page lifecycle, SEO title and transition; redirects return a DVRouteTarget. Every route list passes through dvOrderGoRoutes, which matches a static segment before a parameter and a parameter before a catch-all whatever the source or declaration order; that also fixed file routes, where [id].dart sorted before new.dart and hid it. Build errors: DV-ROUTE-001 the same path twice, 002 one typed target for two routes, 003 an unreadable route, 004 no order keeps every route reachable, 005 a tabs layout whose tabs and pages disagree. Tabs from files: a _layout.dart extending DartvelTabsLayout makes its folder a StatefulShellRoute with pages nested by path, so a detail page is pushed inside its tab, and a detail page beside its list is named with its parameters (libraryBook) instead of stopping the build. A pushed route takes the platform page so the iOS edge swipe works, a selectable DVPageShell no longer swallows that swipe, and a deep link to a page over another no longer throws in its selection area. The generated router is a DVRouter, which paints DVRoutePending while the first location's async guards decide. dartvelRoutes(at:) mounts the whole route set into a host GoRouter at its root or a prefix, and DV.Navigation, navigateToPage and DVNavLink place Dartvel targets under the prefix and leave host paths alone. Not built: a prefix-mounted nested navigator for Navigator 1.0 and non-go_router hosts; typed targets for routes inside DVGoRoutes. Config routes get no DVPageShell, folder layouts, loading and error siblings or deferred library, by design.

A model is discovered by a pattern over its source, and that pattern could not read its own annotation twice over. It stopped at the first close parenthesis, so a string argument containing one -- schemaType: 'Product (beta)' -- ended the annotation early and the model was not found at all: no generated class, no table, no admin row, no graph node, no static paths, on a build that succeeded. Six parsers carried that pattern -- the model generator, the project graph, the admin scaffold, the schema snapshot, the static-paths generator and the kiosk check -- and a model one of them missed while another found it is a table in the database with no row anywhere else. Each is now matched against a copy whose annotation arguments are blanked to spaces, which keeps every offset so the arguments themselves are still read from the original. The same scan skips string literals and comments, because an annotation described in prose is not an annotation: the marketing site describes one in a paragraph above the annotation its page carries, and a parser that searched the file for the first occurrence read the paragraph. Absent: nothing named here yet beyond what the sections for forms, model pages and multi-tenancy record.

The runtime is built (DVRecordTable: versioned conditional writes refused with DVConflictError and every DVConflict strategy, opt-in history with sensitive fields recorded as changed and never as values, revert that adds a change and keeps every entry between, soft delete with restore refused on a held unique field, compensation inside DV.transaction, and DVContext.transactionId). Generated models use it: find, all, save and destroy go through DVRecordTable. A loaded or copied model is saved and destroyed at the version it read and refused with DVConflictError when the row moved. A model built by hand is refused with DV-HISTORY-001 over a row that exists, which is left unchanged, unless the call says save(onConflict: DVConflict.lastWriteWins). A model that created its row saves again at the version it wrote. DVForm's edited model keeps the read of the model it edits through registerDVModelReadCarrier, so the generated admin saves at that version. GraphQL types carry dvVersion, and saveX refuses an update of a stored record that does not send it back. @DVModel(history: DVHistory(keep:)) writes the log with model.history() and model.revert(to:), which is refused for a model that read nothing. @DVModel(version: false) writes without a version check. @DVModel(softDelete: true) makes destroy mark the row, which find and all skip; Model.withDeleted.find and all read it, and Model.restore(id) brings it back and publishes DVModelChangeKind.restored. DVRecordTable.prune logs DV-HISTORY-004 when it removes entries. An erasure on a tenant-scoped table deletes, anonymizes and purges history only on the erased row's tenant. Absent: the build-time DV-HISTORY-002 check; generated form reload-and-merge; the Studio history view; pointing history at a separate adapter; scheduled retention jobs, so nothing in a generated application calls prune; a unique-field declaration on generated models, so a generated restore never meets DV-HISTORY-006; soft-deleted rows left out of search indexes and sync beyond find and all; a generated revert run inside its own DV.transaction; field encryption inside DVRecordTable, which generated models apply before the write, so an encrypted field changes version on every save; and database-level atomic transactions. Where the section and the code disagree: the section writes invoice.delete(), and the generated method is destroy(); the section names no override for a write with no read version, so DVConflict.lastWriteWins, from its own vocabulary, is it; GraphQL's dvVersion checks the version only, and the conflict's base is the stored row rather than what the client read; a subject is named by id alone, so on a tenant-scoped model an erasure reaches the subject's rows on every tenant, which is right when one id names one person across tenants and wrong when ids are issued per tenant.

The client is built (DV.Http and DVHttp over the WinterCG wire types: declared hosts with timeouts, idempotency-aware retries with backoff, per-host circuit breaker, a concurrency pool, bearer credentials resolved through DVSecrets at send time, trace-context propagation, and DV.Test.fakeHttp with stubs, recorded calls and fixtures). The dartvel.http block is read strictly by DVHttp.readConfig, which refuses any key or value it does not understand and names it. dartvel routes reads the block through that reader before it writes anything and emits http.g.dart, whose configureDartvelHttp() the client runtime and the generated web, worker and cron server roles call before application code runs, so backend code reaching const DVHttp() has the same declared hosts as DV.Http on the client. At runtime an absolute URL is sent as the declared host whose base URL covers it (same scheme, host and port, a path at or below the base path, the longest base URL winning) and is refused with DV-HTTP-001 before it is sent otherwise, faked or not. send(allowUndeclaredHost: true) sends on the default policy and never as a declared host, so a URL somebody else supplied cannot borrow a declared credential; webhook deliveries use it and stay pinned to the address their own check approved. dartvel routes raises DV-HTTP-001 for a DV.Http.host literal nobody declared or an absolute URL literal no declared base URL covers, and DV-HTTP-005 for a declared host whose auth.bearer secret is backend-scoped, or undeclared, used outside the backend directory, each naming file and line. Absent: the build reads only literal names and URLs (written directly, through Uri.parse, or as send's second argument), so a URL assembled at runtime is caught only by the runtime refusal; DV-HTTP-005 separates client from backend code by directory (lib/ minus backendDir), not by the import graph; no provider adapter (mail, search, billing, storage, AI, tax) is built on DV.Http yet, and webhooks send through it only as undeclared destinations; fixtures are recorded in memory with no file format or capture command; bearer is the only auth scheme; there is no backend DV facade, so backend code writes const DVHttp() rather than DV.Http. Where the section and the code disagree: the prose calls a client-side use of a backend credential the existing DV-SECRETS-001 violation while the diagnostic table gives it DV-HTTP-005, and the table is followed.

Both @DVBackendCron and @DVClientCron are collected into generated entries, and nothing ran either until this was written. The note here used to say DVScheduler ran them; it did not. DVScheduler was instantiated in exactly one place in the repository and that place was its own unit test, so a schedule travelled from an annotation into a generated list and stopped. The generated schedules file now emits the handler behind each backend entry and a starter that registers them and ticks, and the generated startBackend calls it before it serves. The client half is a second file for a reason -- the generated backend imports the backend one, and a client schedule declared on a page would pull Flutter into a server with no dart:ui, which a show clause does not prevent because the whole library is still compiled -- and the generated client runtime starts it. An application with no schedule starts no timer on either side. A schedule now says for itself whether the occurrences missed while the process was down are run when it comes back, and the annotation could not say it before -- the scheduler took catchUp per task from the day it was written, and the only way to reach it was the hand-written register call that generated schedules exist so nobody writes. Nullable rather than defaulted, because a schedule that wrote false has decided about itself and must outrank the blanket setting a starter is called with, while one that said nothing is leaving that decision to the application: a nightly digest sent four times the morning a server comes back is worse than one digest missed, and a rollup that writes a row per period wants the opposite. The expression is also no longer the whole of the annotation, which is the part that could have failed quietly: the collector's pattern required it to be, so an argument after it did not make the schedule wrong, it made the function stop being a schedule at all. A catchUp the generator cannot read as a literal stops the build rather than being treated as unstated, since the generated entry carries the value rather than evaluating it. A client tick is a wakeup as well as a tick, and that is taken into account now. A timer firing every twenty seconds from somebody's pocket wakes the device for a schedule that could have waited, and the system suspends the timer anyway -- so the periods that passed while the application was away arrived whenever it happened to fire next rather than when it came back. The client ticks only while the application is in front of somebody, stops when it goes away, and ticks once on the way back, because whatever came due while it was away is due now rather than up to the interval from now, and that wait is the whole of what somebody who just opened the application is waiting on. An application that declares no client schedule gets a starter that starts nothing and listens to nothing, since a lifecycle subscription in every application is the same cost as the timer this file already refused to start. Reaching the application lifecycle is also why the client schedules are a file of their own: DV lives in dartvel_flutter, and the generated server reads the other one. Absent: the per-target capability report. DV.Schedules.capability, its granularity/whenBackgrounded/whenTerminated record, the doctor finding for an interval finer than a target honours, and DV-CRON-001 to 004 are designed and unbuilt. What ships is the generated registration and ticking described above, whose platform behaviour is now stated per target rather than implied by the annotation. Backend schedules tick only in a process given no role or DARTVEL_ROLE=cron, and the generated entry point claims each occurrence in the database DATABASE_URL names through DVDatabaseScheduleLease, keyed to the scheduled instant in UTC (DVCacheScheduleLease exists for an atomic cache store, but nothing configures one); a declared cron process with no DATABASE_URL exits 78 rather than start unless DARTVEL_SCHEDULE_LEASE=none says it is the only one, nothing runs when the database cannot be reached, and a SQLite file shares the claim only among the processes of one host.

nothing now, and something was. Seven adapters -- in-memory, database, Redis, SQS, RabbitMQ, Pub/Sub and Kafka -- and the four network ones are verified against a real broker in CI rather than against a fake. Six of the seven were also unimportable until recently: of eight files under src/queues, exactly one was exported from the public entrypoint, so DVSqsQueueAdapter, DVPubSubQueueAdapter, DVKafkaQueueAdapter, DVAmqpQueueAdapter and the transports behind them were public classes no application could reach without writing a package:dartvel_core/src/ path. The tests reached them that way, which is why nothing noticed. They are exported now, and a reachability check in CI fails a section citing a file nothing can call. Absent: DVJobState.completed, which nothing produces. A job that finishes is removed from the queue rather than marked, and the admin counts pending and failed and never asks for completed -- so an application switching on the state will never see that branch taken. Retaining finished jobs to make it reachable would grow without bound, and no retention policy is specified, so the value is named as unreachable rather than given behaviour nobody chose. DVQueueWorker is the loop a DARTVEL_ROLE=worker process runs over DARTVEL_QUEUE: the generated backend registers every handler a server can run from jobs.g.dart, which imports only dartvel_core, and puts every role's queue on the database DATABASE_URL names, where two workers claim a job once; the worker refuses to start with no DATABASE_URL or no handler it can run. Each job carries the tenant it was dispatched under on every adapter, and the worker runs its handler as that tenant or, with none, as the default tenant. In a process whose environment says preview, DVQueues dispatches, works, lists and flushes under DARTVEL_QUEUE_NAMESPACE as <namespace>.<queue> and uses no queue when it is unset; the variable is ignored in every other environment, and a process with no namespace cannot name a queue under a preview- namespace. Still absent: a handler whose code names DV or whose file reaches Flutter is generated into client_jobs.g.dart and runs only in the client; no queue adapter but the database is selected from configuration; dartvel queue work runs the project's worker, but queue failed, retry and flush still act on the CLI process's own queue; retry and discard take a job id without checking its namespace.

Policies are typed, registered and default-deny: DV.Auth.authorization.can returns false for a policy nobody registered, which is the right answer to a question the application never taught it to answer. What this section claimed and did not do until 2026-09-06 is the page half of it. @DVPage has taken a policy since the annotation was written and the specification gives it as one of the two usage examples, and the generator never read it -- the string was parsed in exactly one place in the repository and that place was the backend function generator, while route guards came from a directory convention. So a page carrying the annotation for guarding it was open to everybody and nothing anywhere said so, which is the worst shape an authorization bug takes: an unguarded page that looks unguarded is a decision somebody made, and one carrying the annotation is a developer who has already ticked it off. It is enforced now. The generated router calls one runtime checker rather than an inlined auth call, because a router emitting the exact shape of that surface would pin it into every generated application; a page whose application has configured nothing to answer the policy is refused rather than opened, since treating no answer as yes would reintroduce the same bug as a default instead of an omission; and a directory guard still runs first with the policy after it, because a page can be under a guarded folder and carry a policy of its own and replacing the chain would quietly drop the folder's guard. A policy that is not a Dart reference is refused at build time, since the value is emitted into generated source where anything else either fails to compile or compiles into something nobody wrote. A first attempt at fixing that did not fix it, and this record said it had. The guard builder, the runtime checker and a unit test for each were written and committed, the index was updated to say the router called them, and nothing did: the live generator's own page-argument parser still never read policy, the runtime checker was not exported from dartvel_flutter, and no code outside those two files referenced either symbol. Asserting on the shape of a string returned by an uncalled function is what let it pass. It is wired now -- the generator parses the argument with the same function the test holds to account, the route carries it, the redirect the router emits calls the checker, and the checker is exported. The backend half is built too, and this entry went on saying it was not: a policy on a backend function is parsed, emitted as a gate on the generated route, and answered by the same default-deny surface -- the gate runs after the body is read so CSRF still runs first, and inside the route rather than around the router, because a policy belongs to one function. The last thing this section wrote down and did not do was @DVPolicy(ModelType) itself. It is the specification's headline example of authorization and it appeared in exactly one file in the repository: the one declaring it. So a developer could write a PostPolicy, watch it compile, and have every question about a post answered by default-deny -- the right direction to fail, and still an authorization model that is written down and not the one running. A policy class's conventional methods are registered now, by the client runtime before a page can ask whether to draw an action: a generated table hides an action the policy denies, and a client that registered nothing would hide every one of them. The generated server registers them too, from backend_policies.g.dart before its first route exists, for every policy class in the application and its merged modules whose file does not reach Flutter; the first attempt had it registering all of them until the integration job refused to compile the result. A policy written against the generated models reaches them through the generated barrel, which exports the router and the generated widgets, so such a class is registered in the client only and reported on every build, and a route whose Resource.action only such a class defines stops dartvel routes. A route's quoted Resource.action is refused when the caller's scopes do not cover it or nothing registered it, then answered by DVBackendPolicy.decide when the application set one and otherwise by the registered policy with the caller and no resource; a reference such as DVPolicies.refund is still answered by decide alone, and registrations from policy classes are a layer the application's own register for the same action and resource wins over, on the client and the server alike. The registration tears the method off rather than wrapping it, so Dart infers the user and resource types from the policy's own signature and the registry key is the type the policy actually takes rather than a string this generator assembled. What the annotation's own argument is for is the disagreement: a method on @DVPolicy(Post) that takes a Comment stops the build, because it would register the check under Comment -- Post keeps failing closed while Comment is opened by a policy nobody wrote for it, and neither half of that says anything out loud. A method that takes no resource is refused for the reason the API has one: can(user, action, resource) always carries a resource and the registry is keyed by its type, so a check without one could never be reached by the question it answers. A method that is not a conventional action is left alone rather than registered under its own name, which would put a key in the registry nothing asks for and turn a typo into a policy. The generated admin asks a policy before it draws an action and again when the action is pressed. DVModelAdmin draws New only when T.create allows it, Delete only when T.delete allows it on the open record, and Save only when T.update allows it (T.create for a record not yet stored). A record that may not be saved is a read-only form saying so. Each action is asked again when pressed, so a role removed while the screen was open saves or deletes nothing. An update is asked about the stored record rather than the edit, because ownership is judged on what exists. A model no policy answers offers no action, which is the registry's default-deny. Who is asked about is Model.Admin(as:), the application's own user, and DV.Auth.currentUser without it. The check goes through canAction, which compares the caller with the types the policy was torn off with, so a policy written against the application's User asked with the session's DVAuthUser refuses and logs why once rather than throwing. A caller given with as: is never exchanged for the session user. There is no server write to guard beside it: generated models reach Flutter and cannot load in the server, and no generated route saves or deletes one, so the admin's own save and destroy are its write path. The GraphQL fields generated for a model ask its policy before they read or write: the list query asks Model.viewAny, the find query asks Model.view on the record it found, save asks Model.update on the stored record or Model.create when none is stored, and delete asks Model.delete on the stored record, each through DVGraphQL.authorizeModel, which asks canAction about the request's API key, OAuth token or session user when a server authenticated one and DV.Auth.currentUser otherwise; an action nothing registered, a caller or resource the policy cannot take, and a policy that throws all refuse, nulling the field with a FORBIDDEN error. Absent: the standalone Model.Form asks no policy, because its Save runs the application's callback rather than a model write; the generated GraphQL fields are registered only in the client, so no server route reads or writes a model through them; the client has no application-user resolver, so a policy written against the generated User needs as: passed explicitly to the admin, and the GraphQL fields, which take no as:, can only ask about DV.Auth.currentUser; the admin does not ask view or viewAny before listing or opening a record; a find for a missing key answers null and a delete false without asking a policy, so a refused caller can still tell whether a key exists.

The nineteen DVMiddlewares keys ran nothing until this was written. @DVUseMiddleware had one reader in the repository -- a validator in the backend generator that threw when a name was not on a whitelist -- so it checked the spelling and dropped the list. Nothing was stored, nothing reached the generated router, and no request was ever handled differently for declaring any of them. The implementations were not missing either: rateLimit, securityHeaders, locale, maintenance, tenant, idempotency, featureFlags and auth are all written and unit-tested, through a chain each test builds by hand, and nothing else ever built one. A key now falls into one of three sets and every one of them means something. Nine are built and run in the order declared, wrapped around the handler so a refusal answers before the function runs and the headers the chain resolves reach a response that exists. One, csrf, is already enforced for every state-changing request whether or not it is declared, so declaring it is redundant rather than wrong. Two more cannot be a middleware at all, because the chain runs around the handler and by the time it has anything to say the body is in memory: bodyLimit and uploadLimit are registered with the native server on the route, which answers 413 for a declared Content-Length past the route's number without reading a byte and cuts off a body that grows past it while it is read, and the generated request prelude checks the same number again. A route declaring neither is held to dartvel.server.maxBodyBytes, 1 MiB by default, and the crash endpoint registers its ingest maxBytes. Each shape gets its own number when both are declared, since a JSON body of several megabytes is a mistake and an upload of several megabytes is the feature. One wraps the handler and the chain both: tracing. The helper existed, was tested and was wired to nothing -- the key named it and the generator had never heard of either. It is outside the chain on purpose, because a request refused by a rate limit is still a request and a trace covering only the ones that got through is a latency graph with the slow half missing. csp sends the policy the project configured under dartvel.security.csp, and a route declaring the key with nothing configured fails the build: a policy is a statement about one application own scripts and origins, there is no default that could be right, and an empty header is not no policy -- a browser reads it as one that allows nothing. Five still fail the build as route middleware and each says why. policy belongs on the function annotation, which is the thing that carries a policy name. rateLimitCheckout and cacheTags have no code behind the name at all. cors and compression are answered for the whole server rather than per route -- CORS headers go on every response including the preflight, which never reaches a route -- and the reason they give now names a key somebody can set. It did not before: it said to pass cors: to the serve call, and nobody using Dartvel writes a serve call. The generated startBackend makes that call and read no configuration at all, so an application could not set a CORS policy and could not turn compression off. dartvel.server is read at generation time and emitted into it: the origins, methods, headers, exposed headers, credentials and preflight max-age of the policy, and whether responses are compressed. A caller passing either argument still overrides it; a generated entrypoint passes neither. Saying nothing means no CORS headers rather than answering every origin, because a server that answers every origin is the single setting most likely to be wrong and defaulting to it would put it on every application that never thought about the question. A value the build cannot honour stops the build rather than being ignored: credentials from origins: any, which a browser refuses itself so the policy would allow nothing; an origin written with a path or a trailing slash, which never matches the Origin header and reads as CORS being broken; and compression written as a string, which is not a boolean and would leave compression on for somebody who wrote down that they wanted it off. The example application configures a real policy, so the generated backend emits one and a compiler reads it. The middleware library was also not exported from the barrel, so an application could not import CommonMiddleware or MiddlewareChain without reaching into src. The page half was the same bug one scope over, and the specification opens this section with the page form. The router generator had never heard of the annotation. Its only reader anywhere was that backend spelling check, which walks every file under lib and therefore did validate a page key -- against the sets written for an HTTP chain -- so a page could declare auth and open for everybody, or declare bodyLimit and cap nothing, with a green build and a whitelisted name behind it. A page scope now answers for every key on its own terms, because nine of the backend keys cannot mean anything on a route activation: there is no Content-Length to read before a body arrives, no response whose headers a route could set, and no second party to rate limit, since the page and the visitor are one machine. Two run. A page middleware lives inside the router redirect, which returns a location or lets the route through, so auth and maintenance are the decisions of that shape, and both are emitted into the route in the order declared, ahead of the folder guards and the page own policy. That is the backend order, where the chain wraps the policy gate. Nothing replaces anything, because a page that picks up middleware and silently loses the folder guard it was moved behind is the failure this shape invites. A page guarded only by declared middleware also joins the guarded route list the sitemap writer reads, so a checkout page behind auth is no longer published to crawlers while the specification says authenticated routes are excluded by default. The two defaults point opposite ways on purpose. auth with nothing wired refuses, which is what DVPagePolicy already answers for a policy nobody can evaluate. maintenance with nothing wired reports the application up, because nobody wires that hook until they have a window to declare and reading silence as down would black out every application on the release that added it. Both redirect targets are exempt from their own check, since a sign-in page declaring auth would otherwise redirect to itself until go_router gives up with an exception naming the router rather than the page anybody would go looking at. And the router that carries the auth key carries the answer as well, reading DV.Auth, because a hook nothing sets is the same bug again: the guard would have refused the people who had just signed in, which is not the safe version of a guard but a feature nobody can use. The other seventeen keys fail the build with somewhere to put the thing instead -- bodyLimit at the backend function where the body is read, policy at the DVPage policy argument that carries a name, cors and compression at the server settings that answer for every response. The scope is the declaration rather than the file or the folder, because a file can hold a page and a backend function and one answer per file would refuse whichever came second, while a page can sit outside the pages directory and deciding by folder would let one annotation mean two things depending on where somebody dropped it. Absent on pages: the other three things the specification says page middleware can do. It can redirect and it can block; it cannot preload data, set SEO context, or defer a route bundle, because a redirect returns a location or nothing and has nowhere to leave a value the page would then read. Absent too are the layout, model and storage scopes the specification lists beside pages and backend functions. A DVUseMiddleware on a layout file now stops the build rather than wrapping nothing, which is the honest half of not having the scope: a _layout.dart declaring auth used to have its spelling checked and guard none of the pages under it, so a whole section looked protected in the source and was open in the build. On a model or a storage declaration the annotation is still read by nothing and still measured against the backend sets, because the scope test answers page or not-page. Each needs a scope of its own before its keys can be judged, and the layout one also needs a rule for how a layout key composes with the pages under it -- once for the subtree, or again per page -- which is a decision rather than a missing function. Global middleware has no configuration key at all: nothing under dartvel reads a list of keys to apply to everything. Maintenance has no configured source on the client either, so DVPageMiddleware.isDown is an extension point an application sets rather than something a build reads out of pubspec.yaml, and a maintenance window is code. DVPagePolicy.decide is likewise still set by nothing, which leaves a page policy default-deny until an application wires it; that belongs to the authorization section but sits in the same redirect, so it is named here rather than discovered there. Absent: what the five refused backend keys would do. policy belongs on the function annotation, which is the thing that carries a policy name, so a route middleware form of it would be a second place to say the same thing. rateLimitCheckout and cacheTags have no code behind the name at all, and each is a guess at a different feature -- one names a bucket an application would have to define, the other a set of tags a response would have to carry. cors and compression, if a per-route form is ever wanted, need a rule for how each composes with the server-wide setting -- whether a route's origins replace the server's or add to them, and what a route that turns compression on means inside a server that turned it off -- which is the reason those keys are refused rather than quietly accepted.

Built: GraphQL depth and cost budgets on by default, pricing every operation and subscription before any resolver runs (nested levels, named and inline fragments, aliases, repeated spreads, list page sizes from argument, variable or declared pageSize, and a backend function field's declared cost), refusing the whole operation with DV-EDGE-001 naming budget, limit, actual and excess, with auto values derived from the registered schema (depth from the type graph's cycles allowing one step back into a cycle, cost as the whole schema one relation deep), memoised and arithmetic-capped pricing so a doubling fragment chain is refused rather than hanging, a self-spreading fragment reported as a request error, and DVGraphQL.analyze() pricing without running; the introspection policy (development, never, authenticated); persisted queries off, prefer and require against a sha256 manifest that is rejected on load when a hash does not match its document, refusing unknown documents and hashes under require (DV-EDGE-002) and a known hash sent with a different document in any mode but off; typed WAF rules as middleware (DVWafRule, DVWafSource.anywhere, within and notIn, first matching rule decides) with path normalisation so encoded, doubled or dot-segment paths cannot slip past a rule, an unknown country or failing resolver treated as outside every allow-list, no country header trusted unless named and sent by a configured trusted proxy, refusals carrying DV-EDGE-003, a DVWafAdapter interface for pushing rules to a platform firewall with enforcement kept in middleware either way, and lint() reporting match-all and 90-day-stale rules (DV-EDGE-006); per-account and per-source velocity limits keyed by the case-folded identifier and never by whether the account exists (DV-EDGE-005); LocalAuthProvider, DVLocalAuthProvider and DVCredentialGuard giving an unknown account and a wrong password one identical refusal (AuthException.invalidCredentials) after one password verification either way, against a dummy hash made at construction, with the guard also padding to a minimum time and collapsing providers that still throw the deprecated unknownAccount and invalidPassword; sign-up hashing before the address is looked up; an LDAP miss making the same password bind as a wrong password, against a DN that matches no entry; sign-ups that hit a taken address counted against the source only (DV-EDGE-005); never trying the password once a limit trips, and checking breached passwords at sign-up and password change (DV-EDGE-004) through a k-anonymity range query sending only the first five SHA-1 characters; a bot-protection adapter interface whose challenge fails closed. dartvel routes reads dartvel.api.graphql (maxDepth and maxCost as auto or a whole number of at least 1, introspection, persistedQueries) before writing anything, stopping on a key nothing reads under dartvel.api or dartvel.api.graphql and on a value the runtime cannot use, and the generated buildBackendRouter installs the declared settings on DVGraphQL before its first route, keeping the page size and any manifest the application loaded, while a project declaring none emits nothing; /graphql and /graphql/stream hand the decoded body to DVGraphQL.executeRequest and subscribeRequest, which read the hash at extensions.persistedQuery.sha256Hash, run the manifest's document for a hash sent alone, and refuse a hash that is not the hash of the document beside it under prefer and require. Absent: the build does not extract client queries into a manifest and generated clients do not send hashes, so under require /graphql answers only documents the application loads into DVGraphQL.persistedQueries itself, which dartvel routes says when it reads require; WAF rules are not a generated or named middleware key, dartvel analyze does not run the WAF lint, and rule match times live only in process memory; no real firewall, captcha or breach-service adapter exists (interface plus test adapter by design); the generated sign-in and sign-up endpoints use DVCredentialGuard, and the sign-up endpoint accepts a challenge token for a configured DVBotProtection, but the prebuilt auth pages have no challenge slot and send none; the per-source limit at those endpoints, and the rate limit's default identifier, count the client address DVClientAddress resolves: the connection's peer address, which dartvel_shelf passes over FFI as Request.peerAddress, unless the peer is in dartvel.server.trustedProxies or DARTVEL_TRUSTED_PROXIES, in which case the configured X-Forwarded-For or Forwarded chain is walked right to left to the first untrusted hop; a request with no peer address counts as one unknown source; a source is an IPv4 address, or the /64 an IPv6 address is in (dartvel.server.ipv6SourcePrefix, 32 to 128, checked at dartvel routes), and an IPv4-mapped address counts as IPv4; there is no shared velocity store adapter; the Platform API key scope that permits ad-hoc queries under require is not wired; dartvel doctor --security (DV-EDGE-007) does not exist. Where the section and the code disagree: sign-up cannot give the same answer whether an address is taken or not, because a sign-up that signs somebody in is itself the answer and nothing defers activation behind a verified e-mail, so DVCredentialGuard counts each taken-address sign-up against the source instead; the section lets the adapter decide where a WAF rule executes, but the code also always enforces in middleware so a failed push or a direct origin request is still refused; stale-rule reporting is described as a dartvel analyze finding and is reachable only through DVWaf.lint() at runtime; the section's DVWafSource.notIn has its counterpart named within because in is reserved in Dart; the section does not say what a breach-service outage does, and sign-up proceeds with a log line unless configured to fail closed, while bot challenges fail closed; the auto depth and cost budgets are this implementation's definitions, since the section only says they come from the model graph.
Biometric sign-in, which is a device capability rather than a server one and is tracked under Platform bindings. LDAP, SAML, passkey and Web3 ship.

The runtime is built (DVSessions with tokens stored only as hashes, a new token at every privilege boundary through rotate, elevate and completeMfa, revocation effective on the next request, idle and absolute expiry, device listing and revokeOthers, memory and database drivers; DVMfa policies with step-up and requireMfa; DVSecondFactors with RFC 6238 TOTP, replay refused at the verifier and by compare-and-set in the store, secrets sealed with DVFieldCipher, and salted, single-use recovery codes; DVSessionCookie refusing SameSite=None). The generated backend authenticates a dvs_ bearer token or the __Host-dv_session cookie into DVSessionPrincipal on every route, refusing an unknown, rotated, revoked, expired or other-tenant session with 401 and clearing a refused cookie, and refusing a session still waiting for its second factor with insufficient_user_authentication. It serves sign-up, sign-in, second-factor, sign-out, session, sessions, revoke and revoke-others endpoints (DVAuthEndpoints) that authenticate through DVCredentialGuard, issue a session on the request's tenant replacing one the request carried, deliver it only as the __Host-dv_session cookie to a browser and only as the dvs_ token in the body to a native client that asks, complete a second factor by TOTP or recovery code through completeMfa so only the rotated token carries privilege, revoke on the server at sign-out, and answer for the signed-in person's own sessions on the tenant. DV.Auth signs in through them by default (DVSessionClient, DVSessionAuthProvider), sealing a native token under the application key before it is written and handing it to DartvelClient.setAuthToken; DV.Session is a read-only signal, and DV.Auth.sessions, revoke and revokeOthers call the generated endpoints. The generated backend also serves the signed-in person's factors: TOTP enrollment that answers the secret and its otpauth URI and activates nothing until a code confirms it, recovery codes answered once and kept as salted HMACs with a new set replacing the old and requiring a factor within stepUpWindow, and removal that takes a code in the same request and removes the recovery codes with it; every factor change rotates the session, and a missing or stale factor is DVAuthEndpoints.stepUpRequired (DV-SESSION-001), 401 with insufficient_user_authentication and max_age. @DVPage(mfa:) and @DVBackendFunction(mfa:) take DVMfa.required or DVMfa.recent and are generated: a function checks the factor before its policy, raw handlers included, and a page redirects to a generated second-factor route that returns only to a path in the application; generated calls go through DVStepUp, which suspends a call refused for a missing factor, shows the challenge and sends it once more; an mfa: the generator cannot read stops the build. DV.Auth.SecurityPage (QR drawn by DVQrCode and DVQrImage, encoded in Dart and verified by an independent reader, recovery codes shown once), SessionsPage, SignUpPage (one answer for a taken address), ProfilePage and DeletePage are built from DVBox and DVText; an address change sends a code to the new address and changes nothing until it is verified, and deletion needs typed confirmation, the password through the credential guard and the factor, then runs the DVPrivacy erasure before removing factors, account and every session, answering 503 with the account intact when no erasure is configured (erasure_not_configured) or it could not reach an adapter (erasure_incomplete). The generated backend sends the address-change code through DV.Notifications.mail in a generated, overridable template (install(emailVerificationMail:)), refusing with mail_not_configured before a code is minted when no provider or sender is set, and deletes through the DV.Privacy it configures from DARTVEL_PRIVACY_KEY. The account pages have generated routes (/account/profile, /account/security, /account/sessions, /account/delete behind DVAccountPages.requireSession; /sign-up; SignInWithEmailAndPasswordPage(from:) at /login, setting dvSignInRoute), configurable or turned off under dartvel.auth.pages and checked at dartvel routes, each named by a level 1 heading, and dartvelAccountPages lists their navigation entries. POST /auth/account/password changes the password behind the current password through the credential guard and a factor within stepUpWindow, breach-checks it, rotates the session and revokes every other session of the person, and SecurityPage offers it. dartvel.auth.deletionGraceDays (0 to 29) makes deletion answer 202 with erasesAt and revoke every session at once; a complete sign-in within the window cancels it, a sign-in after it is 403 account_deleted, and a sweep erases due deletions through a DVAccountErasureJob on DVQueues that claims each by compare-and-set, so an erasure never runs after a cancellation. The generated runtime sends x-dartvel-device as the platform and kind of client only, and DV.Session.watch(context) rebuilds a widget when the session changes. A browser client sends credentials only to origins named exactly in DVCredentialedOrigins, which refuses wildcards, null, paths and plain http off the loopback, and the generated runtime names its own backend's origin; a credentialed dartvel.server.cors policy is refused without origins, with any methods, headers or exposed headers, or with a plain http origin off the loopback, and answers content-type and x-dartvel-csrf-token. The session cookie stays SameSite=Lax, so the web build and its API must be the same site. The deletion sweep ticks whether or not a window is declared, so a deletion scheduled under a window the project later removed is erased at the erasesAt the person was given, and signing in before then still cancels it. Absent: the prebuilt account pages have no avatar, which waits on a validated upload endpoint and an avatar field on the account; passkeys as a second factor; per-tenant MFA policy, which waits on Organizations; a Redis driver; clearing a device's DVOfflineStore when its session is revoked, which nothing connects; DV-SESSION-003 as a deploy-time gate rather than a runtime refusal; DV-SESSION-004, which nothing emits; session.location, which nothing populates from a request. Recovery codes are stored as salted HMACs in DVSecondFactorStore rather than as a generated model's sensitive field, because no model path exists for framework-owned auth tables.

Built: DV.Theme.mode and setMode, which is light/dark/system switching and the whole of what DVTheme is -- a mode holder. Designed: the token vocabulary (colour, type, spacing, radius, elevation, motion) that modifiers name, per-mode token resolution including high contrast, fonts declared in configuration and bundled per target with fallback chains, per-tenant token overrides as a model, icon and splash generation from one master, and Figma variable import with two-way drift reporting. The section was labelled Contract/Shipped against a class with one field, which is why the stability drops to Draft: a surface this far from finished cannot promise that a breaking change takes the migration path rather than a spec edit.

binding_names.dart declares 87 names and no platform binds them all, which is the design rather than a gap: a tray is not a thing a browser has, and a resizable window is not a thing an Android application owns. What each target binds is its own capability set, and that set is now checked against the registrations rather than trusted -- android_bindings_test asserts the two agree by reading the source, and the emulator job asserts it again on a device, where a claim with no handler behind it looks exactly like a platform that cannot. Bound today: Linux 63, Windows 41, web 41, Android 36, macOS 36, iOS 7. Android moved from 10 to 36 and web from 16 to 41. Those figures date the moment they were written; dart tool/binding_coverage.dart counts them from the source, and prose here should be read against it rather than trusted. Absent on Android, each with the reason rather than a date: biometrics.authenticate, because BiometricPrompt reports to an AuthenticationCallback, which is an abstract class, and jnigen implements interfaces and cannot subclass one, so the prompt answer has nowhere to arrive until a Java shim is written beside the Context provider; nfc.readTag and nfc.writeTag, because a tag reaches an application only through foreground dispatch or reader mode, both Activity callbacks that fire whenever somebody taps, so a one-shot binding would answer null for ever or hand back whatever was tapped last; bluetooth.connect, disconnect and forget, because Android has no device-level connect at all, connection being per profile and asynchronous, and removeBond is hidden and blocked for ordinary applications; and display.enterFullscreen and exitFullscreen, which must run on Android main thread through Activity.runOnUiThread and so need java.lang.Runnable generated as an implementable interface, which needs an Android SDK to generate from. display.enableKiosk and disableKiosk stay unregistered on purpose, since DVDisplayControls falls back to kiosk.enforce and kiosk.release, which Android binds, and a second registration would be two answers to one question. On web the 44 unbound names each carry a written reason in dvWebUnavailableBindings and a test fails until a newly declared name joins one list or the other, so silence is not available: a tab has no tray, no global shortcut, no watchdog that outlives the event loop it runs on, and no path for a file somebody picked. Nine more are registered only where the browser has the API -- share.text, contacts and the NFC and Bluetooth names are absent from desktop Chrome, detected for rather than assumed -- and a refusal is told apart from an absence, DVWebPermissionDenied carrying the browser own words when somebody taps Deny where a missing API leaves the name unregistered. What has been run is narrower than what is implemented. On web, 32 of the 41 were exercised in headless Chrome, including an OPFS byte round trip and a real 11,315-byte PNG from a fake camera device; the rest need a tap, a modal or an Android Chrome, and Firefox and Safari are reasoned from their APIs rather than measured. On Android nothing below the Dart decision layer has been executed at all, because there is no device or emulator on the development machine, so every JNI call is implemented and unverified until the emulator job runs it. Two contracts disagree across platforms and both are live faults rather than gaps: notifications.sendLocal answers with the freedesktop notification id on Linux and a bool everywhere else while DVNotifications.sendLocalNotification requires a bool, so that call throws on Linux; and files.writeBytes returns a byte count from the shared native binding while DVFiles.writeBytes requires a bool, so it throws on Linux, Windows and macOS where web returns true and works. Sensors are the one place the declared surface is itself wrong: SensorManager has no read-now call and the declared name is singular, so Android binds a genuine one-shot while DVSensors types itself as a Stream that yields exactly once, and a real subscription would need a second name or a stream-shaped bridge.

Migrations run now, and did not: dartvel db migrate discovered a list of table names, printed a line per model saying it had migrated it and a total saying they were synced successfully, wrote a JSON snapshot, and executed nothing. The generated createTableSql -- one per model, correct, carrying the tenant column -- was called by nothing anywhere in the repository. The generator now writes the statements where something other than Dart can read them, built from the same column list the model itself carries, and the command runs them: SQLite because that is the one the framework can reach, through the framework own adapter rather than a second way to open the same file. Any other provider gets the statements written out with the reason they were not run, because the CLI has no connection to a managed Postgres and saying so is worth more than the green line it replaces. A table that already exists gains the columns its model gained, since CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is a no-op against one that is there and a query naming a column the table lacks fails against a database just reported as migrated. The tenant column is the one that cannot be added quietly: rows written before it existed belong to no tenant, a predicate on every read hides all of them from everybody, and the table reads as empty in a way that cannot be told from data loss -- so such a table is left entirely alone, not half migrated, and the command asks whose the rows are. SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL, each with their wire-compatible variants, and TLS on both network engines so managed endpoints are reachable. The framework's own session, account-deletion, queue, purchase, metering and promotion tables declare their timestamps, durations and quantities BIGINT and meter amounts DOUBLE PRECISION, and are exercised against a PostgreSQL service in CI; every column the framework creates declares a type, including tables built at run time and those in a tenant schema, and a static test fails the suite on one that does not; a table an earlier release made with 32-bit columns is widened through the schema planner, in its own schema, when empty and refused with its plan when it has rows. MongoDB, ClickHouse and BigQuery are out of scope by decision, not backlog. Also absent: applying a migration to Postgres or MySQL from the CLI, which needs a connection it does not have; dropping or altering a column, since every generated column is TEXT and nothing has yet needed to change one; and a module tables, which are named at run time by how the module was mounted and are recorded by the parent own generation. The in-memory adapter now runs the SQL the framework itself writes -- CREATE TABLE and DROP TABLE, parameterised INSERT, UPDATE ... WHERE and DELETE ... WHERE, and SELECT with DISTINCT, column subsets, aliases, COUNT(*), ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET, with WHERE joining the six comparisons, IS NULL and IS NOT NULL by AND -- so Studio's page store, the database cache and queue adapters, Studio Pro's stores and DVTest.fakeDatabase() all work with no database configured. It understood four statement shapes before that and threw on everything else, which made the framework's own development adapter unable to back the framework's own surfaces. A join, a subquery, OR, FTS5 MATCH, ALTER TABLE or CREATE INDEX still throws and the message names the statement it refused: an adapter that guessed at a query it had not parsed would return wrong rows that look exactly like right ones.

Built: DVDatabaseAdapter.classify for PostgreSQL, MySQL 8 and SQLite/Turso by server version (PostgreSQL defaults rewrite before 11 and NOT NULL is online from 12; MySQL's INSTANT point releases 8.0.12, 8.0.28 and 8.0.29 respected; SQLite rules from the linked library), with anything unclassifiable treated as blocking (DV-SCHEMA-006); a planner that replaces a blocking type change with a five-phase expand/contract plan only when the expand step itself does not block, and reports what the contract will cost (DV-SCHEMA-001); a production gate needing a reasoned, logged override (DV-SCHEMA-002); production snapshots carrying provider, server version, columns and row counts so a rehearsal classifies as production would; a resumable, pausable chunked backfill running as DVQueues slices; per-chunk hash verification naming a mismatched chunk (DV-SCHEMA-004) and a chunk that verified and later differs (DV-SCHEMA-007); a tier-based throttle that halves under replica lag or write latency and reports DV-SCHEMA-003 once below its floor past its patience; a five-phase tracker persisted in the database whose verify step needs a complete backfill with every chunk verified and no discrepancy in the window, whose read switch needs that verification to still stand, and whose contract and drop are refused while older clients still call, when no client list is given, or while the release being replaced still reads the old shape (DV-SCHEMA-005, decided by the same DVContractDecision as the release gate); its phase exposed to Backend Release Management through DVSchemaEvolutionStore.phaseSource; and dartvel db migrate --plan (applies nothing), --dry-run --against snapshot (gated as production, logs nothing) and --production --allow-blocking <reason> (appends the override to .dartvel/db/schema_overrides.jsonl). Not built: classification for MongoDB, ClickHouse or BigQuery; model generation emitting column types, nullability, indexes or renames, so the CLI derives only create-table and add-nullable-column changes and dartvel build never raises DV-SCHEMA-001; generated dual-write model code; any command that captures a production snapshot; live measurement of replica lag or write latency; backfill progress in Studio; SQL execution of expand, contract or drop steps; DV-SCHEMA-005 connected to the Protocol Versioning client histogram, and DV-SCHEMA-002 wired into dartvel deploy; enforcing that the expanding release raises the protocol version; expand/contract plans for blocking changes other than a type change; live MySQL tests of classify. PostgreSQL classification of a type change is exercised live by the framework-table widening, which runs a blocking change only against an empty table. Where the section and the code disagree: classify is an opt-in DVSchemaClassifier rather than a new adapter member, because a new member would stop every existing adapter compiling; the adapter table lists MongoDB, ClickHouse and BigQuery, which the Database section puts out of scope as operational databases; the MySQL column says MySQL 8 but the rules change within 8.0, and MariaDB and 5.7 are not described; DV-SCHEMA-003 names a floor and a patience that the configuration example lacks, so backfill.floorRate and backfill.patience were added, and the verification window is unspecified and defaults to one hour; whether a backfill survives a restart depends on the configured queue adapter; verification is recorded and a later discrepancy revokes it, and the read switch is its own release inside the verify phase, where the section puts reads moving in phase 5.

Built since: Dartvel reads an OpenAPI document as well as writing one. `dartvel import openapi <file|url>` turns a specification into ordinary source -- a private @DVModel per schema under lib/models/, a function per operation under lib/api/ with path parameters interpolated -- which is the direction people actually start from: an API exists, somebody hands you its spec, and the work is transcribing it by hand. A field the specification does not list in `required` is nullable, which is the difference between a model that matches the API and one that throws the first time a field is absent. A schema the importer cannot map is reported and skipped rather than emitted as `dynamic`: a guess that compiles is found at run time, and a line of output naming the schema is found now. Files already on disk are left alone unless --overwrite is passed, because an import that silently replaced an edited file is an import that gets run once. A Postman collection reads in too, because an OpenAPI document is the tidy case and what people are handed is very often somebody's export of the requests their team already makes. Requests become functions, folders are walked through, `:id` becomes a parameter that reaches the path, and Postman's {{baseUrl}} does not survive: the generated client knows where the API is, and left in it produces a request to a literal "{{baseUrl}}/books" that fails at run time and reads as a network problem. A collection carries no types, which is said once rather than discovered by looking in lib/models and finding nothing. Both importers share the writing half of the command and the naming rules -- two copies of the overwrite rule would be two chances to destroy somebody's edited file.

sections.section: Platform API: Keys, Scopes and OAuth Provider
sections.absent: Built in dartvel_core: DVApiScopes maps a scope name to Resource.action policy actions read from dartvel.platformApi (a list, or {actions, description}), matching scope and action names whole and never as prefixes. DVAuthAuthorization.can and authorize refuse a DVScopedPrincipal's action outside its scopes before the policy runs, logging DV-APIKEY-002, and inside them the policy still decides. DVApiKeys issues a key for an open organization with declared scopes, shows the secret once and stores only its SHA-256, compared in constant time; a key is refused when revoked, expired, presented for another tenant or its organization is closed; rotate overlaps (DV-APIKEY-003), revoke is immediate, both recorded in Record History; requireExpiry raises DV-APIKEY-005. DVOAuthProvider registers clients with exact redirect URIs and declared scopes only (DV-APIKEY-004), requires S256 PKCE, spends a code by a versioned write, rotates refresh tokens and revokes a grant on reuse, supports client credentials as an API key with a grant, and implements introspection (RFC 7662) and revocation (RFC 7009). dartvel routes reads dartvel.platformApi with DVPlatformApiConfig (scopes, ratePlans as {maxRequests, window}, requireExpiry, oauth lifetimes and issuer) before writing anything, stops on a key nothing reads, and stops with DV-APIKEY-001 on a scope action no @DVPolicy class in the application or a merged module defines, by resource and action together; the declaration is generated into platform_api.g.dart as dartvelPlatformApi and parsed again at startup. With it declared, the generated backend installs DVPlatformApi and every route's authentication stage resolves an Authorization: Bearer dvk_ key or dvat_ token on the request's tenant into DVApiPrincipal.current; any other bearer is the application's; an invalid, revoked, expired or other-tenant credential is one 401 with WWW-Authenticate and no-store, and a key over its declared rate plan is a 429. DVBackendPolicy.allows refuses a policy outside the principal's scopes before decide, which sees the principal; @DVBackendFunction(policy: 'Resource.action') is read, where it was silently dropped before; a keyed request is refused on a route declaring no policy action and is not asked for a CSRF token. With dartvel.platformApi.oauth on, DVOAuthEndpoints serves authorize (GET to /oauth/consent, POST recording the answer of the person DVOAuthEndpoints.resolveUser names, CSRF-checked), authorize/request, token (authorization_code with PKCE, refresh_token, client_credentials), introspect, revoke and /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server (RFC 8414); token, introspection and revocation take a form POST only, a GET being a 405 and a JSON body invalid_request before anything is spent; a repeated parameter or a client authenticating two ways is invalid_request; introspection answers only a confidential client or a key or token whose scopes cover DVOAuthToken.introspect, and only on the request's tenant; every token response and error is no-store, CORS is allowed on token, revocation and metadata and not on authorization; an unregistered redirect URI is shown and never redirected to. DV.Auth.OAuthConsentPage, served by the generated router at /oauth/consent, shows the client and each scope's declared wording and approves nothing until pressed. DV.Auth.apiKeys (issue, list, rotate, revoke) and DV.Auth.oauthClients (register, list, revoke) act on the organization on the current tenant through DV.Auth.authorization on DVApiKeyResource and DVOAuthClientResource, refusing with no policy or no user, answering another organization's key or client as not found, and refusing an undeclared rate plan at issue. The generated backend registers every @DVPolicy class in the application and its merged modules that the server can load before its first route exists, dartvel routes stops on a route's Resource.action no such class defines, and the server refuses to start while a route names an action nothing registered, an action on DVApiKeyResource or DVOAuthClientResource included, which has no framework default and is answered by the application's own registration or @DVPolicy class. A request authenticated by the application's own session (a Bearer dvs_ token or the __Host-dv_session cookie) becomes DVSessionPrincipal.current on the tenant the session was issued on, with the application's user from DVSessionAuthentication resolveUser and the organization membership read on every request; the registered route policy is handed that user when its signature takes it, else the principal; no caller on a route whose policy needs one is a 401, any other refusal a 403, and a session-authenticated state change still needs a CSRF token while an API key or OAuth token does not. GraphQL (/graphql, /graphql/stream, /graphql/schema), the crash endpoint, OpenAPI and health run on the request's tenant through the same authentication stage and refuse a bad credential with the same 401; a DVGraphQLField declaring a Resource.action is asked it as a route asks it before its resolver runs, a root field declaring none answers no key, the crash endpoint refuses a valid key with 403, and OpenAPI, health and the schema answer a valid key. Absent: the generated ApiKey model and ApiKey.issue(...); DV.Auth.apiKeys and oauthClients take the user and actor explicitly rather than reading the signed-in user; the consent screen is shown even when standing consent exists; the GraphQL fields generated for models are registered only in the client, and they ask the model's policy inside their resolvers rather than declaring a policy action, so on a server an API key or OAuth token would be refused on them as on any root field declaring none; OIDC (id_token, userinfo, discovery, JWKS), with tokens opaque rather than JWT; the developer portal module; rate plans shared across processes, since the lifecycle enforces declared plans with CommonMiddleware.rateLimit in memory per instance; per-key usage metering and meter dimensions in the generated lifecycle; key last-used tracking; introspection of refresh tokens; RFC 8252 loopback port variance; a diagnostic code for refresh-token or code reuse. Where the section and the code disagree: keys are said to be stored hashed like a password, but they use SHA-256 rather than the PBKDF2 password hasher, because a 256-bit random secret has no dictionary to resist and a slow hash would run on every call; the provider is said to sit over Authentication's session and token machinery, but DVSessions and DVAuthTokens have no client, scope, PKCE or grant concepts, so it keeps its own tables; DV-APIKEY-005 is a warning while its reason says expiry is required, so the key is issued and the code logged rather than refused; scopes name Order.view while DVAuthAuthorization registers view:Order, which is translated; the scope configuration has no place for consent wording, so a description form was added, and no place for an issuer, so oauth.issuer was added; client credentials treat a key as the credential, so client_id is the key id, client_secret is the whole key, and revoking the key ends its tokens; a route's scope check needs its policy written as a quoted Resource.action, since a reference such as DVPolicies.refund names no action a scope can cover; introspection by key needs the framework action DVOAuthToken.introspect, which no application policy defines; the consent answer is returned as JSON redirect_to for the screen to navigate to rather than as an HTTP redirect.

The delivery runtime is built (DVWebhooks: declared events; subscriptions, delivery records and payloads kept in DV.Database in dv_webhook_subscriptions, dv_webhook_deliveries and dv_webhook_payloads, so a delivery that failed before a restart is retried after it as the same delivery with its attempts counted and its place in line kept, whether the queue is DVDatabaseQueueAdapter or was lost with the process, since drain and resume() queue a job for every pending delivery that has none; per-subscription queues on DVQueues that always attempt the oldest undelivered delivery; concurrent drain, so a slow endpoint delays only itself; HTTPS-only endpoints refused at subscribe, at every attempt and at every redirect hop when they resolve to private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, reserved or metadata addresses; each attempt and redirect hop connected to the exact address its check approved through DVHttpRequest.connectAddress, with SNI, certificate verification and the Host header kept on the original name and redirects returned rather than followed by the client; public-JSON payloads with declared sensitive fields stripped; HMAC-SHA256 signing with keys from DVSecrets and a bounded two-signature rotation overlap; dead-lettering; disable after repeated failure; payload retention that deletes the payload row and keeps the record, with replay past the window refused).
