Absent: nothing named here. DVModelChangeKind.restored is published by the generated Model.restore(id) of a @DVModel(softDelete: true) model, and only when the record it restores was deleted.

The runtime is built (DVOfflineStore: a local DVRecordTable written at once, an ordered persisted mutation log, replay that runs once per reconnect, stops on a transient failure and dead-letters a permanent refusal; DVRecordTableRemote deduplicating by mutation id and resolving last-write-wins by the declared clock rather than arrival order; a bound by count and age that refuses rather than drops; DVConflict.ask refused offline; DVOfflineClock correction with skew reported once; DVSyncState per record; DV-OFFLINE-001 to 004). Absent: @DVModel(offline:) is not on the annotation and nothing is generated, so Order.find, save and watch, order.syncState and Order.pendingMutations do not exist; replay is not dispatched through DVQueues and is not carried by the model sync transport, so the log keeps its own dead letters; the local store schema does not come from the migration schema diff; there is no IndexedDB store on web; writes are not routed through the policy engine or tenant scope, and signing out does not clear the store automatically; encrypt: true and sensitive-field encryption at rest are not applied; maxClockSkew and the queue bounds are not read from pubspec.yaml; DV-OFFLINE-005 and DV-OFFLINE-006 have nothing that emits them; DV.Platform.network.status and .since do not exist.

no provider has been exercised against a real APNS or push service. The SMTP provider is exercised against a real SMTP server now, in a container, with the raw source of what arrived read back -- which is the only way to see the half of this that is accepted and wrong, and it found two. The subject went down the wire as raw UTF-8 in a header RFC 5322 says is ASCII: the server took it, the companion assertion that it was still readable at the far end passed because that server guesses the encoding, and the clients that do not guess show it as mojibake to whoever was sent it. Headers are RFC 2047 encoded words now, split on character boundaries rather than on bytes, since a word broken mid-character decodes to a replacement in half the readers and leaves the subject wrong in exactly two places; an address keeps its angle brackets and only the display name is encoded, because encoding the whole thing produces a header no server can route. The body declared no transfer encoding at all, which means 7bit, which raw UTF-8 is not -- a server without 8BITMIME may refuse it or strip the high bit and the message arrives readable-ish, which is the worst outcome to be handed. Each part says what it is now: 7bit where the content really is, quoted-printable where it is not, which also keeps every line under the 998 octets RFC 5321 allows. Dot-stuffing, the AUTH exchange, multipart and the ordinary path were already right and are now proven against a server rather than against a connection this repository wrote. The native transport they depend on speaks HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and is verified live, and the VAPID signature is pinned byte-for-byte to RFC 6979's published P-256 vectors rather than only round-tripped through this library's own verifier -- but a signature a push service would accept is not the same as a request one has accepted. Channel routing is built: DVNotificationMessage.channels used to be read by nothing, so the specification's own three-channel example delivered to the in-app provider and reported success; each channel now picks its own provider and resolves the recipient id to the address that provider needs through DVNotificationRoutes, push tries the native providers and falls back to Web Push both when none is registered and when the registered one fails, quiet hours hold only push, web push and SMS because holding an email drops it, and send returns a per-channel DVNotificationDelivery so a notification that was withheld and one that was lost are different answers. Mail priority reaches the wire as X-Priority and Importance instead of being dropped by all six providers, and SES no longer drops custom headers or recipient display names. Absent for want of work rather than credentials or hardware: delivery receipts and bounce or complaint webhooks as typed backend functions; attachments and tags on DVMailMessage, which the specification lists and the type does not carry; per-tenant sender identities and DKIM or SPF validation checks; List-Unsubscribe headers, so unsubscribe is a preference this framework honours internally and not one a mail client can act on; queued-by-default mail, which still sends inline although DV.Jobs and DV.Queues exist to carry it; a durable inbox and database notifications, since the in-app channel writes to whichever provider is registered and the only one shipped keeps a list in memory; server-side device token storage, rotation and revocation -- the device half of registration is reachable now that PushNotifications is exported at all, but where a token is kept between the device handing it over and a send needing it is still the application's problem, since DVNotificationRoutes only asks for it; per-channel rate limits; tenant-aware branding; and the pubspec notification permissions the specification says are validated at build time, for which no CLI or generator code reads a key -- the declaration does not exist at all, so there is nothing yet being parsed and dropped. The windows, macos, linux, tizen and webos provider kinds are enum members with no implementation behind them; routing will select one the moment it is registered, and until then a push on those platforms falls through to Web Push

Everything on the upload side. There is no @DVModel.imageField, so nothing generates variants for a file a user uploaded, and no upload validation, dimension or byte ceiling, scan hook or signed transformation URL exists -- the endpoint is reachable only for assets the build declared and hosts the application allowed, which is what stands in for signing today. No AVIF anywhere. WebP only from a web-server build, negotiated from the request's Accept for a PNG or WebP source; a static build writes each variant in the source's own format. No provider adapter: resizing is local, in the build and in the server, and there is no path that hands an image to an image service. No video of any kind, by decision rather than backlog -- no thumbnail extraction, no transcode profiles, no DVVideoEncoder. Off the web nothing is wired: the build writes variants for a web build only, so a device ships its original assets and the device-profile rule in the section is a design, not a behaviour. The DV-MEDIA codes are registered meanings and none is emitted yet: the two that describe refusals the server already makes (a width outside the set, a host or redirect that is not allowed) are answered today with a 400 and a sentence rather than with a code. What is real: dartvel build web writes a variant per configured width narrower than each declared raster asset, a web-server build resizes on request and caches, DVImageView asks for its slot's width times the device pixel ratio snapped to the configured set, a link prefetches the variant for the visitor's own pixel ratio into Flutter's image cache under the provider the widget will ask for, and every one of those computes the address through DVImageVariants so the three agree byte for byte. GIF is never resized.

Built: the player and capture state machines as read-only DVMediaSignal values that move only when the backend reports: a player is not playing until the backend says so, a decoder that stops advancing is stalled, a position report from before a seek is dropped, failed is final, and leaving the page releases the backend, audio focus and timers. Protected content with no DRM adapter is refused before the backend sees it (DV-MEDIA-102), an adaptive stream falls back to its progressive version (DV-MEDIA-101) or is refused, and undeclared background audio logs DV-MEDIA-103 and pauses. Capture checks capabilities before asking permission and refuses with a typed error and DV-MEDIA-104; capturing follows what the device confirms; backgrounding, a revoked permission or a lost device ends the session as DVCaptureInterrupted with the partial file rather than a success; disposing aborts and deletes the partial file; recording files are created 0600 in a 0700 directory before the device writes and re-tightened if the device replaced them. Every backend contract has a fake. DVBox.video and DVBox.audio own their player for as long as the box is mounted (a parent rebuild reuses it, a new source replaces it, a controller the application passes in outlives the box), DVBox.controller and DVBox.aspectRatio exist, and DV.Platform.Media.recordAudio and recordVideo return a DVCaptureSession. On Linux, GStreamer over dart:ffi plays files, assets and URLs with duration, position, accurate seek, pause, volume, completion and errors, and records audio to Opus/Ogg, WAV or AAC through the installed encoders, verified into fakesink and from audiotestsrc here and on GitHub Actions, where the Tests workflow installs gstreamer1.0-plugins-base and runs the suite with no skips; a pipeline naming an element that is not installed fails at once with DVGStreamerPipelineError, the player and recorder report it as a failed state naming the missing elements, and capability reports mark a source or format unavailable when an element it needs is missing. Absent: audible output and a real microphone were not verified (the machine has neither); Linux does not draw video frames into Flutter, so DVBox.video plays audio under the poster; camera capture exists on no target and recordVideo is refused everywhere; no player or capture backend for Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, web, Tizen, webOS or tvOS, and eLinux reaching the GStreamer backend is unverified; audio focus is arbitrated only between the application's own players, with no platform focus binding; DVMediaSession lock-screen and now-playing controls, picture-in-picture, AirPlay and Chromecast; captions (DVCaptions does not exist); any DRM adapter, beyond the DVDrmAdapter interface and its refusal; the build generating the background-audio declaration, so every background-audio request gets DV-MEDIA-103 today; remote-control keys run on a television embedder; Media Pipeline's upload validation and variants accepting a capture DVFile; decode offloaded through DV.Workers or DV.Memory; usage metering of playback. Where the section and the code disagree: player.position is written as a DVSignal, but a player exists outside any widget, so its signals are DVMediaSignal values read with watch(context) that do not compose with signal operators; await recordAudio(...) is written as returning a DVFile, and it returns a DVCaptureSession that implements Future<DVFile> and also exposes stop, dispose, state and capturing; DVFile did not exist and a minimal one was added; the DVAudio asset constants and poster generation from Media Pipeline do not exist, so DVMediaSource.asset takes an asset key and the poster is a DVImage; DV.Platform.Media sits beside the existing lowercase media getter.

Tenant resolution is built: DVTenants resolves the current tenant from the configured source, the tenant middleware makes it current for the rest of the chain, presence is scoped by it, and the tenant is held in a zone so it follows async work rather than leaking between concurrent requests. Filtering of generated model queries is built now and was not: the word tenant appeared zero times in the model generator and nowhere in any database adapter, so on the shared-database strategy the specification lists first, a query returned every tenant rows. A model that declares tenantScoped: true gets a dv_tenant column in its schema, a predicate on every read, the current tenant bound into every write, and a delete that cannot reach another tenant row. The schema, the writes and the reads arrive together on purpose -- a column written and not filtered on leaks, one filtered on and not written hides every row, and both look exactly like the feature working. It is opt-in per model because a single-tenant application should not carry a column it never reads and a table deliberately shared across tenants would be broken by a predicate it never asked for, and a model that declares a field of that name is refused at generation time rather than producing a duplicate column when the table is created in a deployment. A model that sets tenantScoped: true and generatePublicPages: true together is refused at generation time: a public page is rendered with no request, so there is no current tenant to scope it by, and the row would be served at a public URL to anybody -- the exact leak the column exists to close, on the one path that never sees it. Which model is scoped is read from that model own arguments now, and was read from the whole file: one tenant-scoped model made every model declared beside it tenant-scoped. The comment two lines above the read names the case it breaks -- a currency list, a country table -- and the symptom is not a leak but the opposite. Rows written before the column existed belong to no tenant, so a predicate the model author never asked for hides every one of them from every tenant. Schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant do something now, and did not: both were an enum value and a name-building function -- DVTenants.qualifierFor, correct, unit tested, and called by nothing anywhere -- so configuring either produced exactly the queries sharedDatabase produces against exactly the same database. Every tenant read every tenant rows on the two strategies chosen specifically to prevent that, and it looked like it worked: every query returned rows and the application behaved. schemaPerTenant qualifies the name, resolved at the moment a statement runs rather than written in, because which schema is asking is a fact about the request and two requests are in flight at once; under sharedDatabase the same call returns the table own name, so the strategy almost everyone uses generates what it always did. databasePerTenant does not qualify the name, since the connection is what differs and a qualified one would look for a schema inside the tenant own database; the adapter is resolved per tenant instead, opened once each and kept, because a connection per query is a pool nobody wrote and on SQLite a second write lock over one file. Configuring that strategy without saying how to open a tenant database is refused, the fallback being the one adapter for everybody -- the leak it exists to close, returning rows the whole time. A migration for an existing table is built too: a table with rows gaining the tenant column is left entirely alone until somebody says whose those rows are, because rows written before the column existed belong to nobody and a predicate on every read hides all of them, so the table reads as empty in a way nothing distinguishes from data loss. A raw query an application writes itself is checked now, and was not: generated model queries carried the predicate and everything else did not -- a report, a dashboard count, a join the generator cannot express, a query written before the model was scoped -- each of which returned rows that looked plausible while showing one tenant another tenant data. The generated client registers which tables are scoped, because the database layer has no idea what a model is, and a statement naming one without mentioning the column is refused. Deliberately coarse: a false positive is a refusal somebody reads and fixes, a false negative leaves the old behaviour, and the one thing it never does is guess in the direction of allowing. Writes are checked as well, the worse half, since a write without the column puts a row in the table belonging to nobody that every tenant then cannot see. Names match on a word boundary, so workorders is not orders -- refusing it would teach people to reach for the escape hatch out of habit, which is how an escape hatch stops meaning anything. Only under sharedDatabase, the other two separating by schema or connection where a predicate on a column that is not there would fail every query. Registration adds rather than replaces, since an application client and every module client run in one process and replacing would leave whichever ran last as the only checked set. DV.Database.acrossTenants is the way through, for an operator report or a support tool: not hard, but written down, visible in a diff and greppable rather than a query that happened to have no predicate. The tenant a request named is held for that request now, and was written to a process-wide field. A server has more than one request in flight and Dart hands the isolate over at every await, so the request that arrived second decided what the first one read: every query the first handler made after its next await ran as somebody else's tenant, returned rows, and rendered. withTenant existed, carried the tenant in a zone, was unit tested, and was called by nothing on the request path. Every generated route is wrapped now rather than only the routes that listed the tenant middleware, because a tenant-scoped model does not care what the route declared -- and the plainest raw handlers had a shortcut registration with no wrapper on them at all. The middleware still makes the tenant current for a hand-written server that runs the chain itself, and stops writing the process-wide field when a scope already carries it, since under a scope that write belongs to no request and reaches every one of them. A request naming no tenant keeps what the process was set to, so a single-tenant deployment on an apex domain is not pushed onto a default tenant with no rows in it. Server rendering resolved no tenant at all, and kept each page under the request path alone. Both halves are one hole and either fixed alone would have looked like a fix and been none: a tenant in the key with nothing resolving one is always the same tenant, and a resolved tenant with a shared key still serves the first arrival page. Under the subdomain source the specification lists first, acme.example.com/orders and globex.example.com/orders are one path, so the first tenant to ask filled the entry and every other tenant read that page until the ttl ran out -- no login and no crafted request, two customers on one server was enough. The preview and web-server handler had the same two faults, which matters because that target exists to promise that the page a developer previews is the page the server sends. An export declared a tenant and narrowed by nothing. DVExportOptions.tenantId was stored, written into the file metadata, and read by nothing that chose which rows were written, while policyFilter beside it in the same object did narrow -- one filter and one label, reading as two filters, and a file that names a tenant it was never narrowed to is worse than one that names none because somebody downstream reads the label. It cannot be narrowed there: the rows were read before the export was called and the tenant column is not a field on the generated model, so there is nothing on an item to compare. A declared tenant that is not the tenant the export runs as is refused, with the order that works, rather than stamped. Full-text search over a scoped table returned every tenant rows. The Postgres provider builds its own SQL and hands it to the adapter, so it went past DV.Database and past the check that refuses a statement naming a scoped table without the tenant column, and the automatic tenant filter the specification names was a hook called filter that every application had to write for itself: one that did not got a search box listing other tenants rows, with their titles and descriptions in the results, because that is what search results are. The predicate is added before the application own filter, so a filter that throws or is written wrong cannot be the reason it is missing. Under a schema per tenant the name is qualified instead and no column predicate is added, and the index is created on the tenant own table rather than in whichever schema the connection points at. Choosing an isolation strategy is possible from a project at all now. It meant calling DVTenants.configure from Dart that no generated entrypoint runs, so schema-per-tenant and database-per-tenant -- the two an application picks precisely to keep tenants in separate schemas or separate databases -- could not be selected, and every deployment ran the shared-database default whether that is what it wanted or not. requireTenant was in the same position: it gated the refusal of a request naming no tenant and nothing anywhere set it. dartvel.tenancy is read at generation time and emitted where the server starts, and a value nobody implements fails the build rather than being dropped, because a misspelled isolation left on the floor runs the default while the pubspec says otherwise and every query still returns rows. A job carries its tenant: DV.Jobs.dispatch records the tenant current at dispatch, and none for the default tenant. All seven adapters store it and read it back (in-memory, database, Redis, SQS, RabbitMQ, Pub/Sub and Kafka, the four network brokers verified against a real broker in CI, Redis only against a local server), and the worker runs each handler inside that tenant's scope, so DV.Database, tenant-scoped models and the per-tenant schema or database resolve what the request resolved. A job with no tenant runs as the default tenant, never as the worker's process tenant, the previous job's, or one a handler set. The durable jobs table gains a nullable tenant column when an earlier release made it, added through the schema planner, and jobs already in it run with none. A schedule's handler is called directly rather than through a queue, so a job it dispatches records the cron process's tenant. Absent: creating the per-tenant schemas and databases themselves, which needs a list of tenants the build does not have. Hosted search is unscoped too: Meilisearch and OpenSearch answer from documents the application shapes, so the tenant has to be a field in the index and a filter on the query rather than something a provider can add to somebody else's schema.

Built: DVOrganizations in dartvel_core. The tenant stays the data boundary; an organization is a group of people on exactly one tenant, a second on the same tenant is refused, and resolving a membership on a personal tenant throws DV-ORG-006 rather than answering no role. Creating an organization on an existing personal tenant makes that person the owner without moving data, and rename, transfer and close never touch the tenant. Roles are typed and ordered by declaration, an undeclared role name throws DV-ORG-001, roles from different declarations refuse to compare, and a declaration must include owner. DVMembership.grants checks the organization as well as the role and works as a DVAuthAuthorization policy. Invitations are single-use, expiring magic links or codes through DVAuthTokens, stored as a hash, expiry checked by the token store and the organization's clock, bound to the invited address, refused with DV-ORG-002 for an existing member, and never issued by a non-member or above the inviter's own role. Seats are a query over memberships under a declared rule (every member, members at given roles, or members active within a period), exposed as a DVLevelLimit refusing with DV-METER-004, with counting and joining under one per-organization lock. The last owner cannot leave or be demoted (DV-ORG-003); transfer promotes the successor first; transfer and close join an enclosing DV.transaction; a closed organization refuses work and can be restored within its grace period (DV-ORG-004). SSO domain auto-join requires a verified domain matched exactly (DV-ORG-005). Every membership change is written to Record History with actor and transaction id. Absent: generated Organization, Membership and Invitation models, Organization.Members(), Organization.Invitations() and the accept-invitation page; DV-ORG-001 as a build error; reading dartvel.organizations (roles, personalTenants, seats); DV.Auth.currentMembership and context.membership on the Flutter facade, with core offering only currentMembership(userId); per-organization SAML or LDAP binding, and any proof of domain ownership, since markDomainVerified records a claim without checking it; a Studio view of organizations, members, invitations and role history; seat and last-owner locking across processes, which would need a database constraint; purging a closed organization after its grace period. Where the section and the code disagree: the section says an invitation is redeemed by whoever holds it, but it is bound to the invited address so a forwarded link grants nothing; single use is the token machinery's guarantee only with a shared token store, so the invitation row is deleted as a second guard; the policy example's @DVPolicy() takes no resource type and uses context.membership, neither of which exists; the section writes DV.Auth.currentMembership as a getter, but core has no current user; seats: paid has no key for the counting rule the section says is declared; the section does not say what a former owner becomes, and they are demoted to the second declared role; no DV-ORG code covers a refused seat; closing is a closed_at column rather than the record table's soft delete, so the clock can be injected, and DV-ORG-004 is listed at info but also covers refusals.

Guarded routes are excluded from sitemap.xml now, and were not until this was written: the sitemap was built by scraping every path: literal out of the generated router with a regular expression, which cannot see the redirect guard block below the path it just matched, so /admin and everything behind a folder guard was published to crawlers. The specification says private routes are excluded by default and it was not true. The generator now writes dartvelGuardedRoutes into router.g.dart and the build reads it. Per-route sitemap tuning is built now, and was not: dartvel.seo.sitemap.enabled, .exclude and .defaults were documented and parsed nowhere, and DVPageSitemap and DVSitemapChangeFrequency appeared in the specification example and in no Dart file, so every route was written out as a <loc> and nothing else. A page tunes its own entry through the annotation and the project sets the rest, a page overriding the defaults field by field so that saying only that it changes daily keeps the project priority. A route neither mentions stays a bare URL: a priority nobody asked for says the same thing as none, in more bytes, and a crawler cannot tell it was invented. A priority outside 0 to 1 and a changefreq outside the seven words sitemaps.org defines are refused rather than clamped or dropped, because a crawler discards the whole url element when a child will not validate. exclude patterns take the section index with the section, since publishing the front door of a hidden area discloses what the pattern was written to hide, and enabled: false stops robots.txt naming a file the build did not write. Adding the argument found a worse thing than the gap it filled: it is a call, and every parser of the page annotation here was written to stop at the first close parenthesis, so a page carrying it was not discovered at all -- no route in the router, no node in the project graph, on a build that succeeded -- and a policy written after it fell outside the captured text and was not read, which generates a page that declared a guard open to everybody. Parentheses are counted now, string literals and comments excluded, and the example application declares the annotation so the real generator reads it and a compiler reads what it emitted. A module mount carrying sitemap: exclude is left out now, and was not: the key was parsed, reached the mount and was written into the generated route index, and the sitemap writer never asked -- so every route of a module mounted to stay out went into the parent sitemap.xml anyway. The same failure as the guarded routes above, in the one place a comment said it was handled. The routes are still answered and still redirected to, because the exclusion is about being advertised rather than reachable and dropping the redirect would break a link somebody already has, so the sitemap and the web server manifest ask different functions. Also absent from the guarded list: module mount routes, which carry that key instead, and generated model public pages, which are public by annotation.

Nothing this section lists is unbuilt. Background sync is exercised in a real browser: the generated worker keeps an IndexedDB outbox of same-origin non-GET requests that could not be sent, answers the caller with a 202 and X-Dartvel-Queued, and replays the outbox in order when the network is back, stopping at the first failure and one replay at a time (a sync event and the client's replay message arriving together sent everything twice until they shared one in-flight promise). dartvel capture pwa-sync loads the built worker in Chrome, takes the server away, makes a POST, brings the server back and expects the POST to arrive; the Runtime verification workflow runs it against the site's own build on every push, and it is what found the double replay. Everything else the section lists is built: manifest, viewport, service worker, offline page, install prompt, and icon generation from web/icon.png through the CLI own PNG codec. The install prompt had two defects in one path until they were found by asking which enum values nothing produces. DVInstallOutcome.dismissed was produced by nothing: show returned a static that only a test seam ever set, so a browser reported accepted whatever the person at the screen chose, and then marked the application installed -- which hides the affordance, so an application somebody declined could never be installed from inside it again. And the binding that calls the browser own prompt was written and called by nothing, so tapping Install opened no dialog at all: the feature flipped two flags and returned. The outcome comes from the browser now, through the bridge like every other platform call, and the binding waits for it, since prompt only opens the dialog and the choice arrives on userChoice afterwards. Anything other than the word accepted is a dismissal, because treating an unrecognised third answer as acceptance would install nothing and say it had. The tests that existed set the outcome themselves and asserted it came back, which proves the seam rather than the path, and is why this survived

Built: the patch path, end to end on Android. DVShorebirdUpdates.register, which the generated runtime calls, binds updates.check, updates.apply and updates.rollback to the Shorebird updater's C API, looked up in the process on Android and iOS and called on its own isolate; check reports a downloadable or waiting patch, apply installs it for the next launch and throws with the updater's message on failure, and rollback runs the check that applies a published rollback. The runtime core is built in dartvel_core and tested, and nothing in a real application reaches it yet. Not built: nothing derives the contract from a project, because the project graph records no parameter types, return types or enums, and no dartvel build step runs the lock check, so DV-PROTO-001 and DV-PROTO-004 fail no real build; there is no command to bump the protocol; the generated client does not send the header or run the handshake before a page's first call; the generated backend neither decides per request nor exposes a handshake route; DV.Protocol, DV.Protocol.state and DV.Upgrade.required do not exist; there is no OTA-first upgrade flow and no generated upgrade page; adapters are applied from the lock's contracts rather than emitted as reviewable source; enum fallbacks, field renames and declared adapters exist only as runtime Dart objects, with no annotation; dartvel analyze does not report DV-PROTO-006; monitoring has no per-protocol session histogram, so dartvel compatibility-check --against takes one as an export through --histogram and refuses without it; and since no command writes the lockfile, compatibility-check refuses every project whose dartvel.protocol.lock was not recorded by hand; the sequencing with Schema Evolution (DV-SCHEMA-005, DV-RELEASE-005) is not connected. Where the section and the code disagree: a version cannot be both derived from the project graph and fail the build for not being incremented, so the shape is derived and the number lives in the lockfile, which the section neither names nor formats; the section does not say when a version's age starts, and it is measured from the release of its successor; the three-result handshake has no state for a client ahead of the backend; callers without a protocol header (raw routes, webhooks) are not covered and pass through as unversioned; the safe-change rules are applied more strictly than written (any removal, widening as well as narrowing, and a new required model field are lossy); DVCrashContext.protocolVersion is a String while the protocol is an integer; DV-PROTO-004 is worded as a requested adaptation, but nothing requests one, so it fires whenever a lossy change exists in the window.

Logs, profiling, performance analysis, error reporting, structured diagnostics with fix-recommendations, structured AI-readable logs, and the DV.log / DV.ObservabilityAndLogging.event API the spec names are all unbuilt -- there is no log sink anywhere in the runtime, so nothing an application logs goes anywhere. What is real: DVMetrics renders Prometheus text exposition and GET /metrics serves it, DVHealth backs GET /health with real checks on a deadline, and tracing carries W3C Trace Context across the request boundary with sampling decided from the trace id alone -- a per-process decision samples a four-service request with probability p^4, which reads as tracing being on and finding nothing. Spans are captured into an in-process ring buffer, served at /_dartvel/traces when diagnostics endpoints are on and nowhere else: there is no OTLP exporter, so no span reaches a collector. Distributed Tracing has the full account. dartvel logs, dartvel traces and dartvel metrics used to paper over this with hardcoded sample output; dartvel metrics now fetches the real GET /metrics endpoint and reports plainly when no server answers or nothing has been recorded, and dartvel logs / dartvel traces now say outright that they have nothing to read instead of inventing a trace id or a log line

Nothing reaches a collector: the exporter interface exists with in-memory, ring-buffer and fanout implementations, and there is no OTLP exporter, so spans leave the process only through /_dartvel/traces when diagnostics endpoints are on. The only span most requests have is the request itself -- dvTraced is the sole place that starts one, so there are no spans for database queries, outbound HTTP, queue publish and consume, transactions or AI calls. Trace context does not travel in the job envelope, so nothing links a job back to the request that enqueued it. There are no client spans and no ingest for them. Span attribute limits and the maximum span duration are unimplemented. dartvel traces reads nothing but the local buffer. The DV-TRACE codes are registered meanings and nothing emits one yet. What is real: W3C traceparent parsing and serialization, spans with attributes, errors and status, a sampler that decides from the trace id so every service in a trace agrees without coordinating, the HTTP middleware that joins or starts a trace and returns the traceparent on the response, and the trace id on every log line.

Generated factories now carry a sequence, so two create() calls produce two records rather than one repeated identifier, with createMany for list-shaped tests and resetSequence so a snapshot assertion is repeatable. Every test mode resolves, and a mode with no tests reports that it has none and where it looked

Algolia is exercised only against a recorded transport: it is a hosted service with no local server, so its request shape is pinned by unit tests rather than by a round trip. Meilisearch and OpenSearch are verified live in CI.

Built: DVSemanticIndex in dartvel_core. A save enqueues an embedding job on DVQueues and embeds nothing inline; long fields are chunked and a record comes back once with the chunk, offset and field that matched; DVEmbedder and DVAIEmbedder refuse vectors of the wrong length; DVVectorAdapter with DVInMemoryVectorAdapter as the reference (exact cosine, real filtering); keyword (default), semantic and hybrid modes; the tenant and where conditions pushed into the vector query and every loaded row re-checked against tenant, conditions and canSee, with a bounded refill (DV-SEMANTIC-005); no default embedder (DV-SEMANTIC-001); generations named by embedder, dimensions and chunking, rebuilt alongside the old one with writes landing in both and queries answered by the old one (DV-SEMANTIC-003, DVSemanticRebuildError); resumable backfill with a checkpoint; DV-SEMANTIC-002 for a scoped model on an adapter that cannot filter; absentRecords() for dead-lettered embeddings (DV-SEMANTIC-004); indexing and queries charged to a DVMeters counter with DVSemanticBudgetExceeded before anything is embedded (DV-SEMANTIC-007); retrieve without sensitive fields, which cannot be embedded. Absent: no @DVModel.searchableField(semantic:) and no generated Model.Search.query(mode:) or retrieve, so the index is wired by hand; the dartvel.search.semantic pubspec block is not read; no pgvector, Meilisearch, OpenSearch or Algolia vector adapter; backfill is a resumable call, not a rate-limited durable job, and Studio shows no progress; no on-device index and no DV-SEMANTIC-006; canSee is a callback, not DV.Auth.authorization policies; retrieve is not wired into AI features. Where the section cannot be followed as written: DV-SEMANTIC-001 and 002 are runtime construction errors, because nothing at build time can see a semantic field yet; the queue has no dead-letter hook and a handler sees only its payload, so DV-SEMANTIC-004 is reported when absentRecords() is called rather than when the job dead-letters; an opaque canSee cannot be pushed into an adapter's query, so a policy-scoped model always takes the refill path.

App-store and Play Billing purchases belong to Purchases and Entitlements, whose server-side ledger, verification and notification core is built and whose store bindings and real store adapters are not. DVStripeBillingProvider.verifyEvent checks the signature for subscription and dispute webhooks alike; Commerce refunds and lost disputes revoke grants only through DVLocalBillingProvider, because Stripe and Paddle keep webhook-driven grants in memory with no revoke API. Stripe and Paddle are built: checkout for a plan, webhooks that grant and revoke entitlements from subscription status, trials, and usage meters. Each webhook is believed only when its own signature scheme matches in constant time within five minutes (Stripe's t=/v1= over 't.payload', Paddle's ts=/h1= over 'ts:payload', and each provider refuses the other's), with the key never echoed in an error and a sandbox Paddle key routed to the sandbox host by the key itself. Nothing here has been exercised against either service; the tests inject the HTTP and the clock. Four things were declared and read by nothing, which is this section's whole history. BillingPlan.priceMinorUnits and BillingPlan.currency were required constructor arguments no provider looked at: both took prices[plan.id] and sent the customer to whatever that identifier costs, so the example's pricing page could render 40.00 while the checkout charged 49.00 after a dashboard edit, and no code was in a position to notice. Checkout now reads the price from the provider first and refuses on any difference in amount or currency, before a session exists rather than after, so a mismatch leaves no orphan checkout that could still be handed to somebody; a tiered Stripe price reports no unit amount and is refused rather than skipped, since treating nothing-to-compare as agreement waves through the exact case. Reading a price needs a GET, so the fetch typedef became DVBillingFetch and carries the method. Trials were in the feature list and on nothing: Stripe takes the plan's trialDays with the session, and only when there is one, because a zero would silently cancel a trial configured on the price; Paddle keeps trials on the price and so checks both directions, since a promised fortnight the price does not give produces a support ticket while a trial nobody declared gives a week away per signup and produces nothing. Usage-based billing existed as two words in the specification. DVUsageMeter names what an application counts, the provider's event name is provider configuration, and recording against an unconfigured meter is an error rather than a no-op -- usage counted by the application and billed by nobody is the failure worth the check. The idempotency key is required because Dartvel's own queues redeliver and a provider counts one meter event per identifier, so a generated default would differ on the retry and double a bill. And the customer key: every provider stored grants under customer.toString(), which for an ordinary Dart object is the constant Instance of 'User', so passing the logged-in user -- what a parameter typed Object invites -- filed every user under one key and one subscription unlocked the plan for everybody, with no symptom except revenue that never arrived. An identity is now required, stated by DVBillingCustomer or by a String, a number or a meaningful toString, and the default toString is an ArgumentError naming the type. One behaviour bug went with them: both providers applied webhooks in arrival order, and Stripe does not guarantee one while a retried Paddle notification lands behind whatever was sent while it was failing, so a stale active behind a cancellation handed a cancelled customer their entitlement back -- signed, genuine, answered with a 200. Each provider now tracks the newest applied event per subscription, strictly older is stale and still acknowledged, and DVBillingWebhookResult.stale says why nothing changed. Invoices list now, through DV.Billing and both providers, with the amount as a DVMoney rather than an integer -- 4000 without its currency renders as forty dollars, four thousand yen or forty of whatever the page assumed -- and a status nothing recognises maps to unknown rather than to paid, since an unpaid invoice shown as settled is a bill nobody chases. A row that comes back for another customer is dropped: the query filters at the provider, so one that does not means the filter did not apply, and rendering it shows somebody another person's billing history on a page that looks entirely normal. Still absent: Usage reporting to Paddle, which bills metered items by adjusting subscription item quantities rather than through anything meter-shaped; it throws rather than accepting a record it would drop. Entitlements live in provider memory, so a restart loses every grant a webhook made and a second process cannot see them -- it fails closed, denying access rather than giving it, but a paying customer is denied until the next webhook. The webhook endpoint is not generated. Verification is reachable now -- DVBillingWebhookReceiver names the contract, each provider says which header it signs under, and DV.Billing.handleWebhook takes the request headers and finds it whatever case they arrive in, so a route no longer has to downcast or write the HMAC comparison itself, which is the version that gets simplified until an unsigned subscription activated is accepted. What is still missing is the route: the application declares the path and hands the payload over, so the specification's generated backend function with signature validation is a facade method a handler calls, not something the generator emits. Entitlement checks are not wired into policies or into any generated UI guard. Conversion rates are set by the application and no provider supplies them, and localisation does not yet choose a display currency on its own.

Built: the server half. DVPurchases verifies a receipt through a DVStoreAdapter and writes a grant only from the store's answer, refusing with DV-PURCHASE-003 when the store refuses, and refusing a receipt bought under another account's token or a purchase already held by another customer; an unreachable store is not a refusal. Store notifications are signature-checked by the adapter, claimed by id so a replay is recognised, and ordered per purchase so a late answer is stale while two notifications in one millisecond both apply; an undeclared product is DV-PURCHASE-004. Play acknowledgement happens inside DV.transaction, where a failure restores the previous grant and releases the claim so the store's retry applies, and checkAcknowledgements retries inside the window and reports DV-PURCHASE-006 past it. Access ends at notAfter, the paid period plus the store's grace; device snapshots always carry notAfter and refuse past it with DV-PURCHASE-005, and a purchase that never expires gets a configurable seven-day snapshot lifetime. Restore checks each receipt on the server and reports refusals per receipt. onChange fires after commit with what was granted and revoked and carries revokedAt, which separates a refund or chargeback from a lapse; DVCommerce.storeRevocations consumes it, reversing only revocations. Store prices are shown unconverted or not at all (DV-PURCHASE-007). Store milliunits and micros become integer minor units exactly or are refused. Routing is a DVStorePolicy adapter with conservative Apple and Play defaults. The ledger has memory and database implementations, a fake store adapter signs its notifications, and DV.Purchases is on the Flutter facade. Not built: real App Store and Play adapters (Apple JWS certificate-chain verification, App Store Server API, Play Developer API, Pub/Sub push authentication, credentials from Secrets); the StoreKit and Play Billing client bindings, so DV.Purchases.buy and the device half of restore() do not exist; DVModel.billable is still a bool, so @DVModel(billable: DVBillable.digital(...)) does not compile and nothing generates products from models; DV-PURCHASE-001, 002 and 008 as build errors (002 is thrown at run time); the generated notification endpoints; generated entitlement models and their sync to devices, so the ledger is a server table read through DVPurchases; the dartvel.purchases.policy pubspec setting; the dartvel dev store sandboxes; dartvel doctor --purchases; consumable products; a scheduled acknowledgement sweep; the in-memory database adapter does not enforce the primary key. Where the section and the code disagree: widening DVModel.billable from bool to DVBillable is a public signature change the generator also reads as text, so it is not done; DVContext carries no request, so acceptNotification takes body and headers as named arguments; a notification for a purchase nobody has verified cannot be attributed, because the account token is one-way, so it grants nothing until the receipt is verified; the section defines notAfter only for subscriptions; DV-PURCHASE-004 is also logged when a verified receipt names an undeclared product; purchases run their transactions isolated, which was needed while the transaction runner held its active transaction in a static and let concurrent requests join each other; the runner now scopes a transaction to the flow that opened it.

The runtime is built (per-tenant counters and gauges in memory or DV.Database, idempotency keys required and deduplicated across periods, fixed and entitlement limits with block, throttle and allowAndBill serialised per tenant and meter, notifyAt thresholds announced once, half-open billing periods with grace and late placement, level limits such as seats, and period reporting to DVBillingProvider under a stable key with a durable retry queue and a reconcile that changes nothing). Absent: @DVMeters and @DVMeter annotations and generated Meters.* accessors; meters instrumented from the project graph (function invocations, storage bytes, queue jobs, AI tokens); DV-METER-001 as a build error; the request and job runtimes do not set DVMeters.withIdempotencyKey; notifyAt is not wired to Notifications; no scheduled period-close job; no provider-supplied billing period; throttle reports but does not delay; hard limits are serialised per process only, and the unique key that stops duplicate records across instances is not enforced by the in-memory adapter; dartvel meters list, usage and reconcile; the Studio usage view; the ClickHouse path.

sections.section: Commerce: Tax, Promotions, Disputes and Payouts
sections.absent: Built, in dartvel_core, tested against fakes and never against a live provider. Tax: DVTax asks a DVTaxProvider and checks the answer before it is charged; a provider refusal, any failure, or an answer whose currency, lines or line sum disagree with the request refuses the sale with DV-COMMERCE-002, and nothing resolves to zero. Only an outage may use the declared offline table, a sale priced from it is marked for re-rating with DV-COMMERCE-001, past asOf plus staleAfter the sale is refused with DV-COMMERCE-007, and a provider refusal is never overruled by the table. DVTaxTable, which ships no rates, is the reference for the rounding rules: exact decimal rate strings with JSON numbers refused, halfUp or halfEven as declared, line or document scope, document rounding allocated by largest remainder so lines always sum to the total, tax extracted from inclusive prices, and a per-jurisdiction discount basis. Promotions: each declares group or exclusive stacking, at most one applies per group and an exclusive one combines with nothing, choosing the largest discount; percentages are rounded once and allocated exactly; eligibility is a DVPromotionPolicy asked on the server, refused with DV-COMMERCE-003; global and per-customer limits hold under concurrency, through a memory ledger that checks and records in one step and DVDatabasePromotionLedger's compare-and-set, tested on SQLite. Sales and refunds: DVCommerce.charge redeems promotions, taxes the discounted amount, records the sale, grants entitlements and captures last through a DVPaymentGateway, so a failure at any step leaves nothing behind; one order id captures once and a capture of a different amount is reversed. DVCommerce.refund reserves against what was captured atomically, reverses tax cumulatively, revokes entitlements on a full refund unless another sale still grants them, and credits through the gateway last; a failure is fully undone, and a compensation that also fails is DV-COMMERCE-004. Store refunds follow the same rule through DVCommerce.storeRevocations on DVPurchases.onChange, acting only when revokedAt is set. Payouts: DVPayoutSplit takes a platform fee and splits the rest by weight so the split always sums to what was collected; DVPayouts credits a sale once, reverses every share cumulatively on refunds and lost disputes, reserves the balance atomically for a payout, transfers under a caller-named idempotency key, excludes sales on hold, and holds an account not verified with payouts enabled without a transfer (DV-COMMERCE-006). Disputes: DVDisputes accepts Stripe charge.dispute events through DVStripeBillingProvider.verifyEvent, applies each once, ignores an older one, keeps a deadline, evidence checklist and timeline, reports DV-COMMERCE-005 once per threshold, holds the sale's payout shares while open, revokes entitlements and reverses shares when lost, and releases them when won; a delivery that fails part-way rolls back so the provider's retry applies. Not built: DV.Tax, DV.Commerce and DV.Disputes on the Flutter facade; Stripe Tax, Avalara or any other real tax adapter; the pubspec reader and generation for dartvel.tax.offline; re-rating of marked sales; provider-issued invoices and customer copies; tax rates by component or postal code; tax-transaction reversal at the provider; promotions as generated models and @DVPolicy(Coupon) wiring; database ledgers for sales, refunds, payouts and disputes (memory only); a real payment gateway adapter; resuming an interrupted refund; Stripe Connect or any other connected-account adapter; onboarding state and identity documents as sensitive model fields with retention and erasure; dispute fees; disputes from providers other than Stripe; evidence submission (deliberately absent); generated webhook endpoints; a scheduled deadline sweep. Where the section and the code disagree: jurisdiction is resolved from a DVTaxAddress value rather than an address model; the section does not say what a dispute does to entitlements or payouts, so holding shares while open, reversing them on loss and revoking entitlements on loss or open are this implementation's choices; DV-COMMERCE-004 is also reported when a store refund's reversal fails; each jurisdiction declares one discount basis rather than one per discount funder; entitlements are revoked through DVEntitlementGrants, implemented only over DVLocalBillingProvider, because Stripe and Paddle keep webhook-driven grants in memory with no revoke API.

Nothing this section asks for is unbuilt. Switch control and hardware-key navigation are built: DVSwitchControl steps focus through a page with one key and activates with another, wrapping, with auto-scan for a single-switch user; DVHardwareKeys maps a remote's D-pad and select onto focus and activation; DVAccessibilityToggle is the attract-route toggle behind DV.Accessibility.switchControl; DVAccessibilityKeys.isExempt names the keys a kiosk hardware-key block must let through, which is the rule Kiosk Mode's native enforcement consults when it exists (that enforcement is Kiosk Mode's gap, not this section's). Waivers are built: dartvel.accessibility.waivers names a route, a rule the audit has (or * for the page) and a reason -- no reason, no waiver -- and a waiver that matches nothing is reported so it does not sit in the file for ever. The release gate is built: dartvel build web audits the semantics tree a real browser produced -- what a screen reader is actually handed -- and fails on a link or control with no accessible name, an empty heading, a page with no headings or no level 1, and a heading level skipped going down; on its first run against the site it found /features going h1 to h3. Generated tables have keyboard navigation, focus that survives a sort, and per-cell announcements naming the column and the row position. Contrast is checked against WCAG ratios and tap targets against Material's minimum

Drag and drop is built: a window accepts drops of the kinds it says it takes -- files, text, or both -- and each drop arrives as what was dropped and where, an empty drop or one after stop reaching nobody; on Linux the toplevel becomes a GTK drop target whose drag-data-received payload is read by its type, so one path serves a file manager's uri-list and a browser's text, and what GTK already took is kept and given back on stop. The uri-list is parsed as RFC 2483 has it, percent escapes decoded and a URI that is not a file left out. Exercised under Xvfb against real GTK, with a real GtkSelectionData built through the clipboard and the signal emitted the way a drop emits it. The tray is built on Linux, as the protocol has it rather than as a picture: a StatusNotifierItem and its com.canonical.dbusmenu menu are exported on the session bus and registered with the shell's StatusNotifierWatcher, which is how a modern desktop is told about a tray icon -- no XEmbed, nothing deprecated, no GTK. The suite stands up a watcher of its own the way a shell would, reads the item's title, icon, status, category and menu path back over the bus, walks the menu layout, sends an Event the way a click arrives and sees it reach the application by id, and watches the name leave the bus on hide. What a runner cannot check is the pixels, and nothing claims them: a desktop with no watcher leaves the item exported and says so. Drag and drop is built on all three desktops. On Windows it is an OLE drop target: a COM object with a vtable of seven functions, registered with RegisterDragDrop, reading CF_HDROP for the files a file manager drags and CF_UNICODETEXT for a browser's text, with the POINTL each method takes declared as the eight bytes it travels in rather than as a struct by value in a callback; the live suite gives it a real IDataObject -- the clipboard's, which is the same interface Explorer hands over, carrying a DROPFILES built the way a file manager builds one -- and calls Drop the way OLE calls it. On macOS the window's content view is registered as a dragging destination and the two dragging methods are added to its class at runtime, reading the whole file list a file manager writes rather than the first of it; the live suite checks that reading against a real pasteboard, files and text, and that a process with no window is refused and says so. What a runner cannot do is drag from another application: on both, the drag is not claimed and everything the drop does is. The file associations register at run time on all three desktops, which is the half an installer normally does and which an application copied into place has nobody to do: DV.Platform.associations writes the user's own desktop entry, MIME package and default-applications list on Linux -- files, so it works on a kiosk with no desktop session -- the per-user half of the registry under HKCU\\Software\\Classes on Windows, and on macOS registers the running bundle with LaunchServices and claims the types its Info.plist declares. Per-user everywhere, because the machine-wide equivalents need administrator rights and an API that asked for them is one most applications could not call. The refusals are stated rather than swallowed: a macOS process with no bundle has nothing to register and says so, and macOS has no public call to stop being the default for a type, so unregistering hands it back to whoever held it before and says when it cannot. Registering nothing, or a type with no extensions, is refused where it is called -- every platform matches a file by its extension. The launch handover is now exercised on both, since the single-instance lock's two-process suite runs on those runners as well as on Linux. The device and fleet APIs are built on Linux: the capability manifest (a provisioned or generated-and-kept id; cores, memory, kernel, display, touch, and the bindings actually registered rather than the names declared), health as a verdict with uptime, load, memory, disk and temperature behind it from procfs and sysfs, a watchdog that restarts on a missed heartbeat and tells systemd through sd_notify so WatchdogSec= works, restart-loop detection reported as DV-KIOSK-008 instead of restarting again, provisioning kept across starts, and a diagnostics bundle. File associations and app links are built on Linux: dartvel build linux writes the desktop entry (Exec with %U, MimeType for every association and x-scheme-handler for every scheme) and shared-mime-info XML for the types the app introduces from dartvel.desktop in pubspec.yaml, and the generated runtime opens what the app was launched with -- DVAppLaunch takes the single-instance lock, maps each argument to a route without trusting it as one, opens it as an external window request, and a later launch hands its arguments to the first and ends. Printing is built on Linux: DV.Platform.Printing draws pictures onto pages through GtkPrintOperation, to a PDF with no dialog (verified under Xvfb, poppler reading the page count back) or through the print dialog. System dialogs are built on Linux: DV.Platform.Dialogs opens, saves, chooses a folder and shows a message through GTK, verified under Xvfb by a seam that answers the dialog from GTK's own loop the way a person would. Built on Linux and tested under Xvfb: global shortcuts, grabbed through XGrabKey on a pump isolate's own X connection with XTest pressing the keys in the test; and the application menu, built as a real GtkMenuBar into the toplevel window with the view reparented beneath it, read back through GTK and activated by id. Both have the Dart side everywhere -- DVAccelerator parsed once, DVShortcuts and DVMenus delivering by id. Built since on Windows and macOS, each exercised on its own runner by the live suite: global shortcuts (RegisterHotKey on a pump thread of its own that delivers WM_HOTKEY by id, proven by posting the message Win32 sends and by a synthesised press where the session takes input; Carbon's RegisterEventHotKey with one handler dispatching by id, registration and the refusal of a duplicate proven, delivery said to need the application's event loop); the application menu (a Win32 menu bar on the process's window, subclassed so WM_COMMAND is dispatched by id, proven on a window the test owns; NSMenu as NSApp's main menu with every item targeting one runtime-defined Objective-C object, read back and activated through AppKit); the tray icon with its menu delivered by id (Shell_NotifyIcon on the process's window, refused where the session has no notification area; an NSStatusBar item sharing the menu's target under a second action) -- the Dart side of the tray now delivers a chosen item to onSelected and the selected stream; and the device APIs, the shared runtime reading through Win32 and through sysctl, Mach and getloadavg, real numbers from each runner. Multi-window and window state persistence are recorded under Multi-Window Startup is measured: the framework marks the phases it goes through -- configure, the generated registrations, the platform bindings, and the first frame, measured after the frame because a router that is built is not a screen that is up -- from one monotonic clock, and the report is the same shape every run, so two runs of the same build are comparable line by line and a budget names the phase that went over. The running application publishes it beside its live window list and the diagnostics bundle carries it, so a fleet asking why a device is slow to come up has the answer without sending anybody to the device; CI reads it back from the Linux run. Boot-to-app packaging is built for the eLinux target: autostart, restartOnFailure and a declared watchdog become the systemd unit the bundle installs, and the generated unit is handed to systemd-analyze in CI, so a directive systemd would reject is found at build time rather than at boot. Update channels for kiosk and device fleets are built: DV.Updates.check and apply take a channel, a staged rollout decides from the device and the version so a device asked twice is answered the same and a device held back can say so, and kiosk.updates decides when a kiosk may apply what it found -- inside a maintenance window that may run past midnight, only with staff present, or immediately, with a required update resetting the session instead of waiting. The serial port is built on Linux: DV.Platform.device.serial lists the ports udev keeps stable names for, opens one in raw mode at a speed the kernel has a constant for, reads with a timeout that survives the signals a Dart VM raises, writes, and closes -- exercised against a real pseudo-terminal in CI, where the bytes, the termios speed and the timeout are checked on real file descriptors. The USB bus is read on Linux: DV.Platform.device.usb lists what is plugged in, out of sysfs, with each device's vendor and product ids as hex, what it says about itself, and where it sits on the bus -- interfaces are not counted as devices, a device with no readable id is not reported with a wrong one, and a bus that is not there is no devices rather than an error. Talking to a device is built now as well, through usbfs rather than libusb -- libusb is a dependency to ship, a licence to carry and a shared object to find on a device that may be read-only, and the interface underneath it is four ioctls. The care goes into those numbers, because they are computed rather than named: one packs a direction, the size of the struct it takes, a type letter and an index into thirty-two bits, and getting any of the four wrong still produces a valid ioctl, so the kernel runs a different call or answers ENOTTY and neither says which field was wrong. They come from one rule and are checked against what the kernel headers define, including the direction bits, where read is 2 and write is 1 -- the opposite of the order anybody says them in. What the errors mean is the other half, and on a device node none of them is general: a permission error is a udev rule nobody has written rather than a fault in the calling code, and somebody handed errno 13 goes and rereads their own transfer loop; a busy interface is a kernel driver already holding it, usbhid on anything that looks like a keyboard, which needs detaching and never yields to a retry; a stall is the device refusing the request rather than the transfer failing; and a timeout is a device that may answer next time, which a kiosk told otherwise stops asking. Callers hold a handle rather than a file descriptor, since a descriptor is shared with every other open file in the process. Closing releases every claimed interface first, because a descriptor closed with one still claimed leaves the kernel driver unbound until the device is replugged -- so the next run finds hardware that no longer works and nothing that says why. Bluetooth is read on Linux through BlueZ on the bus: DV.Platform.Bluetooth answers whether any adapter's radio is on, lists the adapters, and lists every device the machine knows about -- paired, connected or merely seen -- with the name it has given, its signal strength and the adapter that knows it. A device that has never said its name is still reported, because dropping it would tell a fleet a paired thing is not there; and a machine with no BlueZ running says so rather than answering with the empty list that means nothing is paired. Exercised in CI against a BlueZ of the suite's own on the session bus. Pairing, connecting and forgetting are built too, which is the half a fleet needs: a reader that has come unpaired in a lobby is otherwise a kiosk somebody has to drive to. Almost none of it is a plain call, because BlueZ's worst answers look like ordinary failures. Pairing something already paired is an error whose right answer is that the device is paired, since a caller told otherwise retries forever against a reader that works. Pair with no agent registered comes back as an authentication cancellation, which reads as a pairing problem and is not one -- there is nobody standing at a headless device to answer a passkey -- so it is said in those words rather than sending whoever reads it to check the radio, the range and the battery first. Connecting something unpaired is refused before the radio is used at all, so it says to pair first instead of leaving a timeout to be diagnosed. Disconnecting something already disconnected is the outcome that was asked for. And unpairing is the adapter's method rather than the device's, so the adapter the device says it is on is the one asked -- on a machine with two, asking the other removes nothing and answers success. A device is named by address, because that is what is on the label, and matched without regard to case, because BlueZ spells its own paths in upper case and a literal comparison reports no such device for one sitting on the desk. NFC is read on Linux through neard: DV.Platform.NFC answers whether there is a reader that could read something now -- a powered adapter, not merely a present one -- and what is written on the tag currently on it. No tag is null rather than an error, because that is the normal state of a reader nobody has tapped, while no neard at all says so: the difference between 'hold your card nearer' and 'this unit's reader is not running'. Exercised in CI against a neard of the suite's own. Writing a tag is built too, which is the half a kiosk needs to hand somebody a card -- a locker key, a visitor badge, a pallet label. Almost every way it goes wrong still looks like it worked, so almost none of it is a straight call: a URI is written as a URI record rather than as text that looks like one, because a link in a text record reads back as exactly those characters and does nothing when a phone touches it; the scheme is matched against a list rather than taken from anything with a colon in it, so a value like Type2:something stays text instead of becoming a URI no reader can follow; every text record carries a language code, which NDEF requires and some readers show an empty record without; an empty value is refused, since a tag written with nothing on it cannot be told from one never written; and a read-only tag is refused before the write with the reason, because somebody told only that it failed presents the same locked card again. What neard itself says when the chip refuses -- the tag was taken off the reader, the record did not fit -- is passed through rather than flattened. Exercised against the suite's own neard, which records the dictionary it was handed, so what actually reaches the tag is checked rather than that a call was made. Clipboard and selection integration was the one item on this section's own list that nothing had claimed, and it was worse than unclaimed. A copy reported success and put nothing on the clipboard any other application could read. On X11 a copy does not hand bytes to the server; it makes the process the owner of the CLIPBOARD selection, and every other application that wants the text asks this process and waits for an answer that comes out of the GLib main loop. A Dart process runs no such loop, so a Dartvel copy did not merely fail to share -- it took the clipboard away from the whole session, and every paste anywhere hung until the application asking gave up. Nothing caught it because GTK answers the owner out of its own cache: reading the value back inside the process that wrote it returns the text whether or not a byte ever left. It is checked from a second process now, with its own connection to the display, which is the only thing that can tell the difference, and a write starts a pump that drains the main context. Under a real Flutter run the embedder already owns that context on the platform thread and the pump does nothing, which is right, because there the embedder is already answering. The selection half came with it: the PRIMARY selection, where highlighted text goes and a middle click pastes it, separate from what Ctrl+C put on the clipboard, through DV.Platform.clipboard.readSelection and writeSelection. Linux only, and that is a fact about the other platforms rather than a hole -- Windows and macOS have one clipboard and nothing that answers a middle click, so they leave the binding unregistered and say so instead of aliasing it onto copy and quietly destroying whatever the user had copied. A kiosk that locks the clipboard locks the selection too, that being the other way text somebody else left behind gets into one. The refusals arrive as failed futures rather than synchronous throws, which paste got wrong: the signature says Future, so a caller writing paste().catchError(...) never saw the kiosk refusal and it left their frame. The serial port is built on macOS too, and not by copying: macOS's termios has eight-byte flag words where Linux has four, twenty control characters where Linux has thirty-two, and speeds that are the numbers themselves rather than small indices, so a structure carried across would read the wrong fields and set a speed nobody asked for on a port that looks like it is working. Ports are the /dev/cu.* doors rather than /dev/tty.*, because opening the tty door waits for a carrier a three-wire cable never asserts. Exercised against a pseudo-terminal on the macOS runner. The serial port is built on Windows too, which is the third desktop and the last one it was missing from. Ports come from HKLM\HARDWARE\DEVICEMAP\SERIALCOMM, the list Windows itself keeps and the one every serial library reads -- walking the setup device tree instead finds ports that exist and cannot be opened -- and the value under each key is the COM name a caller opens rather than the driver path it is filed under. The list is sorted by number and not as text, so COM10 comes after COM9 rather than before it, and a value that is not a COM name is left out, because that key carries virtual devices on some machines and handing one back produces an open that fails for a reason nobody asked about. Every port is opened through the device-namespace path, not only the ones above COM9: the prefix is legal for all of them, and a rule with an exception at nine is a bug waiting for somebody's tenth adapter. The port is opened exclusively, which is the only way Windows will open one, configured through a DCB with SetCommState and given read timeouts with SetCommTimeouts. An open that fails says which port and why in words -- not there, or held by another program, which are different problems with different fixes -- rather than a Win32 number somebody has to go and look up. The parts that can be wrong quietly are string work and are held to account on any host; CreateFileW itself runs on the Windows runner, where the case worth proving is a machine with no serial hardware at all: enumerating is an empty list rather than an error, and a port that is not there is refused by name. The device APIs come up without a desktop, which is the machine they were written for: the fleet APIs, the serial port, the USB bus, Bluetooth and NFC are registered before the desktop libraries are opened and whether or not they open, because an eLinux kiosk with DRM and no X server has all of them and none of them touches X11. A headless registration claims no clipboard, no window and no tray, because a binding that answers where there is nothing to answer with is worse than one that is absent. Three more options were declared, documented, and read by nothing, which is this section's recurring fault rather than three unrelated ones. A window that said it took files only still handed the application a URL dragged out of a browser: the GTK target list is a request to the desktop and not a guarantee, and the Linux handler read the type off whatever arrived and delivered it, while Windows and macOS had gated the same thing since they were written. The old test asserted the target list, which is the shape of the request; the new ones drop the wrong kind on a real window and check that nobody hears about it. File associations rewrote the desktop entry and the MIME package from nothing on every call, so a second register threw away the first call's types and unregistering one type deleted the entry for all of them -- while mimeapps.list stayed selective and went on naming this application as the handler, leaving the desktop sending files to an entry that was not on disk. Both merge now, and the files still go when the last type does. And a print job title crossed the bridge to Linux and was read by nobody, so the queue showed GTK's own "<program> job #1" while the caller had named the job; Windows had honoured the same option all along, which is what this fault looks like from the calling side -- an option that works on one desktop and does nothing on the next, with no way to tell them apart. What is still absent is inside the items rather than an item, and is worth naming rather than implying. Three declared options are honoured on fewer platforms than they are offered on: macOS registers a file type by its extension alone, so the mimeType and the description a caller declares reach nothing there; macOS flattens every open/save filter into one unlabelled list of extensions, so named filters do not become the chooser's popup they become on Linux and Windows; and Windows' folder chooser drops initialDirectory and opens wherever the shell decides. Each of those is on a runner this machine is not, so each is named from the code rather than measured. On Linux the pages a print reports are the pages that were sent: GTK draws only the pages a user picked in the dialog and DVPrintResult.pages still claims the lot, which is a wrong number that looks entirely plausible and has had no test effort at all. dialogs.message answers true on all three whatever the desktop did, and macOS's PDF export is US Letter by size wherever it runs. The clipboard carries text and only text on every target: an image or a fragment of HTML copied out of a Dartvel application is not on the clipboard at all.

Built: DVPlatformMemory reserves its budget up front in power-of-two segments (native heap through package:ffi malloc on native targets, typed data on web) and hands out DVInt, DVDouble and DVBool scalars and MemorySlice lists over int8 to int64 and float32 and float64 storage, chunked across segments with shift-and-mask indexing and never split when a list fits one segment; native addresses are stable, and a test shows another isolate writing through one with no copy. reset() and dispose() invalidate every earlier handle, including a transformAsync waiting to resume, and new lists are zero-filled. DV-MEMORY-001 (less granted or capped), DV-MEMORY-002 (exhausted, consuming nothing), DV-MEMORY-003 (int64 on web-js) and DV-MEMORY-004 (touchPages refused on mobile or embedded) are emitted and registered. On web-js intList is float64-backed and refuses values past 2^53, checked by compiling with dart2js and running under node. DV.Memory.allocate applies dartvel.memory defaults, per-target ceilings and device-profile overrides and registers each arena for aggregate secured, used, high-water, fragmentation and reset metrics; the generated client installs that configuration at startup; dartvel doctor fails a device profile whose resolved budget exceeds its declared ram and warns on DV-MEMORY-004. Not built: no Studio memory panel, and arena metrics do not feed performance contracts or dartvel analyze performance; the tizen, webos and sony-elinux builds do not pass DARTVEL_PLATFORM, so on those devices the arena takes desktop defaults, including touchPages on, unless DVMemory.configure is given a target; native segments come from package:ffi rather than generated FFI, no Rust binding consumes a slice address, and DV.Workers does not lend arena slices (only DVWorkerBuffer); on web, segments are not aligned to worker transfer boundaries, no SharedArrayBuffer is used, nothing has run in a real browser, and web-wasm has not been executed; JS index math past 2^31 elements is not guarded; dispose() returns native memory when the last view is garbage-collected, not straight away; rawBytes and rawStruct views are not invalidated by reset; an arena allocated in main() before the router is built gets profile defaults; no native target other than Linux has been verified. Where the section and the code disagree: the section lists the DV-MEMORY codes in a text block with no level, so the registry assigns warning, error, error, warning, and the registry check now reads text-block codes; device profiles may override memory settings but no keys are named, and the code reads deviceProfiles.<id>.memory and .ram; allocate() with no size and no configured budget reserves one segment, which the section does not define; segments must be a power of two from 4KB to 1GB; the constructor also takes target and backing.
