Built: DV.Workers.run hands a top-level or static task to its own isolate on the VM and always answers exactly once -- a value, what the task threw, cancelled, timed out, or crashed when the worker exited, died of an uncaught error or awaited something nothing could complete; input, result or captured state that cannot cross fails by name and frees its slot (DV-WORKER-002 for a capture, at run time); cancel and timeout kill the isolate and the slot is held until it has exited, so the bound counts live threads; the pool is bounded and sized from DVWorkerProfile(cores) with one core left for the UI and never more than eight; saturation logs DV-WORKER-005 once per episode; DVCancellation.until(signal, ended) binds a run to a lifecycle so nothing reaches an ended owner; without threads the work runs inline and DV-WORKER-001 is logged once; DVWorkers.capability reports the mechanism, its label, shared memory and zero-copy native. On the web, a web worker per task where the page has Worker: the task crosses by a name registered on both sides, input and result by structured clone, with the first uncloneable value named; a final answer is always posted; a script that fails to load is a crash and cancel terminates the worker; shared memory is reported only on a cross-origin-isolated page, and DV-WORKER-004 is logged once when bytes were copied. That runner is exercised through dart2js under Node with a worker_threads Worker, not in any browser. Zero-copy: DVWorkerBuffer and Platform Memory's DVPlatformMemory arenas can be lent to a worker by address, and while lent they cannot be read, freed, reset, disposed or lent again; they come back with the answer, or after a cancel or timeout only once the isolate has exited; a blocking native call on a worker leaves the caller's event loop free. Not built: DV-WORKER-002 as a build error (nothing checks for captures at compile time, and on the VM a closure capturing only sendable state runs, then fails on the web); DV-WORKER-003 in dartvel analyze performance; pool sizing from dartvel.deviceProfiles (no profile declares cores and nothing generates a DVWorkerProfile, so a build without one sizes from Platform.numberOfProcessors or navigator.hardwareConcurrency, the number the section warns against on embedded boards); generated Rust bindings (none exist, so the Rust kernel in a worker is a lent address plus hand-written FFI); generated worker-script entry and task registration for web builds, which applications do by hand today; a SharedArrayBuffer path even where shared memory is available; the jobs layer adopting DVProgress and DVCancellation. Where the section and the code disagree: it says progress and cancellation are typed events Background and Durable Work already defines, and that section defines none, so they are defined here; a task takes (input, DVWorkerReporter) rather than input alone, because a function that reports progress needs a way to report it; a web worker cannot be handed a function, so web tasks are registered by name, which the section's one-surface example does not show.

The policy, the state machine and the enforcement matrix are built and validated by dartvel doctor, which fails a build configuration whose policy cannot be honoured. The session clock is built: the runtime notices idle, counts down for the warning span on a signal the countdown route reads, and at the timeout resets -- clearing what clearOnReset names through the app's clear callback and telling it to go home -- or only goes home, or nothing, as onIdle says; staff mode has no clock; a clear that fails leaves the kiosk failed. Hardware-key blocking is built on Linux: DVKiosk.enforce grabs every combo that leaves a kiosk through X11, riding the global-shortcut pump, filtered through the accessibility exemption so a kiosk blocks escape and never access, and reports what was held and what the server refused; verified under Xvfb with XTest, where Alt+Tab is swallowed and Tab is not. Fullscreen is asked of the GTK window when there is one. Declared policies parse with their refusals enforced -- a literal exit PIN, `auth` in a display-scope clearOnReset, an idle warning longer than the timeout. Exit attempts count to maxAttempts and lock out for lockoutFor, refusing even the right PIN while locked, and the lockout survives resume(). Enforcement resolves the specification's per-target strengths and reports DV-KIOSK-001, 002, 004 and 010; the runtime reports 003 and 005. The screen-side half is built: DVKioskHost turns any pointer or key into activity, shows the countdown while the runtime warns, sends the app home on a reset, and replaces the page with a diagnostics screen when the watchdog reports a restart loop -- which the Linux device binding does, counting startup arms and reporting the fourth in five minutes as DV-KIOSK-008 (restart-loop detection is therefore built); the watchdog itself restarts on a missed heartbeat and heartbeats systemd through sd_notify, which is what restart supervision under a systemd unit needs. Pointer confinement on Linux is built: DVKiosk.enforce holds the pointer inside the toplevel with a grab on the application's own X connection, verified under Xvfb with XTest warping the pointer outside and finding it inside. Notification suppression on Linux is built: the freedesktop notification the binding sends is held back while the kiosk holds, counted, and let through on release; the in-app inbox is not that binding and continues. System-gesture blocking is not applicable on an X11 desktop, which has no edge gestures to block. Kiosk windows in display scope are built under Multi-Window: DVWindowKind.kiosk, win.kiosk with state, enforcement, resetSession and exit, capability.displayKiosk. DV.Platform.display.kiosk is built: the generated runtime installs the declaration's device-scope policy at start, and the application observes the kiosk's state, reads what this platform honours, resets the session and leaves only through the declared exit method, the platform holding the policy on resume and letting go on exit. Native enforcement is built on the three desktops: Linux (XGrabKey, XGrabPointer, notification suppression), Windows (RegisterHotKey for the escape combos with the secure attention sequence and reserved keys reported unenforced, ClipCursor for the pointer, the window style for fullscreen; notifications never claimed) and macOS (NSApplication's presentation options, one fixed consistent set; a combo reported blocked only because the option covering it is in effect, Cmd+Q unenforced, pointer and notifications not claimed), each exercised on its own runner by the live suite; and on the web (Fullscreen, Keyboard Lock and Pointer Lock, each needing a user gesture and reported refused with the browser's reason when it is absent, a dedicated browser kiosk mode reported through the fullscreen display mode), exercised in Chrome by the browser suite. Android enforces natively now, and what stood in the way was a wrong conclusion rather than a wall: lock task mode belongs to an Activity, the application Context that package:jni hands back is not one, and that was recorded as the end of it. Application.registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks is the public route -- the callback is a Java interface, jnigen generates an implement for it, and the Activity in front of the person arrives in Dart with no platform channel. A declared device-scope kiosk also builds the launcher the specification names: the application becomes a HOME activity, or the home button leaves it, and it carries a device-admin receiver for dpm set-device-owner to point at, or lock task shows the "pin this screen?" dialog to somebody who is not standing there. Proved on the emulator that job has been booting all along: the kiosk is declared in that checkout, the build's own output is checked before the device sees it, the device is made the owner the way a kiosk is provisioned, an integration test asserts what the platform did, and dumpsys is read afterwards -- a Dart-side bool that lied would pass a test that only read it back. What is claimed is what lock task does: the home and recents buttons and the notification shade, wholesale, and no individual key combinations, so each declared combo is reported unenforced with that as the reason. This also found every Android binding dead in every real application -- the generated runtime's switch over the platform had no android case and its default reported success -- so clipboard, haptics and sharing were claimed and unreachable.  Native enforcement is built for eLinux now. There is no window manager there and no X11 -- the application draws on DRM and already owns the display -- so the enforcement is not about which application is on top, it is about the two ways somebody can get off it. A virtual terminal switch leaves the application running and puts a login prompt in front of it, on a unit in a lobby, and the application never finds out; the console underneath is still in text mode and paints kernel messages over the framebuffer while the application draws on it. Both are one ioctl each, both need CAP_SYS_TTY_CONFIG, which the generated systemd unit grants and a shell does not, and each is attempted even when the other fails since a device that allows one should hold the one it can. What was not held is named with the reason and carries DV-KIOSK-007, because a kiosk that could not hold and reports nothing reads exactly like one that did. Release gives back only what was taken, since an application that always releases on shutdown runs it on the path where the hold never happened. What CI can exercise is the refusal, which is the common path and the one that has to be right; the holding path needs a device with the capability. Absent: native enforcement on iPadOS, Tizen and webOS (DV-KIOSK-007 there). Built since: DVWindowKind.kiosk (display-scope kiosk windows, DV-WINDOW-010/011/012); deviceProfiles.<profile>.kiosk goes over the section in the generated DVKioskPolicies.device when dartvel build --device-profile selects that profile; dartvel inspect kiosk [--json] [--device-profile] prints the effective policy per target and per kiosk window with the source of each value (section, profile:<id>, policy:<name>, default). DVKioskPolicies.<name> is generated into the client's config from dartvel.kiosk.policies, each the section's settings with the named entry's over them; DV.lifecycle.kiosk is a read-only lifecycle signal the runtime drives and the kiosk host mirrors, so a reset shows as resetting -> active. DV-KIOSK-009 is built: dartvel doctor warns when onIdle: home has a model with a sensitive field in reach of an allowed route, naming both. kiosk.updates is built: apply reads immediate, maintenanceWindow or staffMode, window reads a span of the clock that may run past midnight, and the policy is in the path of every update: DV.Updates.check reads it -- with the staged rollout, the version lock and the skip -- and answers whether this device should apply this now, why not when not, and when it will be; DV.Updates.apply refuses what the check held back rather than quietly skipping it, and resets the session before a required update lands, which is what the specification says a forced update does outside the window. A maintenanceWindow policy with no window is a doctor problem rather than a kiosk that silently never updates. And dartvel build refuses to start when the declaration cannot be honoured, rather than leaving that to dartvel doctor: a pipeline that builds and does not run a doctor was shipping a literal exit PIN, green. Five containment keys the specification lists were read by nothing: routes.external, input.clipboard, input.textSelection, display.hideCursor and screenDim. The parser reads the routes, input and display maps and pulls three named children out of each, so those five were read straight past and dropped. Reporting them as problems by name was the first step -- an unrecognised enum value always produced one, an unrecognised key produced nothing, and that is the worse of the two, because somebody who writes input.clipboard: disabled into a kiosk has decided the clipboard is locked and silence reads as agreement. Four of the five are enforced now, and they are the four Dartvel can honour on its own in Dart with no platform binding. textSelection overrides what a page declares: the annotation is the page preference and the policy is the deployment decision, and a deployment that has locked selection has not left the question open to each page. clipboard refuses in both directions and before the platform binding rather than after -- blocking copy while allowing paste leaves a kiosk somebody can type into from whatever the last person left there, and asking the platform first would put the text on the clipboard and then report a failure. It refuses rather than doing nothing quietly, because a copy that reports success and copies nothing cannot be told from a broken clipboard. Neither is implied by kiosk mode: an order screen showing a reference number is more useful if the number can be copied, and the specification makes both explicit keys. What they deny follows the kiosk state rather than the process, so staff mode lifts it -- somebody with the exit method has been trusted with more than the person in the queue, and an engineer who cannot copy the error code off the screen reads it down a phone -- while a refused exit lifts nothing, or the way past a locked clipboard is to guess once. display.hideCursor is the third. A pointer nobody can move is what a touchscreen kiosk shows when the cursor is left on: it sits wherever the last mouse left it and reads as a frozen screen. auto is the default and means touch-only, which cannot be read off the build target -- a kiosk on a Linux box with a touchscreen is a desktop build, and a tablet in a keyboard case has a trackpad -- so it asks whether a pointing device is attached, and listens rather than reading once, because an engineer plugs a mouse into a kiosk to service it. always and never do not consult the hardware, since somebody who wrote always has a reason and a mouse plugged in for service should not undo it. The decision is a function in core of the mode and the hardware so the two halves cannot disagree, and the host applies it with a MouseRegion: the half Flutter owns, on every target that has a pointer at all, needing no binding that could be missing. display.screenDim is the fourth, and it is half of what the key asks for. A kiosk shows one attract screen for months and burn-in is what that does to a panel, so after the configured idle the surface is darkened and any touch or key brings it back; the backlight is not turned down, which needs a platform binding, and the field and the signal both say so rather than leaving a feature that looks like it saves power and does not. The dim is checked before the idle action and outside it, because tick returned early when onIdle was none and the one display that wants nothing but the dim would never have got it. The tap that wakes the screen is spent waking it: somebody touching a dark panel means come back rather than buy whatever is under a finger they cannot see. And a dim longer than the idle timeout is refused rather than accepted, because the reset returns the kiosk to its attract route and restarts the clock, so it never arrives -- ever, not merely usually. routes.external is the fifth and it is built now. What it needed was a meaning distinct from routes.allow, and the two keys ask opposite questions: allow picks which of this application's own pages the kiosk shows and defaults to all of them, while external decides whether an address that is not this application may be handed out at all and defaults to none. That default is the one that closes the escape hatch -- a footer link to the company website opened a browser on top of a lobby display, which hands the person an address bar and a machine. An entry on the allow list is an absolute URL: scheme, host and port match exactly, the path globs the way a route does, and a scheme with nothing after it -- tel: -- covers that scheme, which is how a kiosk gets a call-us button. Host matching is equality rather than a prefix, because example.com matched as a prefix also matches example.com.attacker.test. Enforced at the two points where a link actually leaves: DVLinkOpener, the funnel every DVNavLink.external goes through off the web, which returns without opening rather than throwing since a link the kiosk does not offer should do nothing when tapped and an exception out of a tap handler is a red screen nobody is standing there to clear; and on the web the interceptor, which prevents the anchor's default action before the browser follows it on the same click rather than deciding after the tab has opened. The refusal follows the kiosk state as the other containment keys do, so staff mode lifts it. Three declarations that cannot mean what they say are refused by the parser, which doctor and dartvel build already fail on: an allow list under external: block, where every address on it is refused while the list reads as agreement; allowlist with nothing on it, which is block under another name; and an entry YAML turned into something else, since externalAllow: [tel:] without quotes is a mapping and dropping it quietly leaves a list short by one. dartvel inspect kiosk prints every key the running kiosk acts on now rather than a subset chosen by hand -- clipboard, text selection, cursor, screen dim and the two external ones were enforced and invisible, so a kiosk that refused a link or a copy showed no line saying which declaration did it. DVKioskResetReason.startup and .staffExit are passed now, and neither was a label looking for an event. staffExit is the specification's own rule that resume() returns to kiosk and resets the session, which resume() did not do at all: staff mode is a state rather than an unlock, so coming back out of it is where the engineer's diagnostics page, their half-filled form and whatever they signed into stop being on the screen, and until now the next person in the queue inherited all of it. startup is the restart -- a kiosk is supervised on every target that can do it, so a crash mid-order brings the process back in seconds and the parts of a session that outlive a process come back with it. Which arrival it was comes from the state resume() is leaving, so no caller passes it and no caller can pass the wrong one; every other state returns to kiosk without a reset, because a second resume while somebody is part-way through an order must not wipe it, and a lockout still outlasts a resume. session.clearOnReset clears something now. The runtime always called a clear callback and neither production construction supplied one, so the default ran and the default's body is empty: the key parsed, doctor validated it, the reset fired with the right reason, and the set of things to clear reached a function that does nothing with it -- a customer signs in at a self-service screen, walks off, the kiosk times out, and the next person taps through into an account still signed in. Three of the five are the framework's own and are cleared: the client cache through the configured adapter, the auth session through signOut, and the shared store key by key with the reserved dv. and workspace. prefixes skipped, since those hold window layout rather than anybody's session. Scope decides how far the store clear reaches, which is the point of the specification's table: device scope owns the store, a display-scope kiosk owns only kiosk.<name>.*, so DVWindowKiosk carries the declared window's name -- the policy alone cannot say which prefix belongs to this window, and two customer displays running the same named policy own different keys. routes.allow blocks a route now rather than merely describing one. It parsed, doctor read it and scanned the pages behind it for sensitive fields, and DV-KIOSK-006 was registered for a route outside it being blocked -- and nothing blocked one, since allowsRoute had two callers and both were doctor. The gate is the router's global redirect, the one place that sees a deep link, an intent, an address bar and every in-app navigation alike, which is what the specification's rule about deep links not being an exit path requires. It is emitted for every project rather than only a kiosk one, because whether a kiosk is holding is a fact about the running process: a kiosk window carries its own policy and staff mode lifts the list while the same binary runs. The attract route is never redirected even when the list forgets it, because home refused and redirecting to home is a loop rather than a wrong page, on the one screen a kiosk always has to be able to show. Absent: the power half of screenDim, which is a backlight and needs a platform binding rather than a rule in Dart; a clipboard the operating system shares with another application on a desktop; the system cursor outside the application's own surface; and native enforcement on iPadOS, Tizen and webOS (DV-KIOSK-007 there), none of which can be built or verified without that hardware. Absent as well, and deliberately: clearing signals and forms. The reset's navigation home already destroys the page and everything context.signal hung off it, and what survives that is state a project kept elsewhere on purpose -- clearing DV.global would drop the API client registered at boot and stop the kiosk working ninety seconds in. So an application supplies its own clear callback for those, and doctor names them as a warning rather than a failure, because a kiosk whose session lives entirely in the page is correct as declared. Naming it beats a framework default that silently reaches neither.

A Dartvel application renders in a terminal, which it could not before: `flutter build bundle` reads the compiler configuration a project's build hooks need -- every Dartvel application has one, the Rust runtime -- and looks for it at build/flutter_assets/linux/x64/<mode>/CMakeCache.txt, which nothing writes. The desktop build writes one two directories away, so a terminal build runs that first and copies the cache across; it is a configuration step and nothing from it ships. Absent: the fork's own renderer -- the Kitty protocol with an ANSI fallback -- and a distributable runner. Both live in dartvel_cli_flt, a Rust custom-embedder project that no machine here has installed, so `dartvel build linux-cli` still stops at the toolchain check and says so rather than substituting a desktop build. Everything the Dart side owns is now wired end to end. Built: terminal size as a signal (DV.Platform.terminal.size, read from the attached terminal and again on SIGWINCH); DV.Platform.terminal.graphics, which is asked of the terminal rather than guessed from TERM -- Kitty's a=q query paired with a Device Attributes request so a terminal without graphics support answers no instead of timing out, with the reply reader treating a partial reply, an id that belongs to somebody else and an outright refusal as three different things; launch negotiation for a dual-mode build (arguments and display decide, the spec's wording asks when there is no display, a terminal outcome goes to the runner beside the GUI binary); a terminal-only build that generates a main for the binary it is actually producing -- `dartvel build <desktop>-cli` now carries its resolved backends to generation through --render, so the main declares the terminal alone, installs the surface at startup, and never goes looking for the -cli runner it already is; and DV.Window.open in a terminal, which navigates and reports DVWindowPresentation.page with DV-WINDOW-001 rather than asking an operating system for a window on a machine that has no display server

Built: the platform-independent scene runtime. DV3DSceneDocument round-trips exactly (bit-exact doubles; stated units, up axis and handedness; kept node ids and child order; unknown keys preserved and written in sorted order) and refuses duplicate ids, undeclared or wrong-kind assets, non-finite or zero-scale transforms and non-unit rotations with the path to the value. DVSceneGraph converts the basis to right-handed Y-up metres and says when that mirrors, invalidates subtrees on a transform change, and ray-picks each node's true local shape (box, scaled sphere, or model bounds from its file) with hidden subtrees skipped and ties in document order. DVSceneView converts between pixels and rays in both directions and refuses to project points behind the camera. DVGltf counts drawn triangles and bounds through the node hierarchy without decoding geometry, refusing cycles, truncated files and invalid indices. DVSceneAssetPolicy refuses cross-tenant or unprefixed storage keys, path traversal, http, unlisted hosts, credentials in URLs and undigested assets before any request, and DVSceneAssetLoader verifies digest and size, decodes inline or on DV.Workers, shares concurrent loads and reports typed load states. The DVSceneRenderer adapter interface has a headless reference implementation (DVSceneRecordingRenderer, installed by DV.Test.fake3D()) that throws on a double release or use after release. DVSceneRuntime makes one upload per asset, releases each resource exactly once, keeps the previous scene on screen while an update loads, presents the poster rather than a scene with a missing asset, and logs DV-3D-001 once per boot per cause. DVBox.scene provides typed non-widget nodes whose modifiers take a value or a signal, tap picking that respects occlusion and bubbles to ancestor handlers, drag orbit controls, and the poster labelled with DV3DDegradation. @DVModel.model3dField validates format, size (before parsing) and triangle budget; the generator emits model3dFields, viewer3D(), the viewer in page and card, and field JSON, and the generated client analyzes clean. Scene documents are the content workflow's scene kind, with DV3DSceneStore and bundles applied once with forget-and-reship rollback. Not built: any GPU renderer, so no Flutter GPU or Impeller adapter exists and every target presents the poster; PBR materials, IBL, lights and shadows as rendering (lights and environment are carried in the frame only); animations and DVAnimations handles; physics and DVPhysics; syncTransform; the flame_3d adapter and DVBox.scene.game; the dartvel build import pipeline and the generated DVScenes, DVMaterials and DVEnvironments; shader bundling; KTX2 variants; build-time poster rendering and the poster, compressed-variant and upload-processing jobs for model fields; poster use by static generation, noscript fallback and OG images; the scene3d pubspec configuration and budgets; dartvel inspect scene3d; dartvel analyze performance; golden 3D tests; the Studio inspect-and-edit UI for scene nodes; a router serving stored scenes to a viewport; network asset fetching (no default fetcher, and no hosts allowed until configured); triangle-accurate picking; pinch zoom. Only DV-3D-001 is emitted; DV-3D-002 through DV-3D-008 are registered and nothing emits them. Where the section and the code disagree: the scene camera is DVSceneCamera because DVCamera is already the device camera at DV.Platform.Camera; DVModel3D takes a DVSceneAsset because generated DVScenes handles do not exist; the model3dField field type is DVSceneAsset rather than DVFile, because DVFile carries a local path and mime type but no stored key or digest, which are what make cross-tenant and changed-bytes refusal possible; onTap uses CPU ray picking against local shapes rather than GPU picking; DVEnvironments.studio is DVEnvironment.studio because DVEnvironments is specified as a generated class; DVBox.scene is a static callable on DVBox rather than a constructor, so DVBox.scene.game(...) remains possible; a missing asset at runtime is reported as DV-3D-001 with the asset in context, since the table gives it no code of its own; the example's per-viewport aspect ratio is met by DVScene(aspectRatio:) when height is unbounded.

Built: DVWindowKind.volume and .immersive with matching presentations, DVWindowOptions volume, immersion and comfort, and window.spatial holding the session, an immersive space owned by its opener and closed with it; capability.spatial forcing displays and displayKiosk false and tearOut true, with DV-WINDOW-013 for a display hint; DVSpatialCapability for headsets and glasses with strict decoding (a garbled report is DV-XR-006); device poses converted into the scene world by change of basis using the scene graph's basis, with mirroring anchor frames refused; typed plane, image, hand and world anchors on scene nodes that round-trip in the document and are placed, hidden or left at the origin by the graph; the DVXRDevice contract with a strict headless fake and a DVNativeBridge device; a session whose state, immersion, passthrough, tracking and lighting are read-only signals moved only by what the device confirms, which asks for the camera before passthrough (a refusal gives a full space lit by the studio with DV-XR-001), closes camera, space and tracking on background, camera revocation, a broken event stream or close and asks again on resume, keeps immersive spaces exclusive, persists a world anchor only with consent and only as the OS token (a token that does not re-localize is DV-XR-003 and its node stays hidden), stores that token under xr.anchors.* encrypted with AES-256-GCM under the application key whatever cipher the shared store has, inline or spilled, and refuses it (DVSpatialAnchorNotStored, the anchor left unpersisted and an error logged) rather than keeping it in plaintext when no key can be had, with the generated runtime pointing DVWindowSharedStore.defaultAppKeys at the package's application key store, that key held on Android under an AES-256 key generated inside the Android Keystore that never leaves it, with only the nonce and sealed key on disk in the no-backup directory, and on iOS in the Keychain as an item available after first unlock, this device only and not synchronizing, picked by dvAppKeyStoreFor with no application change, refused with DVAppKeyStoreUnavailable rather than kept in a file when the keyring cannot answer, and moved in once from the file an earlier version used, whose removal waits until the keyring copy reads back, shown across a process restart on an API 34 emulator and an iPhone simulator by key-custody.yml; DVConsentSpatialConsent answers consent from a declared, default-denied DVConsent category, so a grant under an older policy version does not count, a withdrawal (including one DVConsent could not record) deletes every kept token and refuses writes still in flight, and enforce() after load() deletes tokens whose grant lapsed; its privacy adapter (xr:anchors) erases the install's tokens for the install or a user its consent records name and exports anchor ids but never tokens; converts hand and controller rays before picking and accepts gaze only as an already-selected node, applies the comfort policy (DV-XR-005, vignette forced) and reports a sustained frame drop once (DV-XR-007), and never puts a pose, anchor position or light probe into a report; a flat viewport reporting DV-XR-002 or DV-XR-001 once for anchors or passthrough; DV.Test.fakeXR. Not built: a native XR binding on any target (Jetpack XR or Spatial SDK over JNI, visionOS FFI, WebXR), so capability.spatial is null everywhere outside tests; anything rendered in space, because 3D Scenes has no GPU renderer and no session drives a DVBox.scene; DVXR.refresh at app boot; parsing the xr: configuration block; DV-XR-004, which nothing emits; DV-XR-005 enforced by dartvel analyze rather than only at runtime; recenter, seated mode and height calibration; onHover, and onGrab and onRelease on a flat viewport (they reach handlers only through a session's attach); shared anchors and cloud-anchor adapters; the immersive fallback page requesting fullscreen; dartvel build android-xr, horizon and visionos, doctor targets, golden renders and simulator end-to-end tests; key custody on a real Android or iOS device, a hardware-backed Keystore key, and a device locked before first unlock, which only the pure-Dart refusal tests cover; a DV-XR code for a token refused for want of a key or consent, which is only an error log line; anything in a running app that builds DVConsentSpatialConsent from the pubspec consent block or calls enforce(). Where the section and the code disagree: the section writes DV.Window, but the code has DV.Platform.Window; DVEnvironments.passthrough is DVEnvironment.passthrough to match 3D Scenes; a spatial fallback sets an existing window degradation while its codes carry DV-WINDOW-014 or 015 rather than DV-WINDOW-001, and bindingRefused carries DV-XR-006 rather than its own DV-WINDOW-006; the section does not say what a second immersive request does, and it is refused as a page with DV-WINDOW-015; the section persists world anchors through the store without consent, and the code requires consent and stores only the OS token; the binding list has no pause, so backgrounding closes space and session and resume reopens them; the xr.* binding names sit in the web unavailable map, bending that map's meaning of what a browser cannot do, and will go stale once a WebGL2 renderer exists; the section says anchor tokens are encrypted with the application key like everything else in that store, but other view state in the store is still unencrypted by default, since only xr.anchors.* is sealed, and without an application key a token is refused rather than stored.

The performance contract is built: open() to ready (real and virtual), tear-out handover, shared-store write rate and coalescing ratio, store size and spill count, and restore-on-launch duration are measured; a call site that always degrades, a key written twice within a frame, a restore over the startup budget and owned windows outliving the frame budget on close are findings, one per subject; the running application publishes them beside its live window list and dartvel analyze performance aggregates degradations per call site, worst first. Built and tested: the generated runtime takes the single-instance lock at start, opens the arguments the process was launched with as external requests, hands a later launch's arguments to the first process and ends the later one (DVAppLaunch, wired through createDartvelRouter(arguments:) and the project template's main); window identity as canonical URL with idempotent open(), the window.open binding on Linux through dartvel_windowing (which is what flips capability.multiWindow), XRandR/Xinerama display enumeration behind window.displays, DVDisplayHint resolution that never falls back to another display, DV.Window.main with promotion, the exit policy (lastWindow/mainWindow/explicit, owned windows excluded), owned windows closing in reverse order with a closed owner refused rather than reparented, modality that degrades honestly where the OS cannot enforce it, the single-instance lock and external open requests draining into the running application, workspace restore dropping routes that no longer resolve, the reserved dv./workspace. shared-store namespaces, DV.Test.fakeWindowing, dartvel inspect windows, and the DV-WINDOW/DV-KIOSK registry behind dartvel explain, checked against this specification's own tables. Every code in the registry has an emitter: 001-013, with 006 the one error, raised when the claimed binding is missing or throws rather than filed under the OS declining (004). The live window list is built: the primary instance publishes what it has open beside its lock on every change, and `dartvel inspect windows` reads it while it is fresh and otherwise says the app is not running and when it was last seen. The Studio window inspector is built: a Windows tab in free Studio lists the window manager's windows live, each with a close. Kiosk windows are built: DVWindowKind.kiosk with a declared policy owns its display (another window asking for it is placed elsewhere, DV-WINDOW-011), is pinned (a close is refused, DV-WINDOW-012, until kiosk.exit satisfies the declared method), presents in place with its policy running when the display is gone or the host cannot pin (DV-WINDOW-010), and has a session of its own; capability.displayKiosk reports whether the host can pin. Still Designed: tear-out. Display enumeration is on all three desktops: XRandR or Xinerama on Linux, EnumDisplayMonitors with GetMonitorInfoW on Windows, CGGetActiveDisplayList on macOS, each through FFI and each decoded into the same spelling, so a panel name, a primary flag and a layout origin mean the same thing wherever they came from. Every one is exercised against the runner's own desktop session rather than asserted from a unit test: a display list that parses and describes no real screen is the failure worth catching, and only a machine with screens can catch it. Where there is no windowing layer at all the list falls back to PlatformDispatcher.displays, which reports no panel name, no primary flag and no layout origin. Device profile display names are carried into the generated client: dartvel build --device-profile becomes the DARTVEL_DEVICE_PROFILE define, DVDeviceProfiles carries every profile's display names, and the runtime installs the selected profile's before any window opens. dartvel.windowing.sharedState is read now, and was not: the specification documents four numbers under it and the build read none of them. Two are constructor parameters on the store already, with defaults equal to the documented values, so a project that set spillThresholdKb: 64 got 32 and one that set debounceMs: 200 got 50 -- accepted, built, and the number in the pubspec was decoration. Kilobytes there and bytes in the constructor, converted at the build, since passing the number through would spill at 64 bytes. Emitted only when a project tuned something, because the store is built lazily with its own defaults and replacing it with an identical one is a line that does what not writing it does; and a value that is not a number is dropped rather than emitted, since a typo in a pubspec should not fail a build with an error pointing at a generated file nobody wrote. A spilled object is deleted when the value that spilled it goes away, and nothing deleted them: removing a key cleared its pointer and left the object, and a value that shrank below the threshold was written inline over the pointer and left the object, so the bytes stayed on disk or in a bucket for the life of the installation with nothing referring to them. The object goes before the pointer, because a crash between the two leaves an object nothing points at -- which the next write of that key replaces -- while the other order leaves a pointer to an object that is gone, and a reader following it gets an error rather than a missing value. Absent: pollMs and sweepAfter. There is no separate-process polling backend, so pollMs has no parameter to reach. sweepAfter cannot be honoured for a sharper reason than having no sweep: DVFileStorageAdapter has list and delete and no notion of when an object was written, so "older than 24 hours" is not a question this interface can answer, and answering it would mean adding age to every adapter -- S3, R2, Azure, GCS, local and memory -- for one setting. windowing.web.inPageViews, windowing.web.openInNewWindow and windowing.android.freeform are read and honoured now, and were documented and read by nothing: the capability hard-coded what each platform can do, so a project that wrote openInNewWindow: false still reported multiWindow on web, still offered the control, and still opened a browser window when somebody pressed it. A declaration narrows what a target offers and never widens it -- a phone does not gain a second window by writing one down, because a capability that lied in that direction would be worse than one that ignored the setting: a caller would offer a control and the call behind it would degrade. Null is not declared, which is the platform's own answer rather than false, since defaulting to false would withdraw windowing from every application that never wrote the block; freeform: auto is the documented default and emits nothing for the same reason. dartvel migrate-code exists and deliberately carries no rewrite of the DV.Platform.Window sugar to the explicit form: DVWindow has setTitle but no persistState or restoreState, DV.Window.current is nullable and DV has no Window alias, so the rewrite would not compile. The sugar is kept, so nothing needs rewriting, and the section says so.

The entry here used to be a copy of Multi-Window's and described the wrong section. Built: the tab strip, reorder, tear-out gated on capability.tearOut with the gesture absent rather than broken where it is false, the empty-window rule, duplicate tabs with DVTab(route, duplicate: true), deduplication by route -- which was by object identity and only worked because const canonicalisation made two literal tabs the same object -- and persistence through persistWorkspace/restoreWorkspace with unresolvable routes dropped. Persistence is scoped: the stored layout is keyed by tenant and user as well as the workspace name, so one person's open tabs are not the next person's at the same desk nor the same person's in another tenant. The switcher is built: on a TV the strip is a row of tiles the D-pad moves between and select chooses, on a watch a stack to tap, and on both moving or closing a tab is an action on the tab's menu rather than a drag; the presentation follows the device and a page can name it. Re-dock is a handover rather than an adoption. Every window is a View in one ViewCollection under one build owner, so a tab carries a key of its own -- belonging to the tab, not to the workspace and not to the route, which is what keeps two deliberate tabs on one route from sharing a half-written form -- and moveTo takes it out here and hands it over there inside a single frame. The element is reparented rather than rebuilt, so the text someone was part way through typing, the place they had scrolled to, the controllers and the requests still in flight are the same objects on the other side. moveTo says which of DVWindowHandover.sameEngine and DVWindowHandover.shared actually happened, and a receiver that already had that route reports shared, because folding a tab into an existing one moves nothing. Absent, and not for want of trying: the drag itself cannot leave a window. A drag belongs to the window the pointer went down in -- the OS holds the pointer there until the button comes up, Flutter routes every move to that view, and the feedback under the cursor is clipped to it -- so at Flutter 3.44 no strip in another window ever sees the gesture, whatever the two windows share. Nor could Dartvel work out which window the cursor was over: it does not track where its windows sit on screen, deliberately, because on Wayland there is no window position to track. So a cross-window move is an action naming a destination from moveDestinations, on the tab menu a long press opens, and it is the arrival that is the real handover. Tear-out is still not one: the new window renders the route through the host route builder, so a torn-out tab is built from scratch and only the shared store crosses. The reparenting is covered by tests with two workspaces in one widget tree, which is the arrangement two same-engine windows are in; it has not yet been run against two real OS windows, which needs a desktop host with Flutter windowing enabled.

Nothing this section asks for is unbuilt; what is not free is Pro, in dartvel_studio_pro in the private enterprise repository, attached through DVStudioSection and the editor's hook and publisher seams so an open-source build has no tab that opens onto nothing. Free: five leaf node types (text, image, button, spacer, divider), the layout boxes, the inspector, undo and redo, publish and revert, code export. Approval before a page goes live is Pro: an editor's Publish submits, an approver's decision writes the page, both audited. Multi-user editing is Pro: the free controller publishes every mutation as a DVStudioEdit and applies one from elsewhere, and dartvel_studio_pro carries them between sessions over a transport with the page's presence channel, viewer/editor roles and an audit trail. Revision history beyond in-session undo is Pro the same way: dartvel_studio_pro keeps a numbered, timestamped, attributed copy of a page at every save and restores any of them from a History tab. Reusable components are Pro the same way: dartvel_studio_pro's Components tab saves any page node as a named template, places instances with fresh ids, and pushes a change to every instance across every stored page. Responsive breakpoints are built: a node carries mobile-first per-breakpoint overrides, the renderer resolves them against context.screen.breakpoint, and the export switches on the breakpoint rather than flattening to one width. The visual backend workflow builder is not absent but Pro: it moved to dartvel_studio_pro in the private enterprise repository and attaches through DVStudioSection, so an open-source build has no Workflows tab. A Figma import -- every top-level frame of a file becomes a DVPageDocument, editable in the builder and exportable as an ordinary @DVPage -- also lives in dartvel_studio_pro, attached the same way, with the frames' auto-layout, fills, text styles and image fills mapped onto the node properties the renderer already paints A box's layout is its direction and how its children sit in it: spacing, main-axis and cross-axis alignment are read from the document, rendered, exported into the generated source, and offered by the inspector. Before this every list and row came out with the framework's default gap packed to the start, whatever the document said, so a design could be described and not drawn. Borders and opacity are in the document's vocabulary, a border being one decision made of two values that apply and export together. And the export writes every style the renderer applies: it wrote two of the twelve, so a page with colours, sizes, corners and weights left the builder as an unstyled skeleton that compiled. The property table is now the single definition -- renderer, inspector and export all read it -- and a test hands the exported page to the analyzer, because text that looks right and will not build is found by the person who just pressed export. An image can be one the application holds rather than one it points at: DVImage.stored names a key in DV.FileStorage and the renderer reads the bytes through an ImageProvider, so the same key in a header and a footer is read once and two keys stay two images. A key with nothing behind it draws the placeholder rather than taking the page down, because a document outlives the storage it was written against. A page's image node says where its image comes from, which it could not: it described a URL and nothing else, so assets, files and stored bytes were unreachable from a page. It is read through DVImage's own reader, so a page node and a model field cannot come to disagree about what a source name means, and the export writes the constructor the page draws. A box says its padding on four sides, casts a shadow and scrolls its own axis. Each was a property the page could draw and the document had no name for: padding collapsed to one number, so a card padded 24 across and 32 down came out 32 all round; every card in every design has a shadow and none of them arrived, so imports came out flat; and almost every screen is taller than the device it runs on, so an imported design rendered the overflow stripe on the first screen. A shadow is one decision made of five values, the colour owning it the way a border's colour owns its width, and each padding edge applies the whole inset because a modifier replaces the padding it is given. The check that every layout property reaches the export asks whether the property changes the export rather than whether it adds an argument, since a flag can change which constructor is written. A text node says its typeface and its line height -- the import already wrote the family and nothing read it, so every imported screen came out in the default font, and paragraphs came out at the font's own leading. Line height is a multiple of the size, Flutter's own unit and the one that survives a change of size. A box can be painted with a gradient: two colours and a direction, the first colour owning the decision, which is what a hero band, a button and a card are painted with in every design system there is. The property table gained a text kind for a value that is neither a number nor a choice, and the check that every style reaches the export sets a property's companions alongside it, because some decisions cannot be stated by one property. A child of a stack says where it sits, an image says how it fills its box, and a box can round some corners and not others. Each was a design a page could draw and the document had no name for: a frame placed by coordinate came through as a heap in the top-left with the right sizes and the right colours, every image took the renderer's default so half of them were cropped or stretched, and a sheet rounded at the top came through as a floating rounded rectangle. Only the edges and corners that are named are written -- filling the others in with a zero would move a child pinned to one edge and square a corner the designer rounded -- and an unrecognised fit falls back to the default rather than refusing to render, because a document outlives the version that wrote it. An exported page imports the generated client from where the file actually sits: it climbed one level whatever the route was, so every nested page the builder exported reached lib/pages/dartvel_client and did not compile -- and the whole point of the export is that the result is ordinary code somebody can keep. Reading a document back from its own JSON is a copy now rather than a view over the same maps, which is what let an export rewrite the document the running application was still serving. A text node says how many lines it gets and what happens to the rest, which a design says per layer: a card title is one line with an ellipsis and a description is three, and a page that said neither pushed everything below a long title down the screen.

Built: DVContentWorkflow in dartvel_core stores versions of any document kind in one DVRecordTable with history, so every state change carries actor, time and transaction id and rolls back with an enclosing DV.transaction. States are draft, review, approved, scheduled, published, superseded and withdrawn; one open version per document; a published version is never edited in place and a new draft sits beside it; review freezes edits; requestChanges returns to draft; restore republishes a superseded version with its approval. An approval records approver, time, revision and a SHA-256 of the canonical content; publishing content changed since then is refused with DV-CONTENT-002, and every transition is a conditional write against the caller's snapshot, so a stale reviewer cannot approve, and a stale publisher cannot publish, what the row now holds. edit, review, reviewOwn, publish and schedule are policy actions checked through DVAuthAuthorization at every transition and never cached, so a role removed mid-review is removed for the next step; a publish or schedule refusal is DV-CONTENT-003; anyone who edited a version needs reviewOwn to approve it, and nothing registers it by default. Scheduled publish and withdrawal are DVContentScheduledJob payloads on DVQueues, dispatched by dispatchDue() with a conditional mark, idempotent under redelivery, doing nothing once cancelled, rescheduled, withdrawn or superseded, and persisted across a restart on DVDatabaseQueueAdapter; at the slot the approval and the scheduler's schedule action are checked again; a slot missed by more than missedAfter is DV-CONTENT-005 and never a late publish. Preview is an HMAC-SHA256 token over kind, document, version and expiry; resolve() serves the named version as noindex, uncacheable and untagged, and an expired, altered or foreign link serves the published version with DV-CONTENT-001; publicVersions() lists only published versions. Cache tag revalidation, onPublished and onWithdrawn hooks, review-request notifications and DV-CONTENT-004 for untouched machine-translated keys all run after commit; history() and diff() against published are built. In dartvel_flutter, DVStudioContent attaches to the Studio editor's publisher so save opens or edits a draft, publish writes DVPageStore and revalidates DV.Cache, withdraw deletes the override, and bundle() carries which version was approved, by whom and when as DVPageBundle.approvals, with old bundles still decoding. DVStudioScreen(content:, actor:) shows the open page's state, a primary action that follows its state and the actor's policy (disabled with the reason when refused), a review panel with the approval record, request-changes and the DV-CONTENT-002 warning in place of Publish, a schedule dialog, History with a node-level DVPageDocumentDiff against published and restore of a superseded version, signed preview links with expiry, and state badges and a Needs review count on the Pages overview, with refusals and stale snapshots shown inline. Absent: theme overrides and translation catalogs as wired kinds (page documents are, and scene documents through 3D Scenes); in Studio, a user directory for choosing a reviewer (the reviewer is a typed id with optional suggestions from DVStudioScreen.reviewers), UI for a scheduled withdrawal or for confirming machine-translated keys, and a view of the workflow's DV-CONTENT-001 and 005 reports, and a reschedule is a cancel followed by a new schedule rather than one atomic move; the router serving a preview link, and excluding preview versions from static generation and sitemap.xml beyond publicVersions(); machine translation through the AI adapters and per-string catalog granularity (marks are per top-level key); DVPageBundleInstaller recording the approvals it applies; a generated default PageDocumentPolicy; dispatchDue() registered as a cron entry automatically; tenant scoping of versions; change capture of content versions; rotating the preview signing key (a key shorter than 16 bytes is refused). Where the section and the code disagree: the section's static DVContent calls take no actor, but core has no current user, so they are instance methods taking as:; draft.state and draft.history read like live properties, but a version is an immutable snapshot and history is async; the policy example's user.membership.role.isAtLeast(DVStudioRole.publisher) names a field and a role type that do not exist (DVOrganizations.hasRole and DVOrgRole do); a review policy sees only the user and the document, not who edited it, so a separate reviewOwn action carries self-approval; the diagram has no approved or superseded state, both of which the section's text needs; preview is said to use the Media Pipeline's signing, which is not built, so the workflow signs its own tokens; DVQueues has no delayed delivery, so a scheduled publish is a stored slot dispatched by a cron-driven sweep; DV-CONTENT-002 also refuses an immediate publish of changed content and DV-CONTENT-005 also covers a missed scheduled withdrawal; an approval does not count as human review of a machine-translated string, which the section leaves unstated.

Nothing named. The dartvel inspect family is registered and runs against a real project: verified by running inspect, inspect routes, inspect models, inspect functions and inspect jobs on the site, not by reading the command table. The dashboard is one per application rather than one per target, and it is the backend's rather than the client's. Every generated page it carried -- studio, models, queues, cache, routes, outbox, policies, telemetry -- was a plain page in lib/pages with no guard, no policy and no role on any of them, compiled into every client the application ships. On web that is bundle weight, on mobile it is app size and review surface, and everywhere it is the admin inheriting the application's own guards, shell and theme, so a module declaring shell: override could change the chrome of the screen somebody administers from. One of those pages is the page builder, and the generated router prefers a stored Studio document over the compiled page by design, so an unguarded builder is a site anybody can rewrite. They declare a policy now and the guard behind it refuses when the application has configured nothing to answer with, which makes the default refusal rather than exposure. The backend mounts it at a path the project chooses, defaulting to a name that is a default and not a constant: a fixed admin path is most of why wp-admin is the most scanned URL on the internet, and a framework shipping one would have created that for every application built with it. A release build does not serve it unless the project asked, because an application deployed by somebody who never read this must not acquire an admin endpoint out of convenience, while development serves it with no configuration at all. A request that is refused because nobody signed in is answered exactly as a route that does not exist, down to the status number and the absence of any header naming it: an admin answering 401 where the rest of the site answers 404 tells a scanner that this host is a Dartvel application with a studio on it, and where, before anybody has typed a password. Everything under the mount is hidden with it rather than only the mount, since one asset answering gives it away for the sake of one file. A page claiming the mount is refused at build time with both the file and the setting named, because whichever registers second is unreachable and which one that is depends on generation order. The artifact exists now: dartvel build web-server writes the dashboard into the directory the server already read from, which no build step had ever created, so a project that turned the admin on used to get a 404 from a mount that was working correctly. It is a static page rather than a second Flutter application, because the backend serving it may be a container with no Flutter toolchain and no route to the internet; it loads nothing from another host for the same reason, since a dashboard that half-renders because a CDN is unreachable is worse than one that was never offered, and this is the page somebody opens when something is already wrong. Every reference in it is relative, so moving the mount to something private does not break it -- the setting that exists to protect the dashboard cannot be the setting that breaks it. What it shows is the project graph: the models, routes, backend functions and jobs the application declares, each with the file it was declared in. One dashboard for the whole application rather than one per build target, which is why it reads the graph, which has no target in it. Absent: the dashboard reads the graph the build captured rather than the running application, so queues, cache tags and the page builder are named in the specification and not in it yet. Also absent: the dashboard during dartvel dev. The dev server serves web/index.html straight from the project rather than a build output, so there is nothing at the mount until dartvel build web-server has written one; the way to see it today is that build followed by dartvel preview.

Absent: PDF export. Export.pdf, DVPdfOptions, the print stylesheet generated pages carry, backend rendering through the headless browser the web build already uses, and DV-EXPORT-001 to 003 are designed and unbuilt. What ships: Resumable imports chunk against a shared tested chunker that reads the header once, skips it as a row and attaches it to every chunk -- without which a worker handed chunk 2 of a CSV had no column order and resumable CSV import could not work at all. Scheduled reports parse their cron where the schedule is declared, so an unusable one fails there rather than silently never running

sections.section: Change Data Capture and Warehouse Sync
sections.absent: Built: DVCapture in dartvel_core records every DVRecordTable write that declares capture as a change with an id, a sequence, the record version, the tenant (explicit or from the withTenant scope) and the transaction id. Sensitive fields are left out before the log row is written and are only named. Deletes, soft deletes and restores are events. Inside DV.transaction a change is staged and gets its sequence only after commit, and a rollback removes it unpublished. Sequences are allocated under a lease and readers are bounded by published_through, so a lower sequence cannot appear after a higher one has been read; publishStranded publishes changes a crash left staged after commit. Retention is declared, and a consumer behind the pruned position is refused with DV-CDC-002, checked before and after the read. DVCaptureConsumer delivers in sequence order with tenant and model filters and moves its checkpoint only after the destination accepts a batch, so a crash in between redelivers under the same change ids; a refused batch is DV-CDC-001 and a destination that cannot deduplicate is told with DV-CDC-004. lag() records dv_capture_lag_seconds and dv_capture_lag_changes and reports DV-CDC-003 past a threshold. Expand and contract entries are placed in the log before the first row that needs them, and a destination that cannot evolve stops delivery there with DV-CDC-005. Backfill is resumable, runs one chunk per DVQueues job, starts from the log head, and sweeps destination rows the source no longer holds. DVCaptureSink is the destination interface; DVWarehouseSink is a reference destination over any SQL adapter that can add and drop columns, applying changes by record version and key incarnation so a key reused after a delete is a new record and an erased tombstone blocks every earlier change. DVCapturePrivacyAdapter wipes the log's values for the rows an erasure reached, captures the resulting delete or anonymized row, and erases each destination directly, leaving the erasure incomplete when one cannot be reached. Absent: the @DVModel(capture: true) annotation field and a process-wide capture log for it to name, so generated models, which now write through DVRecordTable, capture nothing unless a DVCapture is passed to a record table directly; capture of raw SQL writes that bypass DVRecordTable (retention sweeps, erasures, replayed erasures and offline-store erasures do reach the log, through DVCapture.recordErasure, but a capture write that fails after a sweep has deleted a row is recovered only by a backfill); ClickHouse, BigQuery, Snowflake-class and Parquet destination adapters; destination schema driven by the Schema Evolution planner; a Studio view of backfill progress; backfill throttling against database load; an alert rule built on the lag gauges; Product Analytics and Alerting reading this stream; export of destination copies in a subject-access archive; a diagnostic code for a failed log write, which undoes the model write and throws DVCaptureWriteError. Where the section and the code disagree: the section says capture materialises the lifecycle signal every model write emits, but capture is attached to DVRecordTable, which generated models write through, not to that signal; the section defines lag as newest captured minus newest delivered, and the code measures the age of the oldest undelivered change, which is the stale-dashboard case the section describes; contract entries land before the first narrower row rather than in a later release, because capture infers expand and contract from the rows written; a tenant destination needs an explicit tenant column for backfill; erasure also wipes captured values and sends retained rows to destinations as their anonymized values, which the section does not state; a hard delete and a reinsert of the same key committing in reverse order can still leave the warehouse wrong under the compensation-based transaction runner.

Still absent: a hardware-backed Android Keystore key on a real device, and the iOS Keychain on a signed device build; the Android row is exercised on an emulator and the iOS row on a simulator, and a device locked before first unlock is covered only by pure-Dart tests of the refusal. The Vault and KMS adapters the spec describes plugging in behind the same call: there is no resolver interface, so an external manager has to push values in through DVSecrets.configure rather than being asked for one, and writing the adapter against a real server needs that server and credentials for it. Redaction reaches logs and span attributes; the other surfaces in the sensitiveField exclusion set (analytics, AI context, public serialization, search) are not yet matched against resolved secret values. Built and exercised on their own runners: the Windows row -- the key sealed with DPAPI to this user on this machine, the sealed blob being what sits on disk -- and the macOS row, a generic-password item in the Keychain through the Security framework; the Android Keystore row, the application key sealed with AES-GCM under an AES-256 key generated inside AndroidKeyStore that never leaves it, with only the nonce and sealed bytes on disk in the no-backup directory; and the iOS row, a Keychain item written after-first-unlock, this device only and not synchronizing, both read back across a process restart by key-custody.yml; on both phones there is no file fallback, a keyring that cannot answer throws DVAppKeyStoreUnavailable, and a key an earlier version kept in the file is moved in and the file removed only once the keyring copy reads back; and the Linux row -- the Secret Service through libsecret, keyring-backed, exercised in CI on a private session bus with an unlocked GNOME keyring rather than skipped -- the 0600 file store it falls back to, the chooser that picks on what answers, and dartvel key generate|rotate|status, which refuses to replace a key that exists, rotates deliberately recording both fingerprints, and never prints the key. Built on the web, in Chrome: a non-extractable WebCrypto key in IndexedDB seals the application key at rest, the sealed bytes being what IndexedDB holds. Also built: rotation hooks (DV.Secrets.onRotate fires when a resolver reports a new value, every hook runs even if one throws, the same value fires nothing) and DV.Test.withSecrets, which restores values and hooks after a test, on a throw too. Resolution now runs configured values, then the process environment, then .env, parsed by dvParseEnvContents in dartvel_core. Configured values lead so withSecrets is not defeated by whatever the developer has exported; the environment leads over .env so a file checked into a repository cannot shadow the machine actually running the process. The deploy gate had its own reader that did not know the export form and so failed deploys over secrets the runtime resolves; it now asks DVSecrets through dvResolveSecrets and drops the values again before returning. Secret values are struck out of logs and span attributes by matching the values DV.Secrets resolved, not by guessing at key names. That catches a credential inside a connection string under a key such as url, one quoted back by an upstream error, and one typed into a message by hand. PUBLIC_ values are left alone and values under eight characters are not matched, both documented on DVSecrets. The declaration manifest and the diagnostics are built. dartvel build parses dartvel.secrets before any generation, refuses a client-scoped secret without the PUBLIC_ prefix and, now, a backend-scoped secret spelled with it -- the generator decides by prefix alone, so that contradiction shipped the value while the pubspec promised it did not. DV-SECRETS-001 reports a backend-scoped secret reached from client code, DV-SECRETS-002 an undeclared name in client or backend code, and DV-SECRETS-003 a PUBLIC_ variable in an env file that no declaration justifies, which the prefix alone would have compiled into the bundle. One emitter writes env.g.dart for both the CLI and the build_runner builder, with tests: a backend value reaches neither the source nor the exported map, a public value round-trips, output is byte-identical for identical input, and a name that is not a Dart identifier is left out and reported rather than interpolated into the generated source. The web resolver returning nothing at all is pinned by tests that were checked by breaking it each of the ways that look like improvements.

Calling the clouds themselves, which needs credentials rather than code. dartvel deploy --functions writes a deployment artifact per backend function for lambda, cloud-run, container, edge, fly, railway and bare-metal, and refuses to ship an environment whose declared required secrets do not resolve. The monolith is built: dartvel build web-server writes build/server, one executable carrying the backend, the native server library and the web app, which renders pages on request and on its first run creates dartvel_data/data.db with the models' tables when no DATABASE_URL is set; verified by copying the binary alone into an empty directory, starting it twice and reading back what the first run wrote. Absent from the monolith: a binary for any host but linux-x64, because dartvel_shelf ships its native library prebuilt for linux-x64 only and a server binary embeds it; macOS, where changing a signed Mach-O executable's bytes breaks its signature; generated models used from backend functions, because the generated models file imports Flutter and a server cannot compile it, so a backend function reaches the tables through DV.Database; and automatic migration of PostgreSQL or MySQL on start.

Built: dartvel.infra read strictly, refusing an unknown key, a host name ssh or a shell would misread, TLS without a proxy, and a cron line restricting both day of month and day of week, which cron ORs and systemd ANDs; a manifest rendered deterministically into packages, a service user, systemd units that always restart and start at boot, a Caddyfile, units for each backend instance on dartvel.server.port plus its index through DARTVEL_PORT balanced by one Caddy reverse_proxy with lb_policy round_robin and passive health, each naming the address Caddy dials as its trusted proxy through DARTVEL_TRUSTED_PROXIES, worker units per queue and instance as DARTVEL_ROLE=worker with DARTVEL_QUEUE, with cron enabled a DARTVEL_ROLE=cron unit and web instances as DARTVEL_ROLE=web, with cron enabled false no process ticking schedules and a note saying so, and with cron unstated the first backend unit alone ticking, an nftables ruleset that drops everything except the SSH port and 80/443 (or the backend ports when there is no proxy), a pg_dump backup service and timer with the declared retention, and secrets as LoadCredentialEncrypted systemd credentials, never an environment file; a plan recomputed from the host's report so a retry repeats nothing, ordered by dependency, carrying secret names only, digested and refused when a plan file was edited; an apply that runs nothing when the recomputed plan differs from the approved one, when a declaration cannot be honoured or when a removal is unconfirmed, stops at the first failed step naming what ran and what did not, redacts secret values from errors, and succeeds only when observing the host again leaves nothing to do; a rotated secret detected by an HMAC under a random salt without reading the value back, restarting only the units that load it; DV-INFRA-001 for drift including a rule added to the live firewall and a package upgraded underneath, DV-INFRA-003 for a declared service not running, DV-INFRA-002 for a certificate within 30 days of expiry or missing whose renewal is failing, and DV-INFRA-004 when the last verified restore is older than the window or never happened; an SSH adapter that connects only to hosts pinned in the project's known_hosts file (plain, [host]:port, hashed, with @revoked unpinning) under StrictHostKeyChecking=yes against that file alone, pipes each secret to systemd-creds encrypt on stdin, writes files through a temporary file and rename, checks a ruleset with nft -c before loading it, refuses to remove a name or path it does not write, and fails an observation on any line it cannot read; dartvel infra plan|provision|check, which checks the ssh client, the manifest, contradictory secret declarations, required secrets and known_hosts before any host is reached, needs --confirm-destructive in CI or a typed yes at a terminal for removals, and exits non-zero on any failure, an unreachable host or an error finding; DV.Secrets resolves a credential from $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY after the process environment and before .env. Not built: the container and onprem adapters (only ssh provisions); a queue adapter or schedule lease on anything but the database DATABASE_URL names (the generated entry point puts every role's queue on that database and claims schedule occurrences in it, but selects no Redis, SQS or other adapter from configuration and wires no DVCacheScheduleLease, and a SQLite DATABASE_URL shares the claim only among the processes of one host); @DVJob handlers whose code names DV or whose file reaches Flutter, which are generated into client_jobs.g.dart, run only in the client, and are named by a worker at start as jobs it cannot run; a worker or cron health endpoint that reports more than that the process is up (DARTVEL_HEALTH_PORT serves GET /healthz while it runs, with no queue depth or last completed pass); logs.ship; nothing has run against a real host -- the host report is parsed from fixtures, the scripts are only checked with sh -n, and the path assumes Debian or Ubuntu with systemd 250 or later for systemd-creds; nothing writes the verified-restore record DV-INFRA-004 reads, because dartvel db backup and restore do not exist; Backend Release Management does not deploy onto a provisioned host; the provisioner neither installs nor places the backend binary, so services stay enabled but not started until something puts /opt/<app>/server on the host; certificate expiry and renewal failure are read heuristically from Caddy's storage path and journal wording. Where the section and the code disagree: the section names no process roles, so DARTVEL_ROLE (web, worker, cron) and DARTVEL_PORT are added, and a backend given no role is a whole deployment that serves and ticks the schedules; the proxy balances with Caddy's round_robin policy rather than anything the section names; certificate renewal is Caddy's in-process renewal rather than a separate timer; the example has no way to say which host key is right, so ssh.knownHosts (default infra/known_hosts) is added and required; the example names no restore window, so database.backup.verifiedRestoreWithin is added and defaults to the retention; the renewal window is fixed at 30 days; package drift is reported by check and never corrected by a provision, which does not downgrade.

Built: provenance records every field of which is required on read, and a release history that reports DV-RELEASE-006 for a deploy without one and never offers a release that was rolled back from as the previous one; dartvel.deploy read strictly; a planner that asks the adapter whether it can weight traffic and degrades a canary to blue-green with DV-RELEASE-002; a health gate comparing error rate, failures at numbered lifecycle stages and p95 latency with the release being replaced, rolling back on a regression and holding on a first deploy (DV-RELEASE-003), an empty or failing source, too few requests, a declared stage not reported or missing latency; the error-budget, crash release-health, protocol compatibility and schema production gates composed as release gates, each holding where its original reads missing data as a pass; composition with per-gate timeouts, a roll back winning, and holds let through only by an override naming a reason and a person, recorded with the evidence overridden; a rollout that moves one planned step at a time, reads the platform's weight back before promoting, holds on a weight nobody planned, reports DV-RELEASE-001 only once the platform confirms the roll back and retries a failed one, and turns named flags off with a false rule; rollback planning to the previous release, a named one or the one serving at a moment, refusing per-function rollback (DV-RELEASE-004), a target without a record, a target a contract has made unreadable or that is ahead of the database, an unreadable migration phase, and a protocol crossing that strands clients unless overridden, and naming backfills to verify again; rollback execution recorded only when confirmed; a contract-step gate refusing with DV-RELEASE-005, not overridable, while a windowed protocol version reads what it drops, and while the release being replaced reads the old shape. Not built: no dartvel deploy --plan or dartvel deploy rollback command, and deploy_command.dart does not use any of this; no platform adapters (Cloud Run revisions, Lambda aliases, Fly.io, Kubernetes ingress, bare metal); nothing produces per-release, per-stage request counts or p95 latency, so the health gate has no real traffic source, and DVRequestStage numbers the section's stages while the runtime's DVRequestLifecycle is an unnumbered state enum; migration phases come from the Schema Evolution tracker through DVSchemaEvolutionStore.phaseSource, which reports every phase, but the tracker is not told about rollbacks, so a plan that lists a backfill to verify again does not revoke its verified or readSwitched state; DVContractStepGate checks only that the release being replaced reads the new shape, so a drop run on its own while a readSwitched release still writes the old column would break those writes; release history and rollout state are memory with JSON, not persisted; DV-RELEASE-005 is not emitted from dartvel analyze or the schema planner, and nothing maps a schema column drop to the protocol fields it removes; read-replica routing and pool sizing per deployment target are not built; dartvel ci init is not built; no Studio view. Where the section and the code disagree: the section does not say whether errorRate: 1% is percentage points or a multiplier on the previous rate, and it is read as points above it (a multiplier would fail every release against a previous rate of zero), while latencyP95: +20% is a multiplier; a gate section left out takes the section example's numbers as defaults rather than no gate; a first deploy is a hold, and that hold is overridable, since otherwise no first deploy could proceed; a contract refused because the release being replaced still reads the old shape has no code of its own; DV-SCHEMA-005 and DV-RELEASE-005 are one refusal with two codes, both decided by DVContractDecision; crash release health holds rather than rolls back; a rollback onto a release that was itself rolled back from is refused even when named explicitly; a rollout is held while the serving release has no record, which the section does not state.

Built: dartvel.preview is read strictly (database fresh|branch, sanitize required with branch and refused with fresh, ttl, idle, max, visibility members|link|public, schedules). Each branch gets a preview identity whose host label, database, bucket and queue prefix include a digest of the exact branch name, so branches that slug alike do not collide, and names that collide with production's are refused.
