Preview secrets come from PREVIEW_<NAME> or .env.preview; a secret required in production or preview with no preview value, or with a value identical to production's (compared by digest), is DV-PREVIEW-002 before anything is created, and production values are never deployed. DVPreviews creates against a DVPreviewAdapter: a fresh database is created, migrated and seeded; a branch is refused with DV-PREVIEW-003 when sensitive columns exist and no sanitize step is declared and supplied, and after sanitizing any sensitive column still holding a production value is DV-PREVIEW-003 and the branch is destroyed; then the bucket is created and the preview deployed with DARTVEL_ENVIRONMENT=preview. DV-PREVIEW-010 fails the step when the adapter cannot host previews; a preview is not created from inside a preview; the record is written before the first resource exists and a failed migration or deploy tears down what was made. Creating the same branch again redeploys it; at max the oldest idle running preview is suspended (DV-PREVIEW-004); sweep destroys previews whose branch is gone, whose pull request closed, whose ttl since last deploy has passed, or whose create never finished, and suspends idle ones (DV-PREVIEW-005), which a request wakes. Teardown reports DV-PREVIEW-009 only once the adapter confirms deployment, database and bucket are gone, and otherwise keeps the record as destroying for sweep to retry. DVPreviewAccess adds X-Robots-Tag noindex to every response, refusals included, serves a disallow-all robots.txt, rewrites the canonical link to production across streamed chunks, requires a membership check for members (admitting nobody when the check fails), and for link exchanges the URL token for an HttpOnly Secure cookie and strips it from the address, with deployments holding only its digest; public reports DV-PREVIEW-007. After DVPreviewOutbound.activate, DV.Notifications mail goes to a capture inbox and providers are not called (DV-PREVIEW-006), and DVScheduler skips undeclared tasks (DV-PREVIEW-008). dartvel preview create, list, open, destroy and sweep drive this: branch from --branch, then GITHUB_HEAD_REF, then git; sensitive columns from the project graph; a registry in .dartvel/previews/registry.json behind its own .gitignore; non-zero exit on failure; the URL printed last; an empty git ls-remote treated as unknown rather than every branch merged. A process deployed as a preview starts as one or not at all: startBackend, serve() and the worker and cron roles call DVPreviewServer.start, which does nothing unless DARTVEL_ENVIRONMENT is preview; in a preview it switches capture on first, then refuses to start when the preview settings cannot be read, DARTVEL_QUEUE_NAMESPACE is not the preview's own, DARTVEL_DATABASE is missing, lacks the preview's digest or equals DARTVEL_PRODUCTION_DATABASE (which deployments now write), DATABASE_URL cannot be read, or a members preview has no membership check, and only then namespaces the queues and points DV.Database at the preview's database, after which DV.Database.configure refuses any other server database. serve() puts the access gate around the site's files and pages as well as the router. Capture does not wait for startup: a process whose environment says preview captures mail and notifications and skips undeclared schedules from its first send. Absent: any shipping DVPreviewAdapter, so the CLI reports DV-PREVIEW-010 for every create and no preview is hosted anywhere; migrations, seeds and sanitization run where the adapter host runs them, and nothing in the CLI aims them at a preview's database; the membership check a members preview needs must be passed to startBackend or serve as previewMembership, and without it the preview refuses to start; retry and discard take a job id without checking its queue's namespace; code an application runs inside startBackend before serve() is not held behind the database guard; dartvel preview logs --follow, dartvel preview mail and Studio's view of captured mail (the inbox is process memory only); per-preview overrides for mail, push and queues; opening a browser from open; building and serving the web target against the preview backend; a registry that survives across CI runs; rotating a link token. Where the section and the code disagree: max caps running previews, since suspending one does not reduce how many exist; ttl counts from the last deploy rather than creation, so a branch still being pushed to is not destroyed mid-review; the section names no code for a failed migration, a production-name collision or an unfinished teardown, so those fail the step without one; DV-PREVIEW-003 also covers a sanitization that left production values and a declared sanitize step the host did not supply; a preview value identical to production's is reported as DV-PREVIEW-002; a branch with no sensitive columns is allowed without sanitize at runtime while configuration always requires sanitize with branch; membership is a check the application supplies, because core has no request-layer current user or organization lookup; link visibility answers 404 rather than 403 without its token.

Built: a bundle is a signed ES256 envelope over canonical payload bytes, stamped with branch, sequence and the binding manifest it needs; its version is its content digest, so a rebuild is never taken for the bundle already applied. A shell opens a bundle only with the key from its pairing link (dartvel-dev://pair?server&branch&key&token) and refuses an unsigned bundle, another key, another branch, a replayed older sequence, a bundle stating no manifest, and one needing a binding the shell was not built with (DV-DEVCLIENT-002, naming every missing entry); an unreachable or token-refusing server is DV-DEVCLIENT-001. Loading applies through the OTA page-bundle installer, and DV.Updates.applyPages takes the same key check when given signedBy. The shell, dev menu (reload, bindings registered on this device, load log) and loader live in package:dartvel_flutter/dev_client.dart, which nothing reachable from the application barrel imports, so a release build cannot compile them in. dartvel dev always serves the bundle, with no flag to turn it on and whether or not a device is connected, with a fresh key and token per run, prints the pairing link, answers 401 without the token, re-reads pages and resolved plugins on every request, and refuses rather than serve an empty manifest. There is no separate shell build: dartvel build dev-client was removed, and a development shell is dartvel build <target> --profile development, a Flutter debug build (--profile takes development, profile or release, defaulting to release, and replaced the --release and --profile flags). dartvel publish recognises a shell by a marker in the compiled snapshot inside the artifact and refuses it for Play alpha, beta and production and the App Store with DV-DEVCLIENT-003, allowing Play internal, TestFlight and Firebase. An Android development build pairs and hot reloads over the network: dartvel build android --profile development writes a Java tunnel into the debug source set, an activity for dartvel-dev links in the debug manifest, and an entrypoint that starts the tunnel; dartvel dev prints the pairing link as a QR code, runs the local app as before when there is a device to run it on, and with none, or several and no terminal to choose at, keeps serving paired devices instead of exiting; the phone dials out and the server must sign its nonce with the key from the link before anything is sent; flutter attach then reaches the app's VM service back through that connection, so pairing hot restarts the phone onto the current sources and each save hot reloads it. The tunnel is Java so a hot restart, which kills every Dart isolate, does not cut it. The Dev client workflow builds, installs and pairs on an Android emulator and checks that an edit saved while paired runs with the process unchanged. Not built: pairing any development build but Android's, since only Android's gets a tunnel; the dartvel-dev URL scheme outside the Android debug manifest; no preview-environment connection; the dev menu has no dartvel inspect inspectors and no kiosk staff mode; the desktop and embedded launch flag is not built; the token travels over plain http, so the key stops another machine pushing code but the token does not stop a device sniffing the LAN from reading pages. Where the section and the code disagree: the section has a shell load the project's own pages and logic, but a release-mode Flutter shell cannot load compiled Dart, and bundles in the OTA page format carry Studio page documents, which are data, so a shell renders stored pages but cannot run a project's compiled pages, backend functions or other Dart code; OTA page bundles had no signature check to share, so one was added as an opt-in to applyPages and OTA still accepts unsigned bundles by default; there was no on-disk home for page documents, so the dev server reads studio/pages/*.json; the binding manifest is resolved native plugins plus the dartvel_flutter version rather than individual binding names.

Nothing named. DV.$, dartvel sh and dartvel task all work, the last reading tasks from dartvel.tasks in pubspec.yaml -- verified by declaring one and running it, which is how the shell was found to be discarding the output of any command that exited quickly

Absent: most of DV.Rust. The barrels all exist under dartvel_dev and each re-exports its implementation package. The Rust bindings are one integer type: DVRust and DVRustInt in dartvel_flutter, which is enough for the DV.Rust.Int example in the section and nothing further -- no float, no string, no struct, and no way to write a kernel in Rust and call it. Until this audit every import path in the section named package:dartvel/, a package that does not exist and cannot: the name was taken on pub.dev on 2026-08-06.

Built: the half of a home widget that is Dart. @DVHomeWidget on any widget generates the page the specification describes -- a route at /widgets/<id> that centres the widget's content, which is what lets the widget launch the application at itself and a page navigate back to it -- and the application's list of them beside the router, for the packaging that puts them on a home screen. The annotation existed and nothing read it, so a developer could write it, build, run, and find no widget anywhere and no message saying why. The identifier is the class name in kebab case without the trailing Widget, one rule in one place, because a widget somebody has already put on their screen is found again by it and two spellings of the route is a tap that opens the not-found page; two widgets under one identifier are refused. dartvel build honours the specification's sentence about unsupported targets: excluded by default and said, with the names left out and the target that has nowhere to put them, or refused with DV-WIDGET-001 when dartvel.homeWidgets.onUnsupported is fail. A value that is neither is refused rather than read as one of them. Android is packaged now: a declared home widget becomes an AppWidgetProvider, the metadata a launcher reads before anybody places one, a layout, and a receiver in the manifest -- four things, none of which can be added at run time. It draws RemoteViews rather than the Flutter tree, and that is the platform rather than a shortcut: a home screen is composed in the launcher's process, which cannot host a Flutter engine, so a widget claiming to render Flutter would be claiming something Android does not offer. What the specification does ask -- that a home widget can launch and navigate to a page in the application -- is what the tap does: a deep link to the route Dartvel generated for it. That needed deepLinks.initial on Android, which needed the Activity, which is why it arrived with the kiosk work rather than before it; without it a widget's tap opened the application's home route, which is a shortcut and not a widget. WidgetKit is packaged now on iOS and macOS. A widget extension is a separate bundle, so the build writes one -- its Swift, its Info.plist and its entitlements -- and splices a target into the Xcode project that builds it, embeds it in the application, and is depended on by the application so Xcode waits for it rather than racing it. Only one way that goes wrong is loud: a project file Xcode cannot parse will not open. The rest are silent, and each is checked: a target that exists as an object and is not in the project's target list is never built and the app installs without it; an extension with no Copy Files phase into PlugIns is built into the products directory and never enters the bundle; without the target dependency Xcode may embed an extension that is not there yet, which fails on some machines and passes on others; and a second build that appended rather than replaced would leave Xcode two targets with one name. The Info.plist's NSExtensionPointIdentifier is the line with no symptom at all -- without it the target compiles, links, embeds and installs, and the widget never appears in the gallery, because the system never asks a bundle it does not recognise for anything. The App Group is claimed at both ends and derived from the application's own bundle id: the extension's entitlement lets it read the shared container, the application's lets it write there, and one without the other is a correctly signed widget reading an empty container and showing its placeholder forever. macOS signs Release with a second entitlements file, so both are written; and the application's own CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS is only set where it has none, since a macOS project is already pointed at DebugProfile.entitlements and overwriting that would take the sandbox off an application to add a widget to it. The view is SwiftUI drawn by the system, for the reason Android draws RemoteViews: a widget is composed in a process that cannot host a Flutter engine. The tap lands on both now. WidgetKit delivers the widgetURL to the containing application, and on iOS nothing was listening, so it opened at the home route -- which looks like it worked and is a shortcut rather than a widget, the same bug Android had before deepLinks.initial landed there. The URL arrives at the app delegate, so the build writes the capture into AppDelegate.swift: two overrides, because there are two launches and an implementation with one of them works in whichever case somebody happened to try -- a cold launch carries the URL in the launch options and never reaches open(url:), a warm one arrives there with no launch options. willFinishLaunching rather than didFinishLaunching, since the Flutter template overrides the second and a class with two overrides of one method does not compile; and both call super, or every plugin registered for a URL stops seeing one. It is written for every iOS build rather than only where there are widgets, because the capability list claims deepLinks.initial on iOS unconditionally and a binding that is registered and always answers null on a launch that did carry a URL is exactly the drift those files exist to prevent. The Dart side reads it back through the Objective-C runtime and takes it away again: defaults outlive the process, so a link left behind would be opened on every later start, taking somebody back to a page they navigated away from days ago. A delegate somebody has rewritten past recognition is left alone and said to be left alone, rather than written into and broken. The shell properties are the page's now. @DVHomeWidget takes the arguments @DVPage takes, through the same parser on the same names, and the generated page is wrapped in DVPageShell, which is what applies them. Before that they could not even be written: both scanners matched the literal @DVHomeWidget() with the parentheses empty, so giving a widget the properties the specification promises deleted it -- no entry in the generated list, no route, no provider, no extension, and no message, with the annotation still in the file saying otherwise. The pattern lives in core now and both scanners share it, because two of them is a build that reports one set of widgets and packages another, and a test holds one against the other. The title is the shell property that also leaves the application: a launcher's picker and WidgetKit's gallery each ask for a name and each were handed the identifier, so a widget was offered to people as step-counter, a route segment, among the names of their applications. The identifier stays as the fallback, since a widget with no name cannot be picked. Sharing the tree and the state is built as far as the platform allows, and the limit is worth stating rather than working around: a home widget is composed in the launcher's process on Android and by the system on iOS and macOS, and neither can host a Flutter engine, so no arrangement of this can render Flutter on a home screen. What is shared is at /widgets/<id> -- the same widget, in the application's own tree, under the same signals and globals as every other page, which is why the tap opens it there rather than somewhere needing its own copy of everything. What crosses the process boundary is data, and that crossing did not exist: the generated Swift read a key nothing ever wrote and the Android provider drew a constant, which is a widget showing its own name for ever and looks exactly like a widget that works. DVHomeWidgets.publish writes it, and the key is one rule in core that all three halves read -- the Dart runtime, the generated Swift, the generated Java -- because a key spelled twice is a correctly built and correctly signed widget showing its placeholder for ever with nothing to see at either end. The App Group derivation moved to core for the same reason, so the entitlement, the build setting and the runtime cannot arrive at three strings. Android publishes through a generated class in the fixed dev.dartvel.jni package beside the Context holder, since Dart finds it by name and the application's package is an applicationId the framework is compiled without; it is Java because the jnigen bindings have SharedPreferences as a stub and because the redraw needs each provider's class name, which the build knows and Dart cannot. It commits rather than applies, as apply writes on another thread and the redraw broadcast would reach the provider first and show the previous value, which reads as a publish that did nothing. Apple writes into the App Group defaults through the Objective-C runtime, with the defaults object made once and kept, because nothing there runs under ARC and one per publish would leak one per publish. Publishing answers false wherever it could not write -- no binding on a target with no home screen, no entitlement, an APK built with plain flutter build that has none of the generated classes -- since every one of those is silent on the device and reporting success would bury the only signal there is. A launch that was captured is now a launch that navigates. Only the launching half of the specification's sentence worked: dartvel build wrote the capture on both platforms, both registered deepLinks.initial to read it back, and the generated launch path takes the single-instance lock and opens what argv named -- a desktop shape, which returned before reaching either. The whole chain existed and the value at the end of it was read by nothing, so the application came up at its own starting route, which is a shortcut wearing a widget's clothes. The URL shape was wrong as well. A widget's link carries a host saying what kind of link it is, and the general rule for a dartvel:// link folds the host back into the path, so dartvel://widget/widgets/order-status resolved to /widget/widgets/order-status, a route no application has. It is built and read back through one pair of functions in core now, which the generated Java, the generated Swift and the desktop launch path all go through; and startDartvelLaunch asks for the link on the platforms that carry one, after the first frame, because DV.Navigation throws without a router and this runs from the router's own constructor. A class carrying the annotation is a home widget now. The specification puts @DVHomeWidget on any widget, whether Flutter-native, DVClassWidget or DVFunctionalWidget, and the declaration pattern's return-type alternative was loose enough to swallow class _StepCounter extends and take the superclass for the declared name -- so the developer was told to rename StatelessWidget, and a DVClassWidget, the shape the specification names outright, would have come out with the identifier dvclass. The two shapes generate in opposite directions and the privacy rules follow that: a function is lowered into a widget class the generator writes, so the input stays private and the public name is Dartvel's; a class is already a widget, the route names it where it lives, and a private one cannot be named from the generated router at all. The example carries one of each, because the native packaging only runs for a project that declares a widget and without one the class shape would go through CI with nothing exercising it. The generated list of widgets reaches something that reads it. home_widgets.g.dart has carried dartvelHomeWidgets since it was written and the barrel has always exported it, and nothing read it -- not the runtime, and not the build either, which walks the source files again for itself. What needed it is publish(), which takes a bare string: order_status instead of order-status writes under a key no widget asks for, answers true, and leaves somebody looking at a home screen that never changes. configureDartvelRuntime hands the list over now, beside the model, job and module registrations, and publish refuses an id that is not in it and names the ones that are. Thrown rather than answered false, because false is what a target with no home screen says and this is a typo that cannot work anywhere; and an application that declares nothing is left alone, since a test and an older generated client both have no list and refusing every publish there would break working code to catch a typo. The immediate refresh on Apple is built. WidgetCenter is Swift-only with no Objective-C class, so Dart has nothing to message, but a small @objc class compiled into the application does -- and dartvel build writes one beside AppDelegate.swift and splices it into the Runner target's Sources phase. @objc(name) rather than a bare @objc, since Swift mangles a type name otherwise and a mangled name is a class the lookup cannot find; the name and the selector are one constant each in core, because nil from objc_getClass is also the honest answer for an application built with plain flutter build, so two spellings would be indistinguishable from the case that is deliberately tolerated. The Sources phase is found through the application target rather than by taking the first one in the file, since a project with tests has two, and by the object's own line rather than by two tabs anywhere, since a list entry is indented four and carries a two-tab prefix. A Swift file left out of that phase is the silent failure here: never compiled, the build succeeding, and every publish still fifteen minutes late. Still absent: whether that Swift compiles and whether the reload arrives, which needs Xcode and a device -- a file that does not compile fails loudly at build time, and a message that does not land leaves the fifteen-minute timeline every publish had before it; the lock-screen half of the specification's sentence, which on iOS is WidgetKit's accessory families with their own view constraints and on Android is nothing at all; and a home widget declared inside a module, since the scan walks the parent application's lib and a module's own widgets are neither listed nor packaged.

Every step is a real command: create, init, dev, generate, db migrate, test, build, deploy, logs, and for the last step dartvel upgrade --plan, dartvel compatibility-check and dartvel migrate-code. Absent: applying an upgrade. dartvel upgrade without --plan refuses and says so, so the plan lists what to change and the developer changes it, with migrate-code --apply for the source rewrites. What the three commands check and do not check is recorded under Unified Development, Transparency, and Contracts and Protocol Versioning and Client Compatibility.

Built: dartvel init is its own command and no longer an alias of create. It inserts the Dartvel dependency (dartvel_core, plus dartvel_flutter for a Flutter application) and a dartvel: key and nothing else, keeps every original line and comment, and refuses an edit it cannot prove is insertions only. It prints a compatibility report first: the SDK constraint against Dart 3.12.0, an already-declared Dartvel package, and every package shared with dartvel_core or dartvel_flutter against their constraints, with a blocked mix pin naming the dartvel_mix drop-in; a check it cannot make is unchecked, never compatible. It writes pagesDir and backendDir, mapped away from lib/pages or lib/backend when the project's own files would be claimed, and moves nothing. It states DV-ADOPT-001 once. --dry-run writes nothing; applying needs a yes or --yes, refuses a blocked plan, refuses if the pubspec changed after the plan was shown, and replaces the file with one rename; it never adds build_runner. create refuses a pubspec it did not write with DV-ADOPT-005. dartvel routes fails with DV-ADOPT-002 before writing anything when a GoRoute path read from source (nested routes joined, shell routes not prefixing, parameter names ignored) matches a generated page or model public page route, and logs a non-literal path as unchecked. It fails with DV-ADOPT-003 when a @DVModel class carries @freezed, @JsonSerializable or @MappableClass or refers to generated _$Name code, which before produced no model and no message. dartvel inspect adoption reports routes, models, screens and functions as managed and not managed, with --json and a stated counting method per kind. dartvel db pull --local prints @DVModel suggestions from drift tables, isar collections and sqflite CREATE TABLE strings, lists unmapped columns, and never writes or guesses a sensitive field. The generated routes mount into a host GoRouter as a sub-tree or under a prefix through dartvelRoutes(at:), with DV.Navigation leaving host paths to the host router, and an existing GoRoute list mounts into the generated router as DVGoRoutes. Not built: usage-decided linking and dartvel inspect bundle; a nested-navigator mount for Navigator 1.0 and other non-go_router hosts; the signal-as-provider, provider-as-signal and stream bridges; DVAuthProvider adapters for Firebase Auth and Supabase Auth; .arb import into typed keys, ThemeData import, and per-class codemods; OpenAPI and GraphQL typed clients with drift detection, so nothing emits DV-ADOPT-004; DV-ADOPT-002 for mounted-module routes, routers other than go_router, or GoRoute paths built from constants; the unmanaged half of inspect adoption uses pattern rules rather than the analyzer. Where the section and the code disagree: the section says dartvel init refuses a pubspec it did not write (DV-ADOPT-005), but that is exactly the project init exists to adopt, so the refusal belongs to create and DV-ADOPT-005's reason should name create; the section says db pull introspects local schemas like a server, but the local path reads source rather than a database file; dartvel init adds only the runtime dependency, not dartvel_cli, so running the generator needs a globally activated dartvel or a dev dependency added by hand.

Four of the six signals change; two did not until recently and one still does not. DV.lifecycle.kiosk is driven by the kiosk host and context.lifecycle.transaction by DV.transaction, both real. DV.lifecycle.app advances now -- booting when the generated runtime is configured and ready in the post-frame callback, because a router that is built is not a screen somebody can see, which is the same reason the startup profile measures the frame rather than the constructor. DV.lifecycle.build still has a setter called from nowhere but its own test. context.lifecycle.page has nothing that constructs a page context at all, so reading it throws. context.lifecycle.request now exists on a backend function that declares a DVContext parameter, and it changes -- received, executing, then preparingResponse or failed. It does not reach completed, because the response body may be a stream the handler no longer owns and reporting a request complete while it is still sending would be a state that lies rather than one that is missing. context.lifecycle.page reaches a signal that moves now. There was no lifecycle extension on BuildContext at all, so the line the specification writes did not compile in a page, and the getter threw for want of a signal nothing ever created: the enum, the signal type, the getter and its refusal message all existed and none of it was observable. Every generated page route now carries its own -- inside the route rather than around the router, because two pages are alive at once whenever one is leaving as the next enters. It moves through created, ready, active after the first frame, then disposing and disposed. DV.lifecycle.app reports the states the platform gives it now, and reported two of its ten: booting and ready, both set by the generated runtime while an application was starting, and nothing ever set another -- so an application observing it to save a draft on going into the background never saw backgrounded and one refreshing on the way back never saw the return, which reads as an application that is never backgrounded rather than a signal that does not say. Flutter reports it already and the mapping is where the judgement is. hidden is the background as much as paused, because Flutter sends it first everywhere and on desktop it is the whole of it: a covered or minimised window never reaches paused. inactive is not the background at all -- a notification banner, the app switcher, an incoming call, with the application on screen -- so it maps to nothing, since calling it backgrounded would flush an application state every time a message arrived. resumed is ready rather than resuming, being the settled state rather than the transition into it. Still produced by nothing and deliberately: resuming and suspended have no platform event that distinguishes them, iOS suspension not being reported to the process at all, and initializing, stopped and failed would need a distinction the runtime does not make. Absent: the states that belong to a data fetch and a route transition rather than to a widget -- resolving, loading, entering, leaving, inactive and failed are named here rather than emitted at moments that merely resemble them, since a page reporting loading when nothing is loading is worse than one that never says so. The build signal advances now, and did not: setBuild was called by nothing but its own test, so every observer saw idle for the whole of a build and could not tell one that was generating from one that had failed from one that never started. The reason was structural rather than an oversight. The registry was a static on DV in dartvel_flutter, the CLI depends on dartvel_core and deliberately not on Flutter, and the one signal whose subject is the build pipeline was therefore unreachable from the process that runs the build. It lives in core now and DV.lifecycle returns it, which is what the specification means by the CLI, Studio, the analyzer and external tools observing the same canonical state -- one object rather than two that agree by coincidence. dartvel build reports generating through it, completes on success, and fails on the paths that leave without an exception as well as the ones that throw, since a process that exits non-zero in silence leaves the signal on whatever stage it reached.

A backend function whose first parameter is a DVContext is now given one. It was not: DVContext appeared nowhere in the CLI, so the parameter was decoded from the request like any other argument -- the client supplied the context the specification says is injected, and the generated client asked for it. It is injected first and positionally now, excluded from the client signature, and carries a request lifecycle that changes. Absent: completed as a terminal state, for the reason given under Lifecycle Signals.

Built: the runtime registry -- DV.Modules with its ids, lookup that names the registered ones when an id is unknown, a read-only lifecycle signal per module, and paths resolved against the mount point -- and mounting at build time. The build reads dartvel.modules, finds each module's project, takes the module's own route base off and puts the mount point on (the standalone /products/:id is /store/products/:id mounted), and the parent's router serves the module's own generated page at that path; the routes are in the parent's route manifest tagged with the module they came from, which is what the sitemap, the route explorer and the web server's manifest read. A mounted module is generated before the parent, since the parent imports its generated client, and one mounted twice is generated once. modules.g.dart registers every mount and gives each a typed accessor, so DV.Modules.notes is the module the build mounted. A backend-only module contributes no pages; a bad mount or a missing source is a reported problem rather than a crash. The example application mounts a real module, so every runtime job compiles a mounted module's routes and registry. Built since: what a module compiled into the parent contributes is the parent's to run. Its backend functions are in the parent's router at the module's own paths -- which is what its generated client asks for, having been generated against its own project -- its cron functions are in the parent's schedule, its AI tools in the parent's tool table, and its models' tables are created by dartvel db migrate when its data mode is shared. Each file's import is measured from its own project, or a module's function would be imported from a package that does not contain it. A split-backend or federated module contributes none of it: those run in their own deployment, and a second copy built from the source beside the parent would answer with something nobody deployed and would run the night's work twice. Two functions claiming one method and path, or two models one table name, are refused rather than one of them silently losing. The export/inherit declarations are built: the module's own pubspec says what it exports and the parent's says what it hands down, both travel into the generated registration, and DV.Modules.<id>.global<T>() -- the view from outside the module -- reads an exported global out of the module's registry and an inherited one out of the application's, refusing anything else by naming the declaration that would allow it. Nothing read either declaration before, so a module that had written down exactly what it shares shared everything, and a field its author thought was private was already somebody's dependency. Default is empty in both directions, which is the specification's isolation; module code reading its own private globals asks its own registry directly. Built since: a module's assets are the paths that find them in the parent -- Flutter serves another package's files under packages/<name>/, so DV.Modules.<id>.asset() answers with the mounted path and a path the module never declared comes back as itself rather than as a guess -- and its pages are typed targets, named for the route inside the module rather than for the mount, so the same module mounted elsewhere keeps the names and moves the paths. The example application mounts a module with a real asset, and CI checks that the module's screen renders at its route in a browser and that its asset is in the bundle under its package path. The federated module manifest is built: a module publishes its identifier, version, routes, capabilities, assets, shell, auth, theme and data modes, public functions and signals, the parent version it needs and where it is served from, signed over a canonical form with ECDSA P-256, and the parent verifies it before mounting. The refusals are the point and each is tested: a manifest edited after signing, a valid signature by a key the parent does not trust, a document naming a trusted key it was not signed with, a genuinely signed module that is not the one being mounted, an older version replayed over one already accepted, routes that collide with the parent's own, a capability the target does not have, a parent too old for the module's constraint, and an empty key list, which refuses everything rather than waving it through. The manifest is generated from the module's own project by dartvel modules manifest, signed when a key is given, so it cannot go stale the first time a page is added -- and the routes in it are the module's own rather than any parent's mount, which is the mistake that reads as correct because it works in the application it was generated against. dartvel modules list prints what an application mounts. The federated deployment mode is built: the parent verifies the declared manifest against the keys it trusts before mounting anything, takes the routes, version, assets and location from the manifest rather than from the source beside it -- the deployed module is what answers, and building a second copy from source works until the versions differ -- and generates no import and no page for them, listing them in the route manifest with the location they answer from, for a route explorer and anything else enumerating what the application knows about. They are in the parent's route manifest and now in its sitemap and the web server's manifest too, which the specification asks for: a federated micro-site serves its own HTML and still appears in the parent's route index and sitemap. The parent has no page to render for those paths, so the manifest carries the address the module answers from and the server sends the reader there, substituting the matched parameters into the module's own route -- /store/products/7 arrives at the module as /products/7. The sitemap lists the path under the parent's own domain, because that is the address a reader was given. A location that is not an http address is not redirected to, signed manifest or not. An embedded module contributes none of this: it is compiled in, and sending readers elsewhere for a page this build contains would be a broken link with a 200. A federated module with no manifest, no trusted key, a manifest that is missing, signed by an untrusted key, for another module, or naming no location is refused with the reason and mounts nothing.  The four per-module modes are read and carried into the generated registry, so a module can ask what it was mounted as: shell inherit/extend/override/none, auth inherit/independent/federated/public, theme inherit/extend/override/isolated, data shared/schema-isolated/database-isolated/remote. A federated module's defaults are the ones its own deployment can honour rather than the parent's, and an explicit auth: inherit or data: shared on one is refused: there is no shared process to inherit a session from and no shared database, so the module would run with no session and read as a login bug. A backend-only module declaring a shell or theme is refused too, having no pages for either to apply to. The auth mode decides whether the parent's guard applies to the module's routes: inherit puts them behind the guard over the parent's pages, public leaves them open -- a documentation module mounted into an application everybody has to sign into is a documentation module nobody can read -- and independent and federated have their session elsewhere, so the parent's guard is not theirs to apply. This also found the guard over a whole application reaching nothing: `**/` requires at least one directory, so a _guard.dart directly in the pages directory was never matched by the router generator's own copy of the glob, which is authorisation that silently does nothing. The four per-module modes are applied at run time now, not merely known. Data decides what a module reads: DVModule.table resolves what a model actually queries and .database resolves where, so a schema-isolated module reads its own tables in the parent's database rather than the parent's -- which it did, silently, because both queried the same name. dartvel db migrate creates those tables under the same names, and a test asserts the migration and the run time agree on what a table is called, because they are in different packages and neither would notice the other changing. That claim was ahead of the code when it was written: the command executed nothing at all until the migration was made to run its statements, so what the test asserted was that two names matched, not that any table had been created. A module's generated models resolve through DVModuleData rather than a name written in at generation time, since the mode is the parent's decision and the model is generated before there is a parent; an unmounted module is its own application, which is what keeps dart test inside one working. The backend registers the modules it serves, which it did not: registration was in the client's bootstrap, so in the server process every module looked unmounted and its models resolved a table nothing had created -- and backend functions are where model queries actually run. Theme decides what a module's pages render in: a module declares its own through DV.Modules.<id>.useTheme, extend keeps the application's value wherever the module left the framework's default, and override and isolated are one branch because Theme replaces what descendants see either way. Shell decides what surrounds them: the page's own chrome, the module's around it, the module's instead of it, or none at all -- the module's own included, which is what a kiosk screen asks for. The router wraps a module's pages and nothing else, theme outside chrome so a module's header is painted in the module's colours. The split-backend mode is built: the parent declares where the module's functions answer, the generated registry carries it, and the module's own generated client asks the registry for its backend before falling back to the application it was compiled into -- so the same module standing alone calls its own API and mounted calls the service it was deployed to. A split-backend module with no address is refused, because its pages compile in exactly as an embedded module's do and the only symptom would be a 404 from an application that was built, deployed and looks right. dartvel doctor checks the modules a project declares, and a declaration the build cannot honour fails it rather than being carried on from: a module whose project is not at the path it names, or a federated one whose manifest is missing or will not verify, mounts nothing, and shipping an application without the section on a green build is how a rotated signing key goes unnoticed. A backend-only module has no pages by declaration and is not a failure, and a mode that fell back to its default is said rather than refused. The same check runs at the head of dartvel build, so a module that cannot be mounted stops the build rather than only the doctor. The example's module resolves and runs on its own, which the specification says a module is: it had no dependency overrides, so pub inside it failed on the framework's own hosted-versus-path constraints and the one module in the repository could be built only through its parent. dartvel modules manifest was run in it and signed: two routes, its asset under the package path, and the trust line the parent pastes. A module says what it needs -- dartvel.modules.<id>.requires for one built from source, the verified manifest's capabilities for a federated one -- and dartvel build --device-profile refuses when the profile does not provide it or a declared fallback, in the specification's own words. The decision was in the manifest verifier and no caller ever passed it a target, so an image built happily around a module that could not run on it and the first anyone knew was a device in a lobby with a dead section. A profile nobody declared is refused rather than assumed empty, which would refuse every module, or complete, which would defeat the check. The exports block is read and honoured now, and was read by nothing: a module that had written down exactly what it shares shared everything anyway, because a module compiled into a parent contributed its pages to the route index and its functions to the parent router whatever the block said, and an author who wrote pages: false was refused nothing and told nothing. pages and functions are honoured at the two places that consume them. The shared set is the plainly named one -- a mount's routes are what the parent takes and declaredRoutes is what the module has -- because the other way round is the design that produced this gap: a consumer that does not know the block exists then gets the right answer rather than the permissive one. A value that is neither true nor false is refused by name rather than falling back to the default, since pages: yes-please reading as true is how a module silently shares what that line was written to keep. Absent: what models: [Product] governs. What is read is dartvel.module.globals.export and dartvel.modules.<id>.globals.inherit -- globals, and only globals. The specification also writes a broader declaration on a module, exports with pages, functions and a list of models, and nothing reads any of it. That is the same failure the globals declaration had before it was built, one level up: a module that has written down exactly what it shares shares everything, because a module compiled into a parent contributes its pages to the route index, its functions to the parent router and its models to the parent migration whatever the block says. A module author who writes pages: false is refused nothing and told nothing. Named rather than half-built because two of the three meanings are not obvious -- whether models: [Product] governs which types the parent may name, which tables the migration creates, or both -- and guessing one would produce a declaration that appears to work and enforces something nobody chose. The per-module lifecycle signal moves now, and did not: it was created at discovered and moved by nothing, so an application waiting for a module to be usable waited forever and twelve states had one of them ever produced. What registering says depends on where the module runs, because calling every registered module active would be a claim the parent cannot make: a federated module is deployed elsewhere and whether it is up is not something this process knows. embedded and backendOnly are compiled into this artifact and running here, so active; splitBackend is active as well, its pages being compiled in with only its functions answering elsewhere; federated is mounted, the parent having it at a path and no way to see whether it is serving. A registration that declares no deployment stays discovered, since the registry has been handed something it cannot place. The build-time phases -- resolving, validating, loading, mounting -- are not emitted at run time, because the build did all of them long before the process started and a signal reporting resolving for something resolved at build time is theatre.

Built, in the CLI: the six capabilities with exact per-domain and per-key grants, with network: true and wildcards refused; capabilities read from a module's code by a lexical analysis that knows Dart strings and comments, reports targets built at runtime as unresolved, and flags raw sockets, HttpClient and package:http as DV-MODULE-008; a sha256 digest of the module package that refuses symlinks; ES256 publisher signatures over the exact payload bytes, with non-canonical payloads refused; dartvel.module.lock pinning version, digest, signing key, verified publisher and capability kinds, with signatures verified against the pinned key rather than the one a file names; DV-MODULE-004 for a digest or statement that does not match and for a version older than the pin, prereleases included, unless re-pinned with --allow-downgrade; DV-MODULE-005 for a changed key, a stripped signature, a key revoked in dartvel.moduleTrust.revokedKeys, or a publisher change reported by an injected registry lookup, never taken from the module's own claim; DV-MODULE-001 and DV-MODULE-003 checking code and manifest against dartvel.modules.<id>.grant in both directions, with pinning granting nothing; dartvel modules publish, which refuses a declaration that disagrees with the code (DV-MODULE-007), signs, and then runs dart pub publish, with no unsigned path; dartvel modules pin; dartvel doctor --modules; the build's declaration check refusing all of these before generation; modules mounted with package:, resolved through package_config.json; and the docs module map showing each grant with its trust findings. Not built: DV-MODULE-002 and DV-MODULE-006 runtime enforcement, so a module's egress and secret access are not checked while it runs; any pub.dev call, so without a registry lookup the publisher is recorded as null and not verified; an attached manifest on pub.dev beyond the signature file in the package; the Dartvel range checked at mount; the digest honouring .pubignore or .gitignore, so a file present at publish but left out by pub fails verification loudly; trust checks for federated modules, which keep their existing signed-manifest verification. Where the section and the code disagree: the diagnostics registry test forbids codes the section does not list, so revocation and stripped signatures share DV-MODULE-005 and downgrades share DV-MODULE-004; the section's prose makes publish refuse on DV-MODULE-007 in both directions while its table lists 007 as a warning, so the parent reports it as a warning and publish refuses on it; the section defines no revocation, so it is a parent-side list of key fingerprints; the existing federated manifest already uses capabilities as a list of target requirements, which is treated as asking for nothing; the section's reachability analysis is lexical, as it is in Secrets and Environments.

A generated page's favicon is now derived rather than linked as it was written: dartvel build web decodes the image the model or the project named, resizes it to 32, re-encodes it and names the file after a hash of its own bytes, so it can be served immutable and two models sharing a source share one file. A value the build cannot read off its own disk -- a CDN URL, an SVG, an ICO -- passes through untouched, because rewriting it to a name the build invented would point every page at a missing file. Three declarations reached one deployment each before this. @DVModel(favicon:) reached the web server's page resolver and nothing static, so a statically hosted site wore the shell icon on every product and article. dartvel.seo.favicon reached the server and no static page at all. @DVModel(schemaType:) was in the same state, so a static build labelled every product and job posting a plain WebPage, which is structured data that validates and says the wrong thing. All three now reach the written page: model first, then application, with the module level the specification names folded into the first because a module's models are generated from the module's own project. Absent, and named rather than half-built. First, the derivative of a row's featured image: that image is a URL the database supplied, so deriving one means fetching an arbitrary host during the build -- which makes the build depend on somebody else's uptime and on a CDN free to serve other bytes tomorrow -- or fetching it per request in the server, which adds a round trip to a page load in order to save one. Second, the on-demand derivative for web-server rendering: the favicon that path serves is still the raw declared value out of the generated spec. The build pieces are there, since a web-server build writes build/web and could derive into it, and what is missing is a way for the resolver to learn the derived name, because the spec values are compiled into generated Dart before any build output exists. Deriving the files without that would leave icons nothing points at, which is the same bug as a declaration nothing reads.

Built: a page may sit beside <page>.loading.dart and <page>.error.dart companions, which the client generator recognises and wires to the route, and DVTable takes an emptyLabel that an empty table announces once rather than twice. Everything else is designed. There is no page-level error boundary, no generated status pages per code, no skeleton derived from a model's field layout, no offline banner bound to a connectivity signal -- Offline-First Models, which would define that signal, is itself Designed -- and no background-task tray over the typed progress events. The three empty states the section distinguishes (nothing yet, nothing matching, nothing visible to you) are one state in the code, and generated collections take no typed call-to-action slot. DVTable's emptyLabel defaults to the literal 'No rows' rather than an i18n key, so DV-STATE-003 has a finding in the framework's own widget before it has an implementation.

encrypted: true is honoured now. DVFieldCipher seals a field with AES-256-GCM under a keyring read from DARTVEL_FIELD_KEYS in the server process environment, the generator emits the seal at the bound parameter and the open in _fromRow, and a process with no keyring raises rather than writing plaintext. What that covers is the generated model's own read and write path, and nothing else does it. A value reaching the table another way is stored as it arrives -- a raw DV.Database.execute, a CSV import, a migration backfilling a column that already exists. A column written before the flag was added reads back as a decryption failure, since no dartvel db command rewrites one under a keyring. Rotation has the same hole from the other side: the ring keeps decrypting under a retired key, nothing re-seals the rows, so in practice the old key can never be dropped. Also absent: showInAdmin, which gates nothing. The generator justified that by saying there was no generated admin view yet, and that stopped being true: Model.Admin renders the same generated form, so a sensitive field is already excluded from the admin by the form that builds it and the flag has no separate set to gate. Meaning it would need a second set of controls, admin only, so a field could be visible to an operator and not in an application own form -- a real distinction nobody has asked for, and a flag that silently did what showInForms does would be worse than one that does nothing, because it would look like the narrower permission was being honoured. Last, found while wiring the encryption: the generated sync codec encodes with toJson, which keeps sensitive fields, so a model published across a DVModelSync transport carries them in the clear, including one the row itself holds encrypted. Encoding with toPublicJson is not the fix by itself, because the receiving side rebuilds the model through Parser.fromJson and a required sensitive field then arrives null and throws. Whether such a model should be refused by the transport or carried redacted with every sensitive field made nullable is a decision about the sync contract rather than about this flag, so it is named here instead of guessed.

Built: DVPrivacy in dartvel_core. Models declare a subject path (the row itself, a column, or through a parent row), and personal data no path reaches is refused at construction (DV-PRIVACY-001), with a warning for personal data without retention (DV-PRIVACY-002). Erasure resolves every row before deleting any, hard-deletes even in soft-delete tables, purges the erased rows' Record History entries, replaces personal and sensitive fields on rows kept under a retention and reports them with the reason (DV-PRIVACY-003), bumps a kept row's version so an open form conflicts, runs late with DV-PRIVACY-004 and marks itself incomplete when an adapter is unreachable (DV-PRIVACY-009). The receipt is HMAC-signed and names the subject only by pseudonym. A tombstone log re-erases restored backups (DV-PRIVACY-005). Export walks the same paths plus adapter contributions and redacts other subjects' identifiers (DV-PRIVACY-006). Retention has a preview that changes nothing, resumable batched sweeps (DV-PRIVACY-007) and longer retention holding a row (DV-PRIVACY-008). Erasures and sweeps run as DVQueues jobs and are audited through Record History by pseudonym. DVCapturePrivacyAdapter, from Change Data Capture, reaches the rows an erasure deleted through a record adapter hook and wipes their captured values and warehouse copies. Sweeps and erasures write a row only at the version they read: a sweep skips a contended row and reports it in DVRetentionSweep.skipped, and an erasure re-reads it and leaves a row that no longer belongs to the subject. DVOfflineStorePrivacyAdapter erases a device's local rows, server copies and queued writes. Declarations are generated: @DVModel(subject:) takes DVSubject.self, #field, DVSubject.field or DVSubject.through, @DVModel(retain:) takes DVRetention.days(n, from:, then:) or DVRetention.indefinite, @DVModel.retain(years:, because:) marks the field a law requires to keep, and @DVModel.sensitiveField(onErase: DVErase.anonymize) keeps the row and replaces the field. dartvel routes reads them before writing anything, stops the build on DV-PRIVACY-001 and warns on DV-PRIVACY-002, refuses a subject field the model does not declare, one holding a model rather than an id, a path through an undeclared model, a dated retention with no timestamp (from defaults to a createdAt field) and a subject model with no id or slug, and writes the registrations into privacy.g.dart as dartvelPrivacyModels. DV.Privacy in dartvel_flutter is DVPrivacyRuntime, which the generated server configures over the application database from DARTVEL_PRIVACY_KEY (hex or base64, at least 32 bytes, no default), with the analytics adapters installed automatically; it throws naming the key where nothing is configured. dartvel privacy check lists every model with its subject path, retention and legal reason to keep, and fails on DV-PRIVACY-001; dartvel privacy erase --subject model:id --reason walks DATABASE_URL or the existing SQLite file dartvel.database names under DARTVEL_PRIVACY_KEY, erases only with --yes or a typed yes at a terminal outside CI, refuses before deleting anything when a table it reaches is missing or has no _dv_version column, and prints the subject by pseudonym; dartvel privacy export writes the archive to the path --out names and replaces a file only with --force; dartvel privacy retention --plan reports deletions, anonymizations and rows a longer retention holds without creating a table or writing a row, and retention without --plan is refused. Generated models persist through DVRecordTable, so their tables carry _dv_version (NOT NULL DEFAULT 1) and _dv_deleted_at, dartvel db migrate adds both to an existing table with that default through the Schema Evolution planner, a model declaring history: is registered with it so an erasure purges its log, and dartvel privacy erase erases generated models' rows; a table migrated by hand without the column is still refused. The generated server, where DARTVEL_PRIVACY_KEY is set, creates the privacy walk's own tables and registers its erasure and retention jobs, with the codecs a shared database queue stores them under, before a web process serves; worker and cron processes configure DV.Privacy over the shared database as well, and the process that ticks the schedules sweeps retention daily at 03:00 and checks erasure deadlines hourly, each occurrence claimed through the schedule lease. requestErasure records the request in dv_privacy_open_erasures before queueing it and a completed erasure of the subject closes it; the deadline check runs every open request older than a day, reporting DV-PRIVACY-004 for one past its deadline, and one an adapter missed stays open for the next check. Absent: the retention and deadline schedules are fixed rather than declared by the deployment; export is one JSON document, not JSON per model plus the referenced files; fields that are personal without being sensitive, and columns naming another subject, cannot be declared by annotation, so DV-PRIVACY-001 and 002 at build time see only sensitive fields; no Studio view; no File Storage, cache tag or crash report adapters (Product Analytics supplies analytics adapters that erase and export events, unsent events and consent records, keeping consent records and agreement acceptances under the pseudonym and logging DV-PRIVACY-010 from the adapter rather than in DVErasureResult.codes; XR supplies xr:anchors, which runs on the device like the offline store adapter, erasing world anchor tokens for the install or a user its consent records name, including after the consent adapter has replaced those ids with the pseudonym, and exporting anchor ids without tokens); retention sweeps do not reach subject-keyed adapters such as search indexes, caches or file storage, because DVPrivacyAdapter.erase takes a subject rather than the rows swept; export does not decrypt encrypted fields; an erasure started some other way than requestErasure, such as DV.Privacy.erase called directly or the account deletion job, opens no deadline request. Where the section and the code disagree: the section's subject: #user over a model-typed field is refused, since a generated model does not store a model field as its id; DVRetention.days(90) written without from: needs a createdAt field; DV-PRIVACY-001 at runtime refuses any personal data without a subject path, not only sensitive fields; the section does not say what becomes of the subject column on a kept row, and it is replaced with the pseudonym; encryption uses shared keys, not a key per subject, so erasure cannot crypto-shred and removes the ciphertext; auditing through Record History only holds because erasure purges the change log, which the section does not state; how reliably an erasure survives a crash depends on the configured queue adapter; anchor tokens carry no subject, so a subject is tied to them through the install's consent records, and the pseudonym match assumes those records are the device's own.

nothing. `dartvel build web` writes a page per route, expands parameterised routes through the application's own resolvers, and gives each page its head tags, structured data and crawler-visible HTML. A model provider needs its data source reachable at build time, which is how static generation works everywhere; a provider that cannot resolve is named and skipped rather than ending the build. The deep-link verification files are built: dartvel.deepLinks is parsed strictly, the web and web-server builds write .well-known/assetlinks.json and apple-app-site-association from the route index less guarded and excluded routes, an Android build adds an autoVerify intent filter and an iOS build the applinks: associated domains, a platform build with no identity for it stops with DV-LINKS-001, and dartvel doctor --target android,ios fetches what each domain serves and reports DV-LINKS-002, 003 and 004. The server and the Apache configuration serve apple-app-site-association as JSON. Where the section and the code disagree: playAppSigning cannot read the Play signing certificate from anything local, so the project names it as android.playSigningCertificate; without playAppSigning, doctor compares against the certificate android/key.properties names, read through keytool.

The pipeline the section describes is built, and it is one pipeline in dartvel_core that every server renders through: route resolved against the manifest's patterns with its parameters, page data resolved by the declared mode (awaited; cached for a ttl; served stale and refreshed behind the response; deferred to the client), visibility checked (hidden is 404, unauthorized 401, each the shell without the data), the head generated from the data (title, description, image made absolute against the site, canonical), structured data written as JSON-LD, the page's favicon selected, the crawler-visible text generated from the data, the Flutter bootstrap kept, and, with streaming on, the head sent as its own chunk. The resolver is generated: model_pages.g.dart, pure Dart beside the models, names where each public model page's rows are and which fields carry its title, content, image and published flag, and the generated backend builds the route's resolver from it over the application's database and starts its server with it -- so with spaRoot the built site's /users/ada is Ada's page when it is asked for, hidden when unpublished or absent. dartvel.web.server (pageDataMode, cacheTtlSeconds, streaming, cache) travels in the manifest. The kept pages can be shared: given any DVCacheAdapter -- Redis where the deployment has one -- they go there as JSON with when they were kept, so a second instance serves what the first resolved rather than resolving every page for itself, and the manifest's ttl is honoured (the backend's fallback built its cache before reading the manifest, so a declared five minutes lasted sixty seconds). A page is fresh for the ttl and servable stale for the stale window after it, both declarable; a lifetime of nothing is not written, which is what Redis says when it refuses an expire time of zero. Proven against a real Redis in CI: two connections, one cache, one resolve. Structured data is typed per model: @DVModel(schemaType: 'Product') travels into the generated page spec and becomes the page's JSON-LD @type, and a model that declares none is a Thing rather than a guess from the class's name. The declaration now reaches both servers rather than one: streaming split the page in preview and was buffered whole by the backend that ships, because the FFI layer gathers the body of anything not marked a stream; a federated module's location was written by the build and acted on by the backend while preview served the parent's own shell for the module's path; and dartvel.seo travels in the manifest as a site block, because rendering a route replaces the head block the build wrote into the shell, so every served page came back stripped of its description, its social image and its site name -- values the static target keeps. The site's values are a floor a page's own resolved data overrides, and a hidden or unauthorized page still gets neither. streaming: shell sends the shell's head -- every preload, the splash, a preload for each body script -- before the page data resolves, with the resolver started in the request's tenant zone at the same moment; the title and data-written head follow the data, then the body. The early part is what dvHeadParts leaves out of what data writes, and a test renders the same shell empty and full to prove that part is identical in both. The native test holds the data back until the early bytes have reached a socket through the Rust runtime. A guarded route, marked guarded in the manifest from the router's own list, is never sent early and keeps its status; a record found hidden or unauthorized after the flush is a noindex page with none of the data, and a resolver that throws gets the route's own page marked the same way. Each route's own deferred parts and first-frame images are named in the head a server sends: a web-server build writes dartvel_prefetch.json keyed by route pattern beside a shell it leaves alone, and both servers add the matched route's list to the part of the head that goes first -- the first write under shell, before the data. The preview server streams shell-first through the same core function as the deployed one, with the same guarded-route and noindex rules. Absent: rendering Flutter widgets to HTML, which the section does not ask for.

sections.section: Embedded, Television, and Extension Build Targets
sections.absent: tizen and vscode build but have never been run; fuchsia's engine does not build at 3.44.5; webOS and Sony eLinux ship a Dart below the 3.12 floor, so their embedders cannot resolve the example webOS, Sony eLinux and Fuchsia now skip rather than fail, each naming which wall it hit, so a target nobody can build stops reporting a failure about the wrong thing. Present: the two targets exist and are routed -- dartvel build sony-elinux-iso and -img resolve to the eLinux bundle build with a format, and the bundle itself is built and verified on a virtual device in CI. Absent: the image. Dartvel bundles no system-imaging toolchain, so after the bundle is built the packaging step reports DV-ELINUX-IMG and skips rather than writing something that is not a bootable image. That is the whole of it: a complete system image needs a root filesystem, a bootloader and a partition layout, none of which this repository has any of, and emitting a file with the right extension would be worse than the honest skip because it would look like the feature. Absent entirely: dartvel build android-xr, dartvel build horizon and dartvel build visionos. This section's command block lists the three beside targets that are routed, and none of them exists -- no target name resolves in the CLI, and docs/build-targets.md has no row for any of them. XR -- Spatial Presentation carries them as Draft/Designed, which is the honest label, but a Contract/Partial section printing them in the same list as webos, tizen, sony-elinux and vscode gives a reader no way to tell which half runs; the block now marks them. They are the whole of the Android XR, Horizon OS and visionOS build story: the Jetpack XR and Spatial SDK JNI bindings are not generated, the visionOS FFI bindings over the native spatial frameworks do not exist, and no doctor check validates any of the three SDKs.

This section was marked narrative, which is the index's one legitimate way to carry no labels -- and it describes dartvel inspect, dartvel explain and a versioned DartvelProjectGraph, so marking it narrative exempted a real surface from the evidence rule rather than describing a paragraph of prose. Built: dartvel inspect routes, models, model, functions, function, jobs, kiosk and windows; dartvel explain over the diagnostic registry; a versioned project graph carrying graphVersion, routes, models and their fields including sensitive marking, functions and jobs. Absent: the inspectors this section also lists -- module, transaction, schema and generated -- and the node types the graph is described as carrying whose own sections are Designed rather than built: the protocol version and its window, memory arenas, 3D scenes, API scopes, privacy declarations, release plans, analytics events and consent categories, feature flags with owners and rollout rules, per-model subject paths and retention, and usage meters with their limits. Upgrade and compatibility: dartvel upgrade --plan plans against the running CLI's release and writes nothing. It checks the SDK constraint and the installed Dart and Flutter against the floors (Flutter 3.44.0, held to the scaffold README by a test), each Dartvel package's constraint and pubspec.lock version, blocking a project newer than the CLI, shared dependencies against the constraints dartvel_core and dartvel_flutter declare, deprecated names through migrate-code's rules, the generated files this CLI's generator would change on a copy with lines added and removed, a protocol lockfile that fails to decode, and each non-federated mounted module's dartvel_* constraints; it exits 1 when anything blocks. dartvel migrate-code rewrites on Dart tokens (strings and comments untouched, interpolations rewritten), is a dry run unless --apply, skips the generated client, build, .dart_tool and .dartvel, and writes nothing if a file changed after planning; its rules are DVStyleModifier, .styleModifier(), DV.Storage, @DVSearchable, @DVSensitiveModelField and the three Debug providers, each held by a test to the @Deprecated or typedef that makes it safe. Not built: applying an upgrade (dartvel upgrade without --plan refuses); a plan for any release but the running CLI's; checks of the protocol contract (nothing derives it from a project), the database (no record of schema changes between Dartvel releases), plugins and deployment, which the plan lists as not checked; federated modules and modules declared through path or override; module manifests carry no separate compatible-Dartvel field, so the module check reads their pubspec constraints; migrate-code has no rule for the DV.Platform.Window sugar (DVWindow has no persistState or restoreState and DV has no Window alias, so the rewrite would not compile) or for AuthFailure.unknownAccount and invalidPassword (collapsing both into invalidCredentials duplicates switch cases); the rewrite is lexical, so a user method named styleModifier called through a dot is rewritten too. Where the section and the code disagree: the section does not say whether migrate-code applies by default, and it is a dry run unless --apply, as dart fix is.

Built: identical inputs produce byte-identical output, proven by generating a project with pages, a model, a job, flags and a backend function twice and at two paths; no build stamp, timestamp or absolute path in any generated file; the generator version recorded once, in the dartvel_client.dart header; dvGenBuildId, which dartvel dev prints, is a hash of the generated backend routes rather than a time; every directory listing the generators read is sorted; and dartvel generate --check, which generates two scratch copies without writing to the project, reports DV-GEN-001 for stale paths and DV-GEN-002 for paths that differ between the copies, and exits non-zero. Absent: output is not run through dart format; no CODEOWNERS template ships with the scaffold; dartvel upgrade --plan lists the files this CLI's generator would change with lines added and removed, counted as a multiset of lines rather than a minimal diff, and names DV-GEN-003 in its text without going through the diagnostic registry; DV-GEN-002 is checked only by --check, not by every build; the ordering guarantee rests on the sorts in code, since no test can make the filesystem list in a different order; a module mounted from outside the project root is not copied into the check's scratch location. Where the section and the code disagree: the section speaks of committed generated output and a CODEOWNERS rule for it, but the scaffold, every example and the site gitignore lib/dartvel_client and the backend generator adds that line on every run, so by default nothing generated is committed; formatting with the installed dart format would make output depend on the SDK version unless dart_style is pinned; the generator had no provenance record for the build id to move into, so the one value with a reader became a content hash; the section treats dartvel generate as the generator, but the generator is dartvel routes (run by dartvel build and dartvel dev) and generate scaffolds templates, so only --check was added to it.

Built: dartvel docs renders the project graph into a static site covering models and fields (types, doc comments, relations, policies, generated surfaces, and type-derived example data in which a sensitive field is named, marked and never valued), backend functions (signature, doc comment, and the request lifecycle stages in the order the generated backend runs them, held to a really generated handler by a test), the route index (pages, generated model pages, embedded and federated module pages), jobs and backend and client cron, a policy matrix of resource against action with guarded surfaces, the module map with modes, requires, exports and globals, and the diagnostics glossary from the DVDiagnostics registry. Decision records in docs/decisions link to the nodes they name as kind:target code spans, and those nodes link back; DV-DOCS-001 is emitted for a name that is gone and DV-DOCS-002 for a node whose source mapping no longer holds its declaration. graph.json in the site is byte-identical to what dartvel mcp returns, and every node in it has an anchor in the site. Output is byte-deterministic; --fatal-warnings fails on drift; --serve serves on loopback and rebuilds on change. Building it fixed two project-graph defects that reached inspect and MCP: a sensitive field with stacked or parameterised annotations read as ordinary, and a backend function under @DVUseMiddleware read as unannotated. Not built: the site is not mounted as a federated micro-site inside the application and does not inherit its authentication, and is written to a directory instead; model relations are inferred from field types naming another model rather than declared relations; the policy matrix shows which actions a policy class answers, not whom they allow; the module map shows declared grants, not a Module Distribution and Trust evaluation; client cron states that a schedule is a request, not a guarantee, but has no per-target table because DV.Schedules.capability does not exist; no build or dev run invokes dartvel docs, and generate --check does not cover docs output; the graph still reads fields with initializers and functions whose return type nests generics by regex. Where the section and the code disagree: the section says docs and the MCP context are one graph rendered twice, but the graph has no module routes, cron, policies or doc comments, so the site adds them from the generators' own readers and only the shared part is compared; the section speaks of surfaces without a source mapping, but every node is built with one, so DV-DOCS-002 fires only when a mapping stops resolving; decision records are said to name graph nodes with no syntax given, and kind:target code spans were chosen.

sections.section: App Store Publishing and Privacy Manifests
sections.absent: Built: dartvel publish takes a built application to Google Play, App Store Connect, TestFlight or Firebase App Distribution, declared under dartvel.publish in pubspec.yaml. Host support, then the tooling, then the work -- and here the work is an upload of a binary that took minutes to produce, so every refusal comes before it: a track nobody publishes to is refused rather than corrected to the nearest, because "staging" could mean internal or alpha and guessing puts a build in front of the wrong people; Play credentials that were never declared are refused rather than left to fastlane, which stops to ask and a pipeline has nobody to answer; App Store Connect is refused off macOS at the start rather than with "command not found" at the end of a long build. --dry-run prints the command instead of running it. The upload uploads and nothing else, because a publish that also promoted the build would be two things under one word. Designed, not built: privacy manifests and Play Data Safety generated from the model graph and the native binding manifest, with dartvel doctor reporting drift; store metadata and screenshots versioned in the repository, screenshots taken from declared goldens; credentials resolved by name through Secrets rather than held. Absent: the stores are driven through their own tools -- fastlane, xcrun altool, the firebase CLI -- rather than their APIs directly, so a machine without one is told to install it rather than having it fetched; no store has been published to from CI, which needs an account and a signing identity; and metadata, screenshots and staged rollouts are deliberately not touched.
